News.title: Gunman ‘opens fire’ on busy motorway in latest horror shooting in Costa del Sol as car flees scene
News.content:
HOLIDAY SHOCK Gunman ‘opens fire’ on busy motorway in latest horror shooting in Costa del Sol as car flees scene







Next

A GUNMAN has allegedly opened fire on a busy motorway in the latest wave of violent crime on the Costa del Sol.

Shots rang out near Estepona early Sunday morning, with the suspect’s Audi fleeing the scene before police arrived.



No one was injured and police have been left puzzled by who or what the intended target was.

This is the latest in a string of recent shootings to cast a shadow over the sun-soaked destination.



Chief Superintendent Roberto Rodríguez previously said gun violence in the region is “a ticking time bomb”.

And as criminal behaviour grows more flagrant, members of the public are increasingly exposed to violent crime.



Last month a man – later unmasked as a prolific football ultra – was shot in the face at a packed restaurant.

Umit Yalcin , 47, was having dinner with three friends when a man suddenly approached the table and opened fire.

Masked attackers rushed the terrace of the Lounge Bar Plaza in Malaga, horrifying onlookers and diners.

According to Turkish media, Yalcin moved from Turkey to Spain in 2024 to focus on organized crime.



Around 400kg of cocaine belonging to Yalcin’s gang was stolen last year, sparking a feud on the Costa del Sol with a rival Turkish group known as the Dalton gang.

Experts warn it could be a sign of escalating turf wars.

Just days before the terrace attack, two men were injured in a shooting that investigators believe stemmed from a botched drug rip off.

Police found bullet holes piercing the front door of the house in Alhaurín el Grande, near Marbella.

Two days prior to that, a construction worker was shot multiple times in the leg and back as he sat on a bench in broad daylight in Barcenillas, an area in Malaga.



Malaga resident Nacho, 20, had no criminal records or gang ties and was mistaken for a rival hitman.

He was able to crawl to a supermarket after being shot, where witnesses heard him shout: “They are killing me, they have shot me twice.”

Customers in the store attempted to help Nacho, but his injuries were critical and he later died in hospital.

As violence spills onto the streets, residents and tourists live in constant fear of the increasingly common encounters.

The surge in violence has prompted police to step up their presence in the Malaga area.



Policia Nacional have launched additional checks at various points around the city as part of efforts to combat organised crime and other offences, although officials have declined to say how many extra police officers are being deployed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

This week, the cops unveiled a new plan designed to tackle organised crime in the city of Malaga.

The Government sub delegate in Málaga, Javier Salas, highlighted that: “this operational plan brings with it an increase in the number of National Police agents who will provide regular service in the Málaga capital with the purpose of combating organised crime and common delinquency.”

News.title: Seven-year-old girl stabbed to death on sidewalk by stranger as video shows horrified bystanders racing to detain woman
News.content:
Next

A SEVEN-YEAR-OLD girl has been stabbed to death as she walked along a sidewalk in a horrific broad-daylight attack.

Edimari Hernandez Chacon from Chatham, Chicago, was stabbed multiple times in the back by an apparent stranger just before noon on Saturday.



Surveillance footage from the scene captures the moment bystanders raced to detain a woman who is the suspected attacker.

In another video seen by ABC News, the girl was walking hand-in-hand with a woman before the attack.



Cops say another woman then came from behind and stabbed the child multiple times in the back with a sharp object.

“The poor baby had nothing to do with what was going on,” one woman told the news outlet.

The girl was rushed to Comer Children’s Hospital where she died of her injuries.

The suspect, who has not been named, is in police custody, and criminal charges are expected to be filed soon.



She was taken to a hospital and treated for injuries she sustained while being detained by witnesses.

Investigators are looking into a motive and determining if the girl and suspect knew each other.

“I am deeply saddened by the senseless stabbing of a 7 year old child in our neighborhood,” said Alderwoman Michelle Harris.

“My heart goes out to her family, friends, and everyone who is affected by this horrific incident.

“No child should ever have to experience violence or fear while simply walking down the sidewalk.



“I also want to recognize and thank the bystanders who quickly intervened—helping to detain the suspect and get assistance on the way,” she added.

“Their quick actions may have prevented further harm.

“I urge anyone with information to contact the Chicago Police Department.

“Our community must come together to support the victim and hold the perpetrator accountable.”

News.title: Labour MP admits they have no clue how many of 700 early-release lags have tags
News.content:
TAGGED OUT Labour MP admits they have no clue how many of 700 early-release lags have tags







Next

THE Justice Secretary Alex Norris was unable to say how many of the prisoners released this week have been tagged.

On Thursday, some 700 inmates walked free from jail as part of the controversial early release scheme.



Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg today, Mr Norris said: “for the first time there is a presumption on tagging” for those up for early release.

But he added: “Day four is too early for me for the numbers”.



This comes after a report found some criminal offenders were left unmonitored for five months due to delays in fitting electronic tags.

The significant delays are creating a “false sense of assurance” for victims and are leading to repeated breaches of curfews and court orders, the report said.



Inspectors also found just over half of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, while just 60 per cent of alcohol monitoring tags were fitted promptly.

GPS location tags are used to confine sexual offenders and domestic abusers to “restriction zones” which are mapped out with the victim of the crime.

Mr Norris said this morning: “With domestic abuse we would like to have gone further.”

“We haven’t been able to because the alternative would have no prison places which would have meant the perpetrators being bailed back to home.”



The report, published earlier this week, also found that in only 46 per cent of cases were major violations raised and explored.

Despite the findings, Mr Norris insisted today that “safeguards” are in place which mean “if those individuals do breach their licence they are going back to prison.”

This comes after it was reported last month that the majority of prisoners being freed under the early release scheme will not be fitted with monitoring tags.

The Ministry of Justice has insisted those released will be under the “toughest supervision in British history.”

The tranche of offenders released on Thursday were the first of 4,500 prisoners who will be released over the next year in an effort to tackle prison overcrowding.



Several of the newly released prisoners thanked the PM as they walked out of jail.

One man leaving HMP Cardiff, who was asked if he had a message for the PM, said: “Thank you very much and don’t get me back here again, bro.”

Under new regulations, offenders will be banned from entering pubs, clubs and public events as part of the “biggest-ever” expansion of electronic monitoring.

Some victims remain fearful that the system cannot manage the hundreds of early releases.

One mother, whose son was stabbed to death by a robber released on licence said: “They’re letting people out too early with not the right resources.



Donna Thompson’s son Shane, 32, was murdered by Robert Goodwin, who had left jail two weeks earlier.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She added: “When they come out, there’s no drug rehabilitation, probation isn’t knocking on the door for surprise visits.”

News.title: Death row killer Christa Pike ‘may not fully recover’ after botched execution, lawyer reveals as he gives health update
News.content:
Next

DEATH row killer Christa Pike is under guard and “may not fully recover” from her botched execution, her attorney has revealed.

Pike, 50, remains hospitalised and critically ill after surviving a double dose of lethal injection on Wednesday.



Her lawyer Stephen Ferrell told CNN: “She is guarded. I’m not sure who may have seen her.

“I know I have not seen her. The state of Tennessee has not yet said whether it will ultimately try to execute her again.”



Pike would have been the first woman in Tennessee to be executed in over 200 years.

But the failed attempt has left her relying on a ventilator as doctors try to get a massive dose of the barbiturate pentobarbital out of her system.

Her attorneys said prison staff struggled to find a vein and used several needles to try and gain venous access to execute Pike.

Her arms remain burned, blistered and swollen after her attorneys say she was struck with at least seven needles.



And if they don’t execute her, Ferrell believes Pike “may not fully recover”.

“I think one of the main things that will leave this up in the air for a while is the fact that we don’t know what the prognosis is, as in the long term prognosis”, he added.

Several witnesses to the botched execution reported hearing Pike snore in the nearly two hours before prison staff closed the curtain, shut off the microphone and ushered the media out.

“We are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” Ferrell previously told TMZ.

“We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”



Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the brutal murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

She carried out the deadly attack with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who Pike said Slemmer was trying to steal from her.

Carved with satanic pentagrams and badly beaten, Colleen’s corpse was first mistaken for an animal.

Pike has never denied killing Slemmer but said she was “a mentally ill 18-year-old kid”.

She has been on death row at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville since she was convicted in 1996.



Ferrell said Pike’s “biggest fear” was not death, but rather “a prolonged death, and that’s what happened, minus the death.”

Her lawyers raised concerns about lethal injection months before her day of execution, saying she had small veins and a blood condition that could make it more difficult to insert an IV.

Pike asked to be executed by firing squad, which the state does not do, or by hanging, for which officials said they did not have the equipment.

She also asked for a physician not employed by the state department of corrections to be present, in addition to an ICU ambulance if needed for “resuscitative measures.”

What comes next remains unclear, as Dr Joel Zivot – a medical advisor to Pike’s legal team – told The Sun there are situations where an inmate is took sick to be put to death.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said if Pike’s health “can never be restored to some degree where it would be conceivable that she could actually be executed again, then she may not face that.”

However, if she recovers to a certain degree, there is a chance she could face a second execution attempt, Zivot said.

News.title: Green Party vote to brand Zionism ‘racist ideology’ in toxic row as Zack Polanski ducks controversial vote
News.content:
CIVIL WAR Green Party vote to brand Zionism ‘racist ideology’ in toxic row as Zack Polanski ducks controversial vote







Next

THE Green Party has voted to adopt a motion that Zionism is racism as a “racist ideology”.

Exactly 1,022 party members cast their votes in favour of the proposal compared with 813 on Sunday afternoon.



It comes after Green Manchester councillor Asma Alam told campaigners to dress modestly and speak Arabic to win Muslim votes – with an expert describing it as “bigotry”.

Zionism, the pursuit of a single independent Jewish state, is now considered racist by Zack Polanski’s party.



The Green leader ducked the controversial vote, claiming he was busy campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

“Zionism is Racism” motion calls for the abolition of the Jewish state and the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian state in all historic Palestine and Jerusalem as its capital”.

It also urges for a full arms embargo against Israel and harsher economic sanctions.

Supporters of the proposal have also called for the de-proscription of terror group Palestine Action.



Green MPs and politicians have spoken out against the motion and have raised the alarm it could alienate Jewish voters.

Deputy leader Rachel Millward called it “problematic” while the party’s first MP Caroline Lucas described it as “divisive”.

A Green Party spokesperson said: “The Green Party is an anti-racist party and has consistently opposed the illegal occupation of both Palestinian and Syrian land, called for an end to arms sales to the Israeli government and spoken out fearlessly about the devastating situation in Gaza and the West Bank.



“Those positions remain central to our approach.

“So too does our deeply held commitment to equality, justice and human rights for all and opposition to racism in all its forms.”

A statement from Israel’s foreign ministry read: “The shocking resolution adopted today legitimises armed struggle, calls for a Palestinian state ‘from the river to the sea’ – meaning the destruction of the State of Israel – and labels as ‘racist’ the aspiration of the Jewish people for self-determination.”

They added: “Every political party in Britain, first and foremost the governing Labour Party, must unequivocally reject this twisted resolution.”

News.title: Woman rushed to hospital after ‘stolen’ BMW flees cops and smashes into car at junction in late-night horror crash
News.content:
CRASH HORROR Woman rushed to hospital after ‘stolen’ BMW flees cops and smashes into car at junction in late-night horror crash







Next

A WOMAN has been taken to hospital after a suspected stolen BMW crashed into her car following a police pursuit.

The BMW reportedly failed to stop for police and was pursued before smashing into the Vauxhall.



It happened in Bartley Green, Birmingham, just before 10pm yesterday.

A woman in her 30s, who was driving the Vauxhall, was treated by paramedics on the scene and then taken to hospital.



A man in his 20s, from the BMW, was also taken to hospital.

Their injuries were not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.



The crash has been referred to the police watchdog.

The man has since been arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving, theft of a motor vehicle, and driving without a licence or insurance.



West Midlands Fire Service sent crews from Bournbrook and Woodgate Valley to deal with the aftermath and make the vehicles safe.

West Midlands Police said: “A man is under arrest following a collision in Bartley Green.

“A suspected stolen BMW, which had previously failed to stop for police, collided with a Vauxhall, on Clapgate Lane near the junction with Jiggins lane, shortly before 10pm yesterday.

“Road closures were put in place as we carried out further enquiries, but the roads have reopened this morning.

“As is standard procedure, we have referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).



“Anyone who saw what happened, or who has footage from the area including mobile phone videos and dashcam or doorbell footage, should contact us.

“You can call 101 or use Live Chat on our website, quoting log 4887 of October 3.”

News.title: At least 2 dead and 35 injured as gunfire breaks out at homecoming party
News.content:
Next

A HORROR shooting has broken out killing at least two people and leaving up to 35 injured.

Gunfire broke out at a homecoming party in Vienna, Georgia, at around 1:20am on Sunday.

Dooley County Sheriff Craig Peavey said that over 1,000 people were gathered at a block party when the celebration turned violent.



Officers had already been sent to the scene to monitor festivities when shots rang out in at least two different locations.



Two people have been pronounced dead, and around 25 of those injured have been hospitalized.

The identities of those who have died have not yet been released.

However, the Coroner has confirmed they are both men aged 20 and 23.



Their families have been informed, officials have said.

The conditions of those injured are currently unknown, and no suspects have been publicly identified as the investigation continues.

News.title: Schoolkids as drug mules, ‘zombie apocalypse’ claims and no-go zones… how the shine came off Britain’s ‘greatest’ city
News.content:
CRIME WAVE Schoolkids as drug mules, ‘zombie apocalypse’ claims and no-go zones… how the shine came off Britain’s ‘greatest’ city







Next

DRUG deals in plain sight, kids coerced into dealing crack cocaine and now four reported rapes in just three weeks – welcome to an area of Glasgow city centre chillingly described as a “no-go zone”.

Four Corners, seconds from the former European City of Culture’s main Central Station where over 90,000 tourists and commuters travel each day, has faced increasing scrutiny recently… just months after a trendy magazine described it as one of “the greatest places to visit in Europe“.



In fact, it’s become so dangerous – with one man even describing the area to the BBC as being like a “zombie apocalypse” – police have increased patrols and extended a “dispersal zone” until December.

The order grants officers the power to ban groups of two or more people from the area for 24 hours if they threaten the safety or well-being of others.



They’re now looking at setting up a permanent base there too.

But still videos on social media show vandalised phone boxes and children fighting. More footage – claiming to be from a road just outside the dispersal zone – showed a brawl with one man slashed and another stamped on.

A person screamed: “He’s got a knife. Get out of the F way. Run for your life.”

The BBC spoke to one shopkeeper in the area, which comprises Union Street, Jamaica Street, Argyle Street and St Enoch Square, who claimed he was racially abused at least 20 times a day.



Meanwhile, police warned of a “lot of child exploitation”, with vulnerable kids involved in drug-running carrying wraps inside their mouths.

And since just August they’ve issued public appeals for information about the “serious assault” of a 43-year-old man in Four Corners and confirmed they’d arrested people for crimes including assault, racially aggravated breach of the peace, drugs supply, possession of offensive weapons, an attempted wilful fire-raising and breach of a City Centre Exclusion Order.

BBC footage also showed a man throwing traffic cones at a helpless dog as startled people looked on.

PC Steven Gemmell said: “If they have a few wraps of drugs, a lot of the time they’ll conceal it in their mouth. So, if I walk up to someone tonight, maybe one of the younger dealers, they’ll noticeably swallow. It’s a risk they’re willing to take even if that bursts in their stomach.”

In August at the High Court in Glasgow, drug dealer Matteullah Siddiqi, 20, was convicted of exploiting a 14-year-old schoolboy after meeting him at a games arcade in Four Corners.



The lad was forced to skip school and stay in drug dens, only admitting what was going on when teachers became worried after he was truant for 11 days.

The court was told Siddiqi initially approached the boy and asked him “if he wanted to start making money”, but he refused, thinking it was drugs.

However, he eventually convinced him by saying he could use the cash to help his mum. He was then given Siddiqi’s Instagram handle and mobile number and taught to bag Class A drugs. The youngster told the court: “I feel betrayed by an adult who I trusted, but who lured me into trouble.”

Details of the reported rapes, the latest in a long line of crime, emerged this week following a report to Glasgow City Council’s Safe Glasgow Partnership by the police.

It said: “The Greater Glasgow Public Protection Unit undertook challenging inquiries into four rape investigations. In a three-week period there were four incidents of rape reported that either occurred in or were linked to the Four Corners area of Glasgow City Centre. Through thorough investigations, all of the crimes were detected.”



Officers said arrests were made in connection with each case.

General Secretary of the Scottish Police Federation David Kennedy previously said: “We are seeing so many areas that people don’t want to visit and see as no-go areas.”

Labour councillors for the area said they too were concerned.



Councillor Elaine McDougal also expressed her concern, warning: “Someone arriving by train from Edinburgh, London, Manchester or elsewhere in the UK walks straight out of Glasgow Central into the heart of the city.

“We have to ask ourselves what impression we want to give them, but ultimately this is not about tourists. It is about the people who use the city centre every day. A woman should feel safe coming into town at night. Families should feel comfortable bringing their children. Young people should have positive places to go. Workers should be able to travel home without intimidation.”

The Sun, which previously visited Four Corners, saw for itself how antisocial behaviour contrasted sharply with tourists visiting the area.

We witnessed as stunned onlookers watched a beer-swilling yob scale a statue of the Duke of Wellington.

Another man was slumped on a bench, while an intoxicated woman stumbled along Argyle Street before passing out on the pavement.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

With Time Out naming Glasgow the greatest city to visit in 2026, it should have been given a welcome boost.

But can the antisocial behaviour that currently grips it be taken under control?

News.title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.

The party's two deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".

Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813.

They also voted to commit the party to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian State", after they rejected an amendment that had been backed by party leader Zack Polanski.

The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.

It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council.

In a letter to the party sent ahead of the vote, the organisations said Zionism was an anti-racist movement, adding that "modern Zionism was formed in part as a response to antisemitism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

It also raised concerns about the safety of Jewish members in the Green Party, as well as the implications for Jewish institutions in areas represented by the Greens.

Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership following Polanski's election as leader last year.

On Friday, Polanski said he believed Zionism, as it was defined in the motion, was racism.

However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."

He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.

A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.

Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates can be found here.

Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion.

Three of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".

On Friday, former leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC: "I think there is no single definition of Zionism and, irrespective of the intentions of those who put that motion, I think there is a real risk that it will be divisive and could be seen as a sign that Jewish people aren't welcome in the party."

Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".

He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

News.title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than Â£100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.

The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to Â£1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.

Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see".

"Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

News.title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping of jury trial plan, minister says
News.content:
The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

News.title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
News.content:
The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.

The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.

Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption.

One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.

The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.

From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.

The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition.

Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.

News.title: Daughter of MP murdered five years ago tells BBC politicians still at risk
News.content:
Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

News.title: Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
News.content:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - Â£408, including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

News.title: Why Canada is preparing for an unlikely US invasion
News.content:
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

So what would it be like if it happened?

The first phase of a war could be quite short.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

News.title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors

"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."

That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.

His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.

Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.

It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.

We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.

News.title: Sinn Féin will co-operate with PSNI investigation over Drumcree protest, says McDonald
News.content:
Sinn FÃ©in will co-operate with the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) over any potential investigation into the protest on the Garvaghy Road, the party president has said.

Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since Sunday 27 September as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues, and rallies on both sides of the dispute were held on Saturday.

Mary Lou McDonald has said that "there's no question with us co-operating with any process that will unfold".

Speaking on Sunday, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said police confirmed to them that Saturday's gathering on the Garvaghy Road was "unnotified" and police were "taking evidence".

McDonald and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are among those who have attended the protest, which police have described as unnotified and "therefore illegal".

The Portadown District has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday.

The Portadown District attempted to march again on Sunday morning.

The PSNI said that anyone "found to have broken the law will face criminal justice consequences".

However, speaking on the BBC's Sunday Politics programme, McDonald said: "There are moments in politically life where you have to take a stand, and this is one of those moments."

When asked about the legality of the protest she said: "Others will determine whether or not that is in fact the case."

The Parades Commission's decided that the parade - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - could go ahead on Sunday 27 September with restrictions.

A fresh legal bid by the residents to prevent the march was due to be heard on Friday - but has now been postponed until Monday.

News.title: Missing woman found 'safe and well' after appeal
News.content:
A missing woman has been found safe and well after a police appeal to find her.

Leicestershire Police said Charlie Ryan was reported missing on Friday morning.

The force said the 31-year-old was found in the Leicester area on Sunday.

Officers thanked the public for sharing their appeal and contacting them with information.

News.title: Family of teenager killed in crash to sue acquitted driver
News.content:
The family of a teenager killed in a car crash near Stirling two years ago are launching a civil case against the driver who was cleared of causing death by careless driving.

Kyle Marshall, 19, and Jayden McConnell, 17, died when a car driven by Charles Gray spun out of control and into the path of a lorry on the A91 near Bannockburn Interchange in March 2024.

Gray, who had passed his test a month earlier, was acquitted of causing the deaths of his two friends after a five-day trial at Stirling Sheriff Court last November.

According to the Scottish Sun,, external the Marshall family are now suing Gray for a six-figure sum, alleging negligence.

A spokesman for Digby Brown, the law firm representing the Marshall family, confirmed: "A civil action has now been raised in the Court of Session on behalf of the loved ones of Kyle to help them secure answers, support and recognition.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further at this time however we will continue to support the Marshall family during this time."

News.title: Medieval leprosy hospital uncovered in Lincoln
News.content:
The walls of what is thought to be one of medieval England's earliest and largest leprosy hospitals have been uncovered in Lincoln by Time Team archaeologists.

A three-day dig started on Friday on the South Common at the site of the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which housed up to 20 people with leprosy around the late 11th to early 12th Centuries.

Time Team's Prof Carenza Lewis said they had found traces of square features where it is thought people were housed, which "haven't been excavated before, anywhere".

The dig marks the beginning of a three-year project backed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The remains of the building were found last year during a Local Landscapes and Hidden Histories project.

More than 100 volunteers were involved in excavating test pits which uncovered what were thought to be the medieval boundary walls of the hospital.

News.title: Train station returning to village after more than 100 years
News.content:
Work is beginning on bringing a train station back to the heart of a Greater Manchester village more than a century after its original station closed.

Cheadle in Stockport had a station just off the high street up until 1917.

Funding for a new hub, which would be built next to Alexandra Hospital, was given the green light in 2022, with planning permission granted in 2023 but concerns about its effect on the timetabling of trains elsewhere on the network led to delays.

Stockport Council said the issue had now been resolved and council leader Mark Roberts said it was "a hugely significant moment for Cheadle and for Stockport".

"For years we've fought for this station because we know the difference it will make to residents, businesses and the future prosperity of the area," he added.

Roberts said he was delighted that the initial highways work could now start on site thanks to the persistence and partnership of all involved.

Services are expected to run from Cheadle into Stockport town, Manchester Piccadilly and Chester, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The project had been held up by an unresolved timetabling issue over concerns the new station could impact trains elsewhere on the network, with a previous proposal made to remove services at Ashley and Plumley.

Stockport Council said the latest assessment by Network Rail and Northern Trains concluded that Cheadle Station could be introduced without removing a significant barrier that had put the project at risk and these plans have now been dropped.

News.title: Wales' Elfyn Evans wins his first World Rally Championship
News.content:
Solberg, whose father Petter won the WRC title in 2003, won the rally by almost a minute ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier.

He and English co-driver Elliott Edmondson were also on course to win the final stage and collect a maximum 35 points for the weekend to take the title by two points.

However, his crash meant he finished five points behind Evans in the overall standings.

A third Toyota driver, Sami Pajari, finished a further one point behind in third - having seen his own title challenge evaporate on the final weekend.

An inconsolable Solberg remained in his car for some time at the end of the stage before being encouraged to take to the podium by Gazoo Racing team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and team-mate Ogier.

"Two corners, two corners," said an emotional Solberg.

"First congratulations to Elfyn, he has been very consistent all season. That I even had a shot after my rollercoaster of a season is incredible.

"I tried everything. I knew I was pushing but didn't know if it was enough. I pushed even more and I couldn't save the car. I tried my very best."

Evans, from Dolgellau in north Wales, had previously missed out on the title on the final day three times and in two of those seasons he had taken a lead into the concluding rally before losing out to Ogier in 2020 and 2025.

"I don't really know what my reaction is. It's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief," he said.

"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done."

For Toyota sporting director Kaj Lindstrom there were mixed feelings.

"That was the hardest thing. The ending was quite something, I didn't expect it," said the Finn.

"It was a good fight and we all saw that Oliver was all or nothing. It held all the way to the end.

"Oliver still has time but Elfyn finally got his title so we're really happy for him."

News.title: Porridge makers from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship
News.content:
The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt.

She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quickly realised it "really brings out the nuances and different aromas".

She believes her secret weapon may have been the water which she brought with her from her home city.

"It's very soft, and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it. I'm not sure - but it worked last time and this time as well, so maybe it's the water".

In the Speciality Porridge category, Rob, from Sydney, came up with his recipe just a few weeks before competing in the Australian national porridge championships - the Pearly Spurtle - after realising how seriously everyone was taking it.

Tapping into his family heritage - his father is Scottish and his mother is Sicilian - he decided to make a porridge cannoli.

"I then had to engineer it," the 36-year-old told BBC Scotland News.

The cream uses the traditional mix of ricotta, mascarpone and sugar but he blended in porridge, sieved it and added some ground toasted oats.

It provides the filling for shells, made like brandy snaps but using Sicilian Marsala wine instead.

News.title: Man rescued after car crashes into house
News.content:
A man had to be rescued by firefighters from a house that partially collapsed after a car crashed into it.

Police officers, paramedics and firefighters were called to the property on Ninefields, in Waltham Abbey, Essex shortly before 23:00 BST on Friday.

Upon arrival, they found a silver Skoda, which had smoke coming out of it, that had smashed into the corner of a house, leaving it badly damaged.

Essex Police said a man was arrested on suspicion of being unfit through drink or drugs and taken to hospital for treatment.

Another man was safely removed from the rear of the property by fire crew using a ladder, while a woman was also taken to hospital for a "precautionary assessment."

Lewis Hamilton admitted his “heart sank” when he realised his Ferrari team had put him on the wrong tyre strategy at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The Ferrari driver, who started second on the grid, was on soft ‘slick’ tyres when the race eventually started after a 90-minute delay due to torrential wet weather in Sepang.

However, it soon became apparent that the correct tyre choice was the wet intermediates, with plenty of standing water still on the circuit and, as a result, Hamilton dropped more than one minute behind the leaders and down the order as he opted not to pit for fresh rubber.

Yet once the track eventually dried out, the seven-time F1 world champion worked his way back into contention and a late safety car gave him the opportunity to overtake Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and claim a well-earned third-place behind winner Max Verstappen and second-placed Kimi Antonelli.

Asked if he feels as if a win got away from him on Sunday, Hamilton told Sky Sports: “Yep! Mixed emotions. On one side: very grateful to get back on the podium. And the other side, with the [tyre] debate in the background, to see the covers come off ahead and they be on wets and the track was dangerous and tricky… my heart sank.”

“I thought: ‘we’ll stay out until this place bloody dries!’ We kept pushing; I didn’t think to get back to P3, we were over a minute down. But the team made a really good job on pit-stops, wish we had longer and more opportunities to get further ahead.

“The safety car was a blessing.”

open image in gallery Hamilton recovered to finish third ( Reuters )

It was Hamilton’s first podium finish since the British Grand Prix in July, though he still trails championship leader Antonelli – who now has an 86-point lead over George Russell after his unfortunate late retirement – by 106 points.

“Fundamentally, we have a great car and that’s down to an amazing group of people back to the factory,” Hamilton said, looking ahead to next week’s race in Singapore.

“We have been innovators this year but we’re down on power. We’ve got to catch up for next year, we’ll live with that deficit for this year.

“But the car is improving and we just keep trying. I’m enjoying the racing, still feel fit, today we got some good points.”

Gypsy Rose Blanchard has started a petition to combat online harassment after the death of her fiancé and father of her child, Ken Urker.

Urker was found dead at his Louisiana home on Thursday, the day of his 34th birthday. A cause of death has not been revealed pending an ongoing investigation.

On Sunday, Blanchard, 35, created a petition for “Kenan’s Law” to help combat online harassment and cyberbullying. She claimed that Urker had faced “an overwhelming amount of online scrutiny” before his death.

“Reports were made across multiple platforms, and far too often, the response was simply: ‘No violation,’” she said in an Instagram post.

“Kenan’s Law is about changing the way social-media platforms handle repeated reports of harassment. This is not about silencing criticism or taking away anyone’s freedom of speech. Public figures can and should be criticized, but public figures are still human beings, and fame should never erase someone’s humanity.”

Blanchard said that Urker’s death had made her “determined to turn pain into purpose.”

open image in gallery Ken Urker was found dead at his Louisiana home on Thursday, the day of his 34th birthday ( Instagram via @gypsyrose.insta )

“I cannot change what happened, but I can advocate for a better system for the next person who feels like no one is listening. Please sign and share the petition to support Kenan’s Law,” she said.

The Change.org petition has received more than 900 signatures at the time of writing.

The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office confirmed in a statement shared with The Independent that police found Urker dead at his Louisiana home after receiving a call at 6:15 p.m. Thursday. Investigators found him next to “a brown powdery substance,” a syringe, handgun and two shot glasses.

“At this time, we are continuing the death investigation,” a police spokesperson said. “To this point, we have discovered no signs of foul play.”

open image in gallery Gypsy Rose Blanchard has started a petition to combat online harassment after the death of her fiancé and father of her child, Ken Urker ( Getty )

“Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved,” Gypsy said in a Thursday night statement to TMZ. “He will forever be my soulmate and my red string, a connection that time, distance, and even death can never erase.”

She told People that Urker was subjected to intense online harassment about their relationship.

“Ken endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit,” she told the outlet. “The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure.”

Blanchard and Urker began their relationship as pen pals when she was serving nearly eight years in prison after pleading guilty to second-degree murder for her role in the death of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard, in 2015.

Urker proposed in October 2018, but the couple later called off their engagement. Blanchard married Ryan Anderson in 2022, but announced their split four months after her release from prison and reconciled with Urker shortly after in April 2024.

Blanchard and Urker welcomed their daughter, Aurora Raina Urker, in December 2024.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you

UK households should keep small supplies of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home in case of emergency or war, the Defence Secretary has warned.

Wes Streeting said Britain faces a growing threat of being disrupted by fires, floods, and enemy attacks, including cyber warfare.

He called for a "whole society approach" to strengthen national resilience, though he insisted people should remain "alert not alarmed" regarding potential risks.

Speaking to The Sun ahead of the Labour Party conference, he said: "It’s just a simple ask of people.

"Do they have what they need indoors, should they lose access to their online banking for a period? Should they have a power cut?”

open image in gallery British households are being advised to stock up on tinned food. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

It comes as the government releases a list of supplies for an emergency kit they say everyone should keep at home.

Here we look at the key items you should stock up on in case disaster strikes.

What should people stockpile?

Wes Streeting has advised the British public there are certain items they should store for emergencies.

He said: "These are basic things, and of course, you know, a lot of people just have that in their cupboard naturally.

"It’s having some cash at home, having a supply of bottled water indoors, having some tinned goods that you can access if your electric goes and you’re not able to cook on the hob or in the microwave.”

Nutritionists and “preppers” on social media also say people should consider intake of carbohydrates and protein, and so suggest items such as oats, rice and pasta be included in any stockpile.

Kidney beans, peanut butter and tinned fish provide high levels of protein.

open image in gallery The government has asked people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water. ( Getty/iStock )

What should I keep in my emergency kit?

The government says people should put together an emergency kit that includes key provisions you and your household would need during a short-term incident lasting several days, such as a power failure or a disruption to your water supply.

Recommended emergency kit supplies include:

A battery or wind-up torch – torches are safer than candles.

– torches are safer than candles. A portable power bank for charging your mobile phone.

for charging your mobile phone. A battery or wind-up radio to get updates during a power cut – a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside.

– a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside. Spare batteries for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on.

for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on. A first aid kit (or some first aid items) including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.

A minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day is recommended by the World Health Organisation for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets.

Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets. Non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets.

that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets. Baby supplies such as nappies and baby formula – ready made or ‘ready-to-feed’ formula is best as you may not be able to boil water or sterilise bottles.

Rather than buying all the items at once, you could just add to your emergency kit when you are able and build it up over time. You should try to store these items together in a single location in your home, ideally in a spot that remains simple to locate if the lights are off.

open image in gallery Keep some batteries, a radio, a torch and tinned food in your emergency kit at home. ( Getty Images )

Maintaining a supply of prescription medication to cover several days is also essential. For those who depend on any medical devices or equipment, ensure that printed physical copies of all operating instructions are kept on hand. Furthermore, any available back-up batteries ought to be kept fully charged at all times.

What threats is the government worried about?

Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia.

The government is also concerned following the record-breaking heatwaves the UK has experienced this summer, plunging the country into drought and causing numerous wildfires.

According to the FT, the government is accelerating work on its “war book” – a manual for the defence of the nation against external threats – as well as a social media campaign with advice to help people to deal with the impacts of extreme weather.

It also updated its national risk register last month, with the risk of interference in the UK’s democratic process added to it.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin’s government warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia. ( AFP/Getty )

The national risk register is the government’s assessment of the most significant risks facing the UK.

It is a planning tool designed to help professionals prepare for risks and is not intended to be a prediction of future events.

Vladimir Putin’s government recenty warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia.

The Independent also reported that rogue drones are targeting Britain’s military bases almost daily, leaving the UK vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran.

Some 340 security incidents involving drones were reported at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026, data obtained under freedom of information laws show. In 2025, there were a total of 250 incidents recorded – double the 126 recorded the year before.

open image in gallery The Government also plans to advise people on how to deal with the impacts of extreme weather ( Getty )

Why are the heatwaves a concern?

Analysts have warned extreme heat and ongoing droughts are putting Britain at risk of its “worst food security crisis in decades”.

The knock-on impact of five back-to-back heatwaves and prolonged dry conditions could destroy farmers’ harvests, leading to food shortages later this year and increasing reliance on foreign imports, according to analysts from the investment bank Shore Capital.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) warned the situation is “increasingly concerning” and that dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing.

A small boat carrying migrants is being tracked by French coastguard and rescue vessels as it moves towards the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.

The vessel is heading for the south coast, and authorities are preparing for its arrival.

Ship tracking data suggested the dinghy set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.

HM Coastguard said it is “currently liaising with French authorities about a small boat within French waters of the Channel, south of the UK central south coast”.

Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Gosport, said there is “nothing to suggest” the boat will be landing in Hampshire but that police are “making preparations should that situation change”.

Ms Dinenage said in a social media post: “I am aware of reports of a migrant boat crossing from Normandy towards the south coast of the UK.

“I have contacted the Home Office border security minister and requested an urgent update.

“At present, there is nothing to suggest that the boat will be landing in Gosport.

“Understandably, local police will be making preparations should that situation change.”

open image in gallery A group of people thought to be migrants are brought in to the Border Security Command compound in Dover, Kent, from a Border Security Command vessel following a small boat incident in the Channel. Picture date: Sunday October 4, 2026. ( PA )

George Madgwick, a Hampshire Reform UK councillor, shared images on social media of coaches and police, which he said were in the Fareham area of Hampshire ready for “a small boat due to land locally”.

A Government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”

Departures from as far west as Normandy have been rare in recent years.

But this is the third such crossing in the space of a month.

In September, British rescue boats collected the passengers of a migrant dinghy which had spent around 30 hours at sea after setting off from Normandy.

The 51 migrants on board had refused help from the French coastguard.

They arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats.

At the time, the migrants were expected to be taken to Gosport, and hundreds of protesters gathered after coaches and ambulances were spotted in the area.

Six people were arrested by officers during the evening.

The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451.

That figure is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the number at this stage in 2024.

News.title: ‘I’ve finally got my son back – but my cruel IPP sentence means he could be taken away again at any time’
News.content:

A mother whose toddler was removed from her care over a petty crime she committed 20 years ago has finally been reunited with her son after a months-long court battle.

Joshua*, who was not yet two, had never spent a night away from his mother when police knocked on her door in January and hauled her to prison, forcing social services to put him in foster care.

Rachel* had been recalled under a draconian Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) jail term, which she received for a street robbery she had committed two decades earlier.

The recall was triggered by a single call to police from a teenage neighbour over an alleged alcohol-fuelled altercation with a family member days earlier, which she disputes ever happened and has not resulted in any charge.

Although she was released in just eight weeks after Ministry of Justice officials ruled the recall was not needed, Rachel has spent almost nine months battling to prove to a family court that Joshua can be safely returned to her care in a series of hearings which The Independent was given exclusive access to attended.

After nearly a year of heartache, a family court judge this month ruled that parental responsibility can be returned to the mother.

“I am just so happy, I can’t even find the words,” Rachel told The Independent, as Joshua played happily in the background, having seemingly bounced back from the separation.

“It should never have got to this. There’s no need to be here over an allegation, which is why it's all happened.”

open image in gallery Rachel says the day her son was taken away was the worst of her life ( Getty/iStock )

Despite her relief, she lives in constant fear of the hair-trigger recall process under the terms of her strict IPP licence, which still threatens to rip her family apart.

“What scares me is the fact that they will keep using my IPP for my parenting,” she said, adding she is constantly on edge that the slightest slip up could land her back in prison.

“I have been on it 21 years now. I feel like I am being treated like I have killed somebody.”

Rachel is among thousands of people still trapped under the controversial jail terms, which were outlawed in 2012, but not retrospectively. The open-ended punishments, introduced under New Labour in a bid to be tough on crime, were handed to many repeat offenders, even if their crimes were minor.

The ill-conceived sentence has left thousands trapped in prison for up to 22 times their original minimum term, while others – such as Rachel – have found themselves in a vicious cycle of recall, often for breaches of strict licence conditions.

Unlike most prisoners, who serve a fixed 56-day recall, IPP offenders are returned to prison indefinitely. On average, they serve 25 months in jail each time they are recalled, regardless of whether licence breaches or other allegations are proven.

Rachel was handed an IPP following a string of previous convictions after being groomed into sex work as a child and struggling with drug misuse. She was told she must serve a minimum of 17 months when she was sentenced in 2006 for the robbery, but has spent two decades in and out of custody until she fell pregnant with Joshua, who was her “chance” at a new life.

The IPP licence was cited in court papers as a reason for Joshua’s removal from her care, noting: “IPP recalls are sudden and unpredictable, creating ongoing instability for Joshua, who is a very young child.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has pledged to end the injustice of IPP sentences ( PA Wire )

Prime minister Andy Burnham has promised to finally end the “long-running injustice” of IPP jail terms before the end of this parliament. And justice secretary Alex Norris last week described the legacy of the sentence as a “grotesque spectacle”.

But plans to put it right are expected to take time and, for now at least, Rachel must wait until 2028 until she can apply have her licence terminated.

“I can’t wait for it to end,” she added. “I have been on it that long, it would just be a relief.”

Rachel described the day she handed Joshua to social services as the worst of her life. In the weeks that followed, she said it felt like her “heart had been ripped out” as she anxiously waited to find out if she would be re-released, only seeing Joshua during weekly visits at the prison.

When she was freed, Rachel’s time with her son was limited to four “intrusive” supervised visits a week. This was relaxed to supported visits after five weeks, during which Joshua is dropped off for three hour-long visits, with regular checks from social workers.

She was anxious that Joshua would struggle when he was first allowed home full time on an interim basis in July, after six months in a foster placement. But the Spiderman-obsessed toddler is already thriving, according to assessments by the local authority.

Despite the glowing reports about her parenting, Joshua’s appointed guardian during the family court proceedings had urged the judge to impose a care order, which would have given the council shared parental responsibility for Joshua long-term.

This was opposed by both the local authority and Rachel, whose lawyer insisted he had never seen a more “robust and rigorous” supervision plan in his entire career in the family courts.

open image in gallery The mother is being monitored 24/7 by GPS and alcohol tags ( Getty )

The mother, who wears both a GPS tag and an alcohol tag, is being monitored by probation 24/7 and is subject to a 12-month supervision order, with multi-agency support.

She is being watched so closely that she was reported for buying cans of beer for her neighbour in her local shop, even though it is accepted that they were not for her, the court heard.

“Where she is and what she’s doing is very, very closely monitored,” the judge pointed out, before he declined to impose a care order. The judge told Rachel he was “delighted” to read reports of her progress as he restored parental responsibility to her.

The mother said she welcomed the pledge from the prime minister to finally end the injustice of IPP sentences, adding that officials should stop “acting on things without finding out the facts”.

She has never been arrested or questioned over the alleged incident which led to her recall.

“It's hard because obviously I am not committing a crime, I am not taking drugs, I am not hanging around with negative people, I have moved into a new area,” she said. “It’s just this IPP scrutiny is constant.

“I think they need to look into the people that it has affected. It’s affected my mental health, because it's like I am not in charge of my own life.”

The uncertain nature of the IPP sentence has been described as “psychological torture” by the United Nations, which has raised repeated concerns with the government. At least 96 people have taken their own lives in prison after losing hope of getting out, with a further 37 suicides in the community where offenders live under the constant fear of recall.

*Names in this article have been changed to protect the family’s right to anonymity

Stores are cutting back on self-checkout lines - and shoppers aren’t mad about it.

Around a third of 340 small and midsize retail operators (36 percent) said they used self-checkout this year - down from 43 percent in 2025, according to an April survey from Toast, a point-of-sale and restaurant management platform.

The rethink on self-checkout comes even as three-quarters of the group of convenience stores, grocery stores and bottle shops polled said they would continue investing heavily in other technology, including, of course, AI.

While retailers pointed to self-checkout problems with efficiency and theft, social media is also awash in shoppers airing their frustrations, from having to scan and bag their own purchases - tasks traditionally handled by employees - to being subjected to loud and sometimes embarrassing prompts from machines.

One infuriated X user posted Wednesday about going through self-checkout, only then to be stopped by an employee who asked to see his receipt.

open image in gallery Self-checkout use among small and midsize retailers fell from 43 percent to 36 percent this year, according to a new Toast survey ( Getty )

“I handed it to him, but I’m standing there thinking... wait a minute. You trusted me enough to do the cashier’s job, but now you need to check my work before I can leave? If you don’t trust customers to scan their own stuff, maybe don’t make self-checkout half the store,” he fumed.

“I’m not mad at the employee. He’s just doing his job. But somebody needs to explain how I became the cashier and the suspect at the same time.”

Others on social media complained about feeling watched by store employees or surveillance cameras while using self-checkout.

“I hate when Target and Walmart employees stand there watching me at self-checkout,” one user wrote.

“Like b*****, you can do this s*** yourself! Why am I doing YOUR job while YOU watch me scan my own groceries and take my money?” another X user wrote.

There is little data on whether shoppers overall prefer self-checkout or a human cashier. One common perk of self-checkout is avoiding interaction with other people, particularly after a long day or when not in the mood to chat. But for others, that lack of human interaction is exactly the problem.

“There's nothing wrong with self-checkouts. Some of us don't like waiting in line like cattle when we just want 2 or 3 items,” one user wrote Wednesday. “Many employees would like the opportunity to be productive in other ways than just zombie scanning consumers all day. Having both as an option is best.”

A popular argument for traditional cashier roles is letting humans keep their jobs instead of losing them to machines or robots.

“They installed self-checkout in my local Publix a few months ago and I refuse to use them. I will wait in line to have a human do the job. You know why? Those cashiers' hours are based on how productive their lines are, so to speak,” another X user said Tuesday. “If you can help show the store that those lines are still needed, those sweet old ladies get to keep their jobs.”

open image in gallery A popular social media argument is that traditional cashier roles preserve jobs that could otherwise be replaced by automation ( AFP/Getty )

Retailers have reported increasing losses from self-checkout.

A June report from ECR Retail Loss, a retailer-backed research group, found that grocery stores experienced an average 22 percent increase in merchandise losses in the year after installing self-checkout. Those losses include both theft and accidental errors, such as missed scans and incorrect product selections.

Grocery stores with self-checkout had average losses that were 33 percent higher than stores without it, according to the report.

In 2024, some major retailers began limiting the number of items customers could bring to self-checkout - with Target setting a 10-item limit nationwide and Walmart testing a 15-item limit at some stores. Supermarket chain Schnucks limited self-checkout to shoppers with 10 items or fewer.

Other retailers have scaled back self-checkout over concerns about “shrink,” a metric that includes theft but also accidental errors, damaged merchandise and other inventory discrepancies. Dollar General removed self-checkout from about 12,000 stores in 2024, while Five Below also reduced its use of the technology that year.

Some local communities took their own steps. In Long Beach, California, a 2025 ordinance required stores that offered self-checkout to limit the lanes to 15 items and maintain at least one staffed checkout lane.

Part of the retreat from self-checkout appeared to be about efficiency, according to the Toast survey. Some 31 percent of operators listed simplifying operations among their top three business goals, up 12 percentage points from the previous year.

A quarter of respondents cited the use of new technology. Retailers are investing in technology that can reduce manual work and give them more control over prices and orders. Digital shelf labels make price changes faster and easier, while order-ready boards help streamline the process of preparing and handing out orders.

Electronic shelf labels rose 11 percentage points year-over-year, while the use of order-ready boards increased 9 points, the survey found.

Retailers are increasingly experimenting with AI in large numbers - with 88 percent of those polled saying they believe the technology will make their businesses more efficient.
