Sports.title: Amusingly triumphs in Jean-Luc Lagardere clash with Folsom Blues
Sports.content:
Amusingly oozed class in beating the colts to land the Qatar Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere at ParisLongchamp.

Francis-Henri Graffard surprised many when switching his Juddmonte-owned filly from the Prix Marcel Boussac against her own sex, but the decision was well and truly vindicated.

Colin Keane dropped his mount out last in the early stages and she tracked the odds-on favourite Folsom Blues, with both travelling ominously well.

Joseph O'Brien's National Stakes winner had no answer to the finishing burst of Amusingly, though, and the daughter of No Nay Never pulled away to win in tremendous fashion.

Graffard said: "She beat the filly that finished second in the Marcel Boussac (Data) very easily, so I was hoping I didn't make a mistake.

"She shows a lot of speed this filly, so I said to Barry Mahon (Juddmonte racing manager) she's more of a Commonwealth Cup filly than a Guineas filly for next year.

"I've no idea if she'll go to the Breeders' Cup, I need to speak to the team.

"Today is a big win so I just want to enjoy that and winter well and we have a lovely filly for next year, but what she has done today is wonderful."

The Lagardere at seven furlongs was a furlong shorter than the Bousaac, and Keane said: "I think the decision to run in this race rather than the Boussac was a bit of a combination of everyone, it just looked like the last day over a mile she failed to see out the final half-furlong.

"She's a filly with a lot of class and lot of pace, she did a lot on the bridle before being run out of it close home (last time) so that was in the decision to bring her back to seven, albeit we were taking on the colts.

"She relaxed a lot better today, she wasn't as fresh and gassy and did everything right in the first half of the race, when she did that part we thought she'd run a good race and she showed how well she can quicken."

He added: "Time will tell if she's a Guineas filly, she does have a lot of pace but I don't see why she won't get a mile."

Green Empress rules in Prix Marcel Boussac

Green Empress provided Joseph O'Brien with another big-race success when narrowly holding off Data to win the Qatar Prix Marcel Boussac at ParisLongchamp.

Never out of the first two in her career, she was paying the ultimate compliment to the brilliant Sun Goddess, who to date has been the only filly to beat her - on no less than three occasions.

Ridden confidently by Christophe Soumillon, Green Empress hit the front with half a furlong to run and looked set to win comfortably before Christoper Head's Data made her pull out all the stops close home.

O'Brien said: "It's really special for us to have a Group One winner on this day and she has been progressive - she's only ever been beaten by Sun Goddess all year.

Image: Green Empress won the Qatar Prix Marcel Boussac (Cal Sport Media via AP Images)

"She has a super pedigree, being by Saxon Warrior out of a Sea The Stars mare. We see her as a miler that might go 10 furlongs at some stage.

"We'll see how she comes out of today and discuss with the owners whether she'll go to America (Breeders' Cup) or whether we wait for next year."

The success was the latest Group One triumph in a stellar year for O'Brien, who added: "We're very lucky to have the support of some great people and a wide variety of owners.

"For us it's about performing and executing at big meetings. It's fantastic to have a big winner on Arc day."

Sports.title: FIA explain 'unprecedented' glitch that caused Bahrain GP start chaos
Sports.content:
The FIA revealed an “unprecedented” glitch caused several cars to stop in the chaotic start to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Heavy rain in Sepang caused a delayed start but when the drivers left the pit lane, multiple drivers almost grinded to a halt including race leader Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton with several drivers in the midfield also experiencing issues.

The start procedure was abandoned and the Grand Prix eventually started properly with the original grid order almost an hour after the carnage.

"On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars," said the FIA in a statement.

"As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the Power Unit before the start of the race.

"This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A chaotic formation lap halted race start at Bahrain GP in Malaysia

Formula 1 and the FIA have new technical regulations this year which saw the introduction of new power unit which is almost 50 per cent electric.

Some drivers have criticised the new power unit due to its complexities that require an unusual driving style where you can be punished for getting on the throttle early or braking later into certain corners.

Malaysia saw the first wet conditions of the season and Sky Sports F1's Anthony Davidson explained the slow speed of the cars leaving the pit lane in the rain caused the stoppages.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Intense rain delayed the start of the Bahrain GP in Malaysia

"Basically, if you run the engines too slowly, the turbo spools down because we don't have the MGU-H anymore," he said.

"What's effectively happening is if you are off throttle for too long, the turbo spools down and when the drivers puts their foot back down it uses all the engine juice.

"As soon as the battery goes flat, you are down to internal combustion engine power only. And because it can't reach the drivers' torque demand anymore, because the engine is not creating the power because you have no turbo, you go outside of the FIA regulation.

"It's all there to stop teams having traction control. It's incredibly complicated and you fall into this horrible trap where the engine can't reaccelerate because you are being penalised by this regulation."

Image: The Bahrain GP in Malaysia was the first time enough rain saw drivers use intermediates in a Grand Prix this year

'Not good enough' - Drivers react to bizarre scenes

Most drivers were unimpressed by the scenes and the extra hour's delay it took for the FIA to implement new software into the cars before the proper race start.

"At first, I thought that the Safety Car had switched off the light," said Ferrari's Charles Leclerc who was running fourth on the first formation lap.

"I couldn't see the Safety Car. There too much spray and I thought the Safety Car had gone, and Max was taking the gap to warm up the tyres.

"Then they told me on radio, 'we think Max has a problem', then Max went then Lewis was slow. I waited then at one point was like, 'okay I'm going to go' then when I went on the throttle, I had exactly the same problem and I realised everyone was in the same boat and we were stuck at 20kph.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton revealed his heart sank when Ferrari chose to start on soft tyres while the majority of other cars started on intermediates

"It's a little bit scary to see that with an F1 car. That's a bit of our worry with these cars, not to that extent, of course, this was a problem.

"But when you get out of the corner, sometimes you can have 100 horsepower more, 100 horsepower less. You are not completely in control of the power you are given, and then with this kind of visibility, like at the start of the race, you can have big shunts because of that."

In the press conference, Verstappen joked it felt "like the Lego race" in reference to the drivers' parade at this year's British Grand Prix when the 22 drivers raced in Lego-made cars.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the best bits of the chaotic Lego parade at the British Grand Prix

"It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power!" said Verstappen, who went on to win the race in Malaysia.

"At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on. Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you [Hamilton] by yourself crawling."

Hamilton replied: "I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen added "that's not what you want for the sport". Hamilton agreed: "I hope there is a lesson learned".

Sports.title: Roosters hold on to break Newcastle hearts in NRL Grand Final
Sports.content:
Hull FC-bound Daly Cherry-Evans kicked the crucial drop goal as the Sydney Roosters held on by one point to break Newcastle Knights hearts in a dramatic NRL Grand Final.

The Roosters overturned a 12-point deficit to deny Newcastle a fairytale ending to their Cinderella season and claim a 16th premiership after a thrilling Grand Final in Sydney.

Inspirational captain, James Tedesco, and a show-stopping performance from Mark Nawaqanitawase, who could represent Australia at ‌both the league and union World Cups over the next 12 months, handed the Red White and Bluesters their first title since 2019.

"I had so much belief in this club, the players, the coach. This is what it's all about. And we did it. And I'm so, so proud to be here, and I just can't wait to go see my family."

Cherry-Evans, the oldest Grand Finalist in history, used all his experience to nudge over a simple field goal to extend his side's lead beyond a converted try.

And it proved a vital score with Greg Marzhew breaking a couple of tackles to roll over for Newcastle with Sandon Smith converting brilliantly from the touchline. But the 'Chooks', one of the two clubs remaining from the first season of what became the NRL in 1908, held on, to secure ⁠their fourth title under ​long-term coach Trent Robinson.

"Credit to the Knights, they fought for 80 minutes there," ​said Nawaqanitawase, after lifting the Provan-Summons Trophy.

"This is going to last me a lifetime, it's sad to go but I love everyone here, I love all the boys, ‌and let's celebrate this win, ​far out."

The Knight headed into the match just a day after CEO Peter Parr expressed his deep concern after a vehicle drove into a crowd of people supporting the NRL team on Saturday, as they prepared for their Grand Final.

Police said 10 people were injured in the incident in Wallsend, New South Wales, including several children, while the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle was arrested.

Two of the injured, a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, are in critical condition, and the other eight are in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales Police.

Sports.title: Bellingham stands out for high-grade England but Uefa sends out wrong message on racism | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
So … can we play another World Cup, then? Can we just undo and rewind? Forget whatever it was you thought you saw in Atlanta. We’re actually ready now.

Although not, repeat not, if any part of this involves playing football in front of 6,000 excitable children, the combined effect of which was to create an atmosphere in Rijeka the adult human ear is simply not designed to process.

This was a dreamlike occasion on many levels, from its quietly farcical staging, to a relentlessly high-grade England performance and a deserved 7-0 win, all of it glossed in the moment by the striking beauty of the setting.

Rijeka is a gently crumbling Italianate coastal town, the stadium lodged up in the hills facing into the blue of the Adriatic. From the stands here you could switch between watching Jude Bellingham cruise about the pitch like a human superyacht to following the cargo ships crawling across the curve of the bay, the grey-green fade of the hills below, white towers by the shore, like a pocket-sized Balkan Rio de Janeiro.

Against this background, two key things happened. The first was an administrative abomination. At 6pm Croatia and England kicked off this closed-doors, stadium-banned Nations League game in front of a packed and boisterous home crowd with barely a spare seat in the house.

The ban was imposed as punishment for a mass fan march to the Stade de France in Paris last March, accompanied by Nazi salutes and the discovery, later, of a stash of combat-ready weapons, including “iron rods, telescopic batons and sharp wooden sticks”.

In response to this, the Croatian Football Association said no to racism here by saying: yes, come along to the game you’re not allowed to come to because of racism. A very simple suggestion to Uefa. If you’re in any way serious about making this point, just close the loophole that allowed the stands here to be filled with 6,000 children plus their designated “handlers”.

View image in fullscreen Adult Croatia supporters were not allowed in but 6,000 children were, plus ‘handlers’, but it was not a pretty sight for the locals.

Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

It is at the very least a confusing message. It seems to say: racism and children, this is a good combination. And given this seems to happen quite regularly, that racism is now a kind of children’s holiday event around here, football Christmas. And here’s your bonus bag of free tickets, brought to you by today’s matchday sponsor, racism.

Playing the game in Rijeka also punished England’s fans, with just a hundred allowed to make the two-hour drive down a two-lane highway from Zagreb. Although this was still a lovely place to be, with its jaunty open stands, the haze of sea, land and sky merging in the middle distance, and not forgetting the Brutalist away end, a fully enclosed steel prison cage, albeit so scenically placed you could probably Airbnb it in the off-season.

On the pitch things were clearer, as England produced a sustained and genuinely high-grade performance from first to last. They did so in an interesting way too. Often England teams can look good but flawed. Here they were tight and mobile, just a powerful, high-technique modern team. They looked like what people imagine Premier League-era England teams might look like, but never really do, a team with the capacity to take on anyone, playing like this.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And yes, steady on there. They did all this against a Croatia team that gave a performance, given the audience, that verged on child cruelty. But who else around the world is good in exactly this way? France, perhaps. A balanced, focused England team, with Bellingham and Kane, is a serious proposition.

Thomas Tuchel fielded an interesting team, with much to like in a fluid-looking Alex Scott-Elliot Anderson-Bellingham midfield trident. And with seven minutes gone England were 1-0 up. The goal was made by Scott’s drive, Bellingham’s slick pass and Harry Kane roofing it with a zing you could hear from the stands.

England pressed busily, smothered Croatia everywhere and looked assured in their touches. And Bellingham duly made it 2-0 on 20 minutes after some nimble stuff from Anthony Gordon. The goal was his eighth in eight games for England after six in his previous 37. Bellingham just looks irresistible right now.

It was 3-0 on 38 minutes, Gordon heading in a whipped cross from Jarell Quansah, then 4-0 with another brilliant breakaway goal just before half-time, Bellingham running 80 metres to retake the ball, then crossing for Bukayo Saka to tap in.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham slots the ball past Dominik Livakovic to score England’s second goal. Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Modric came and went after half-time, a slightly sad spectacle in itself. For the majority of his career he has looked like a little boy dressed up as a witch. He doesn’t look like this any more. Now he looks like a gnarled middle-aged footballer dressed up as a witch. He still has the brilliance, and the touch, but not in this team of old men. It was 5-0 shortly after, Kane getting his second after a good cross from Anderson, who was just too much for Croatia here. Saka got another, set up by Kane.

By the end, 7-0 really didn’t seem very flattering. And yes, yes, the opponents were poor. But the real point was the style, the balance, the intensity of England’s performance. It felt repeatable. It certainly felt like progress from the World Cup.

The final takeaway, as the shrieks died away, was that Croatian children are far better behaved at football than their adult counterparts. And Croatia does have a genuine problem here. We’re not talking cultural misunderstanding or disputed micro-aggressions. These are macro-aggressions. It’s far-right, actual Nazi-adjacent stuff, and domestic ultra culture still pegged out around white supremacy symbols and references to the wretched Ustase, the notably vicious puppet regime of the second world war.

As Gianni Infantino would say, football unites the world. Sometimes it even unites it in fascism. Filling the stands with kids is not taking your sanctions seriously. Although here the occasion was saved by another kind of punishment and by a genuinely gripping England performance.

Sports.title: Jesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’
Sports.content:
Peak leaf hasn’t yet arrived in Montreal but the bursts of gold and butterscotch up on the hill that gave this place its name still mushroom out by the hour.

Sitting in a glass-panelled hotel mezzanine at the foot of Mount Royal, Canada men’s coach Jesse Marsch has his mind on another harvest. When this extended autumnal international window ends, he will decamp to Italy, where the olive crops at his Tuscan villa are ready for reaping.

Flight paths between Canada and Europe have been busy lately, and figurative transatlantic distances are closing fast. As Canada’s relations with the noisiest neighbour to the south stretch and fray, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is forging alliances with the EU so close that the bloc is apparently inventing new membership categories.

As an American residing in Europe who is also a Canadian leader with robust approval ratings, Marsch is watching. To him, it feels right.

“I’ve always thought Canada was a little bit more European than the US anyway. Right?” Marsch tells the Guardian. “But certainly now there’s enough happening politically and economically that you would say, we’re looking much more like that. There’s talk of [Canada becoming an associate EU member] even actually happening. I like that aspect.

“There’s a uniqueness to Canada in terms of how truly multiethnic this country has become. You can see that Canada is not just a North American country any more, you know? That bodes well for our sport and for the makeup of our team, the makeup of our fans.”

Having led Canada’s men to historic highs at this summer’s World Cup, Marsch is feeling his way into his second act in the job. Some of his sideline displays – we’ll get to that meme – may have irked outsiders, especially in his homeland, during the tournament. Yet, having extended for four more years, Marsch is someone an overwhelming majority of Canadians are happy to have at the helm. There are more than a few cross-points between Marsch and Carney.

“My impression is that first of all, he is a really smart guy, but a really normal guy,” Marsch says of Carney, who attended a number of Canada’s World Cup matches. “Sometimes you meet a US president, and you’re overwhelmed, maybe by their presence, the position itself. I’ve met Clinton, George Bush Sr, Obama, Trump, Biden. Oh, and Carter. Six in person. Carney, compared to all of them, the closest would be Obama. A real air of intelligence, but a real air of being a regular guy. I think that that’s perfect for this country and this moment.

“He has shown great support for us. I made a joke with him that ‘I heard you’re an Everton fan?’ and he goes, ‘Yeah’. And I go, ‘I’m sorry about that’. He replies: ‘Why does everybody say that? Everybody has to pick their team and stick by them.’ I said, ‘I appreciate that you don’t switch from Everton to Arsenal or Liverpool, like everybody else’. There’s something so genuine [about] that. Could a president of the US ever be an Everton fan? No chance.”

View image in fullscreen Canada prime minister Mark Carney greeted Marsch’s team in the locker room after the team’s win over Qatar at the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty Images

Circumstances, as well as natural impulses, have led Marsch to play statesman during this prolonged cooling of relations between Canada and his home country. He’s been defiant – lashing out at Donald Trump’s “51st state” barbs – then more deft. Sometimes, especially when it comes to the US Soccer Federation he said led him on with a job offer only to renege, he finds it hard to hide his disdain.

This window is the start of turning the page to the next phase of his Canada project. He admits, with a chuckle, that the four years stretching ahead feel long but there are imminent goals – a first trophy in 25 years, cracking and consolidating inside the world’s top 24.

A win over Chile in Toronto and 2-0 win over Peru here on Saturday afternoon in games billed as The Homecoming made for a solid start. New caps have been handed out. Key players arrived thriving in new surroundings, none more than Jonathan David at Atlético Madrid. Extended injury absences and the awkward non-attendance of captain Alphonso Davies (skipping the window to honeymoon) have been overcome.

But Tuesday’s clash with the US in Saint Paul means more American questions are coming. Looking back, the Folarin Balogun affair feels absolutely tailor-made for a Marschian verdict. He, of course, has thoughts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Well, this is a deep conversation,” he says, leaning back. “We, as Americans, have been inundated with propaganda since we were young. We’re the No 1 country in the world, we deserve everything, we dominate everything, No 1 in every aspect of life. This is what we’ve been told. So, when things happen and we don’t feel like we’re in control of it … we feel like we deserve to be treated differently because we’re Americans. That is one of the things that infuriates the rest of the world about Americans. And Americans don’t know that if they don’t ever leave the country.

“So what I feel when the Balogun ruling happens is that would never happen in any other country in the world, and this is why everyone around the world hates America. That was proven to be so. The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”

The meme is another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”

He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.

“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

Sports.title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.

Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.

Sports.title: Alexander’s absence weighs heavy as Bradford try to keep promotion push on track
Sports.content:
It was a bruising start to the week for Bradford City when news filtered through to the players that Graham Alexander had stepped down as manager. They were top of League One and his departure was a sudden and unexpected blow for a side that had started to let imaginations run wild about a return to the second tier for the first time in 23 years.

The coaches Mark Trueman and Colin Doyle took interim charge and called a meeting with the squad last Monday. “Some of the players were a little unsettled, didn’t know what was going on or who was taking the team,” Trueman said. “But the players have just got on with business and that’s the key. It shows the mentality of the team. This could quite easily derail them, but they’ve continued to do the right things.”

If any caretaker can keep Bradford on track, it is Trueman, who has now stepped in temporarily five times since joining the club as an Under-18 coach six years ago. This time, though, is different. Previously, his job was to raise the team during low periods. Now the task is to maintain the upward trajectory that began the moment Alexander arrived in 2023.

Bradford were stuck in the bottom tier of the EFL and sitting in 16th when Alexander took over. They finished ninth in his first season, then third in his second to earn automatic promotion, followed by a stunning fourth-place finish back in League One, losing in the playoff semi-finals last May.

It has been a thrilling ride rarely enjoyed by Bradford fans. They twice reached the EFL Trophy semi-finals in successive seasons. At one stage, they won 10 consecutive home games, breaking a club record set in 1953. Last year they had the best home record of any side in Europe’s top five leagues. Alexander won 79 times in 158 games – the best win rate of any Bradford manager in charge for at least 65 games.

The chief executive, Ryan Sparks, said Alexander and the assistant manager Chris Lucketti, who has followed him to Preston, delivered “some of the most incredible moments in our recent history”.

They looked set to deliver more, with Bradford top of League One when the Preston opportunity came out of the blue. Alexander told the club he had ambitions to manage in the Championship, but you wonder if he might have achieved that with Bradford had he stayed. Perhaps he realised two promotions in two years would leave them relegation fodder in the Championship, whereas Preston presents a more stable platform. Ultimately, the lure of a club that he once captained – playing 400 games during an eight-year spell from 1999 to 2007 – d in the city where his children were raised proved too strong.

View image in fullscreen Graham Alexander’s sudden departure has left Bradford to rebuild early on in the season. Photograph: Paul Thompson/ProSports/Shutterstock

On forums and social media, fans shared a mixture of sadness, anger and anxiety. Most believe Alexander has left the club stronger, but frustration is shared among a sizeable minority about the timing – less than two months into a season after a summer spent recruiting specifically for his aggressive, direct, high-pressing football. After Jake Beesley headed Bradford into a fourth-minute lead at Reading on Saturday, the 1,118 supporters who made the 400-mile round trip sang about being top of the league, but did not chant for their departed manager once.

Rapid developments in the space of a few weeks leave a huge hole. Bradford now find themselves in unfamiliar territory: it is the first time in 43 years they have lost a manager mid-season, and fans are nervous about the executives’ aptitude for finding a suitable replacement, given the shaky record before landing Alexander.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In the opposition dugout at Reading’s Select Car Leasing Stadium stood one of the favourites to take over. Before the match, Leam Richardson faced questions about whether he was interested. His response – that he would be in the Reading dugout for the match – neatly sidestepped the prospect that he might not be beyond this weekend, though he insisted he had not been contacted.

Nonetheless, Sparks and the sporting director David Sharpe would have been watching closely from the directors’ box to see whether Reading showed signs of a style of football that would fit the framework Alexander built. Plenty makes Richardson a logical candidate. He previously worked with Sharpe, who was chair at Wigan when Richardson was manager, and he has also coached Callum Connolly, in the Bradford starting XI, and Nick Powell, who came on from the bench.

Others are in the frame, including the Plymouth manager Tom Cleverley, the former Manchester United midfielder – a Premier League winner in 2013 – who at 37 has quietly built his managerial reputation these past two years. Udoka Godwin-Malife’s second-half equaliser meant Plymouth moved above Bradford on goal difference. The next appointment is crucial. Getting Alexander so right makes getting it wrong so much more costly.

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start
Sports.content:
Lamine Yamal says he feels like Superman or Spider-Man sometimes, and Spain’s fans are starting to wonder if he just might be. There is something comic book hero about what the teenager is doing right now, some unexplained super power swelling inside him. For the third consecutive game he scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain completed their World Cup homecoming in Oviedo with a 3-1 win over Czechia that leaves them a single point from the Nations League quarter finals already. Spain’s manager, Luis de la Fuente, put it simply: “Lamine Yamal is on course to become a legend.”

And yet in a game which seemed to have been done at half-time, when Spain led 2-0 after Rodrigo Hernandez had added the second and Lamine Yamal was withdrawn, his show seemingly over, the danger returned. Czechia, vastly improved after the break, pulled one back through Jiri Slama on 69 and then were denied a 79th-minute equaliser when Vassilis Fotias, the referee, who rescued Spain, harshly ruled out a Ryan Naderi goal – apparently for a foul on Robin Le Normand as the free-kick that led to it was swung in.

Reduced to 10 men soon after, still furious, Czechia finally fell with two minutes left when Mikel Merino made Spain safe. The seleccion’s first visit to the Carlos Tartiere in 11 years had ended the way they had hoped. Welcomed back as world and European champions once more, they were applauded off as winners again. A night that had begun with Rodri being presented with the World Cup by Santi Cazorla and Juan Mata, academy products at Real Oviedo and members of the generation to which all others would forever be compared, ended with a jeopardy no one anticipated when it started in a way that has become implausibly, absurdly familiar.

Lamine Yamal had scored after 104 seconds at Wembley and 70 in Seville, as Spain defeated England and Croatia. And the silly thing was that here, his goal might have come even sooner. Fifteen seconds in, the first frisson of excitement went round this place as he chased down the goalkeeper and after just fifty-seven Oviedo almost exploded. But, running on to a Dani Olmo pass, Lamine Yamal calmly guided a shot past the goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky … and past the post.

He would just have to wait until the sixth minute was up instead. Playing a quick one-two with Dani Olmo, Lamine Yamal took possession on the top right corner of the area and curled another outrageous shot into the far corner, the ridiculous becoming routine. They had been playing five minutes 20 seconds, another stadium letting out a roar that spoke of delight but also a kind of disbelief. 320 seconds he had been out there, taking him to 494 seconds to score three.

View image in fullscreen Rodri reacts after scoring Spain’s second in Oviedo Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

Spain weren’t hurrying but they were controlling, and the chances were accumulating: by half-time they had taken 13 shots to one, and enjoyed 70% of possession. They had also added a second on 32 minutes. Rodri collected near the centre circle and did something he rarely does. The man who sometimes seems to be walking, effortlessly controlling the game with his mind and without fuss, happy enough to drop the ball off to others to do their thing, went off on a run. Advancing through the midfield, he slotted to Pedri whose return, with the help of a defender’s touch, set him up to shoot high into the net.

Next Lamine Yamal slipped in Alex Baena, denied by Kinsky. A little dinked pass from Baena then found Lamine whose shot, slightly scuffed, went wide. At the break Baena, who had drawn “oohs” with one glorious touch, was withdrawn and so too was Lamine Yamal, his work here done, another show over. The game, on the other hand, was not. That at least was Czechia’s intention and it should probably have been their reward too, the visitors taking a decisive step forward and a degree of control. They also reduced the deficit with 20 minutes to go.

The move began deep: as it progressed up the right and through the middle, Jiri Slama was sprinting to catch up. Adam Hlozek saw him coming and played the ball into his path for him to steer it low and true beyond David Raya.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A first error from Spain’s keeper almost gave Czechia an equaliser when Raya stepped out to play and his misplaced pass only found Ondrej Lingr, and a second error really should have done soon after. But if there was relief for Spain when Lingr’s shot drifted wide of an unguarded goal, it was even greater when the referee ruled out Ryan Nadel’s effort.

For Czechia there was disbelief. Michal Sadilek’s long cross had been headed goalwards by Ladislav Krejci, and Raya, reaching by the bar, could not hold on. The ball dropped on the line, where Nadel nudged it in. The referee, though, had blown. For Santi Denia on the touchline it was hard to take and it was equally difficult not to feel sympathy. All the more when Krejci was soon sent off and then Víctor Muñoz was sent clear, dashed into the area where Kinsky blocked and Merino, forever alive, finished off the festivities.

Sports.title: Bowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North Macedonia
Sports.content:
This was an occasion on which Scotland dare not stumble. By the time Kieron Bowie smashed home a seventh minute opener against a North Macedonia side not without its troubles to seek, it was already clear they would not. Bowie afforded Sébastien Pocognoli his first goal as the Scotland manager. Later, the Belgian had his maiden victory confirmed. Anything else, against such a dismal level of opposition, would have been worthy of significant Scottish embarrassment.

John McGinn’s 22nd goal for his country, coming from the penalty spot, meant the scoreline at least almost reflected Scotland’s dominance. Only Scott McKenna’s late sending off and a failure to notch three, four or five could have irked Pocognoli. Scotland remain alive and kicking in section B1 of the Nations League while aware they will face far, far stiffer challenges. Scotland needed to be professional in North Macedonia and met that task appropriately.

On the occasion of Andy Robertson’s 100th cap, it appeared in the early stages that the Tottenham full-back had been stung by criticism of recent performances in Scotland colours. Robertson marauded forward at will, including inside five minutes where he forced Stole Dimitrievski into a fine save. McGinn, like Robertson, has been the subject of some scathing words. McGinn’s response was as forceful as his teammate.

It was Bowie, though, who afforded Scotland crucial early leeway. Jack Hendry’s red card in the early stages of Tuesday’s loss to Switzerland led to Bowie being withdrawn from the Scotland attack. Pocognoli retained faith in Bowie in Skopje. Bowie had plenty to do when collecting Billy Gilmour’s pass, 25 yards from goal and with two defenders in close proximity. He set himself before firing a terrific left-foot shot beyond the helpless Dimitrievski.

McGinn’s outrageous pass from the right-back position to Robertson, who was operating as a left winger, should have ensured a Scotland second. Robertson opted to shoot and dragged his shot wide when a square pass to Oli McBurnie was the more sensible option. As Ben Gannon-Doak and Bowie missed opportunities, North Macedonia opted for two substitutions with just half an hour played.

View image in fullscreen Kieron Bowie fires Scotland ahead during the first half. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Scotland’s lack of ruthlessness was their only concern. Gannon-Doak was clean through on Dimitrievski within five minutes of the restart but shot tamely at the goalkeeper. Gannon-Doak and Scotland soon believed they had won a penalty, only for the video assistant referee to rightly highlight the Bournemouth player had stood on the foot of Matej Gashtarov rather than vice versa. North Macedonia were clinging on as Bowie tested Dimitrievski from close range.

Officialdom was soon to smile on Scotland. The match referee had originally given a foul against McKenna as the centre-back nodded the ball down towards Bowie from a Scotland corner. Not only was that decision reversed but Bojan Miovski was penalised for blocking Bowie’s shot with an arm. McGinn finished low and hard to close this game as a contest. Only three players have scored more Scotland goals than the Aston Villa midfielder.

Ryan Christie’s arrival at half-time added composure and creativity to the Scotland midfield. He looks the ideal candidate to link play in Pocognoli’s final third. It will be a surprise if Christie does not start when Slovenia visit Glasgow on Tuesday. Angus Gunn, whose position as the Scotland goalkeeper was questioned before this game, had nothing whatsoever of consequence to do.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McKenna will miss Slovenia’s visit after upending Agon Elezi, six minutes from time. The episode was regarded as the denial of an obvious scoring opportunity. Robertson’s slack pass had landed his teammate in bother.

Robertson later admitted he owes McKenna an apology before reflecting on his cap milestone. “It means everything to me and my family,” said the 32-year-old. “It has been an unbelievable journey. It is emotional for me because I love this country and this is a special achievement. I believe I still have a lot to give.”

Handily for Pocognoli, Scotland did not need 11 men to win. McGinn was denied his second of the evening in stoppage time. North Macedonia, who have now gone seven games without scoring a goal, are a desperate lot.

Sports.title: Zigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSL
Sports.content:
Julia Zigiotti Olme’s sixth-minute lob proved enough to earn the Manchester United coach, Eva Olid, a second Women’s Super League victory of the season with a 1-0 home win over Liverpool.

Zigiotti Olme capitalised on a mistake by Liverpool goalkeeper, Khiara Keating, and, despite some late pressure by Gareth Taylor’s side, United held on to make it back-to-back league wins.

After a shaky start under the new head coach, Olid, the Spaniard has now masterminded four consecutive victories in all competitions and United are unbeaten in five matches.

This was United’s 250th match since the team reformed in 2018 and Olid watched her side mark the occasion with the breakthrough after six minutes.

It was a moment to forget for England goalkeeper Keating after her pass out from the back was intercepted by Zigiotti Olme, who composed herself and chipped home in superb fashion.

Liverpool pushed for a leveller and drew a double save from the United goalkeeper, Phallon Tullis-Joyce, midway through the first half. Cornelia Kapocs had a low effort saved by Tullis-Joyce, who got up quickly to deny Beata Olsson on the rebound as well.

United’s Jess Park hit the crossbar before half-time with a left-foot strike from the edge of the box before Keating saved at her near post from Andrea Medina on the rebound. Liverpool’s best chance of an equaliser came 20 minutes from time when Jenna Clark found herself free at a corner but she could not direct her header on target.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The win moves United level with Liverpool in the WSL, with both teams three points off the European places.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel finally solves problem position thanks to six cap England star
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel finally solves problem position thanks to six cap England star

Lewis Hall has more than seized his opportunity to be England's left-back - he deserves a run in Thomas Tuchel's team now.

That is the verdict of Henry Winter on talkSPORT's Sunday Edition, in reaction to the Newcastle defender's impressive form over the break.

3 Hall completed the joint-most dribbles (4) with Jude Bellingham in the 7-0 win over Croatia Credit: AFP

The 22-year-old was a surprise omission from Tuchel's World Cup squad this summer and had to watch the tournament from home.

Lewis Hall revival

Hall paid the price for a downturn in his club form at the back end of last season, which started when he was hooked at half-time of a 2-1 defeat at home to Bournemouth in April.

He was then made an unused substitute for the Magpies' 1-0 loss to Arsenal a week later, and only made a brief cameo in the Premier League match after that - a 3-1 victory over Brighton.

Hall fought his way back into Eddie Howe's XI, but was forced to play out of position at right-back as Dan Burn - who did make the World Cup squad - continued to deputise on the left flank.

The former has now drastically changed his fortunes for both club and country after enjoying a new lease of life under Matthias Jaissle.

Hall earned an England recall after scoring once and registering an assist in five Premier League outings this term.

The ex-Chelsea starlet, who was the subject of considerable transfer interest from Manchester United, is now understood to have signed a new contract at St James' Park.

He has since taken full advantage of Nico O'Reilly's injury to make the England left-back spot his own in the past two matches.

Manchester City's O'Reilly started the first fixture of the break, but endured a howler as he gave away a goal in the 3-2 defeat to Spain.

Hall has since helped England keep successive clean sheets in the victories over Czechia and Croatia, while displaying a strong connection with his former Newcastle teammate Anthony Gordon.

3 Hall and Gordon took their former Newcastle partnership onto the international stage with England Credit: Getty

England's left-back problem

A mixture of fitness and form has meant Hall has been capped just six times for his country and, before this month, had never made an international start under Tuchel.

The Three Lions boss has had significant challenges finding a permanent solution to his first-choice left-back since he took charge.

Shaun Custis told talkSPORT: "One player I think we do agree on about playing left back is Lewis Hall, who of course didn't go to the World Cup.

"I would say I thought Nico O'Reilly had a good World Cup, but Lewis Hall in a kind of orthodox left-back role looked really, really good and has a link-up with Anthony Gordon.

Football journalist Winter added: "Yeah, absolutely. Ever since he was linked with stepping up into the England team, because we've seen the good work that he's sort of done in the England age groups.

3 Hall has now firmly established himself as Tuchel's best left-back option, provided he remains fit Credit: Getty

"England, their starting left-backs: I went through it early this morning," Winter continued.

"[Ben] Chilwell, [Kieran] Trippier, right side, but playing on the left, more so left wing back.

"[Luke] Shaw finally got fit for the Euro final.

"[Levi] Colwill, [Trent] Alexander-Arnold, Lewis, Rico Lewis, now playing left back for the under-21s.

"[Reece] James, [Tino] Livramento, [Myles] Lewis-Skelly, [Djed] Spence and O'Reilly. And I think we should give Lewis Hall a run now."

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel calls up Premier League star as late Nico O’Reilly replacement
Sports.content:
Rico Lewis has been elevated to the England senior squad from the U21s before the clash against Czech Republic.

The 21-year-old has been announced as a late addition after the Three Lions revealed an injury to Nico O'Reilly.

2 Lewis has been brought into the England squad from the U21s following the injury to his club teammate O'Reilly Credit: Getty

O'Reilly has returned to Manchester City after he missed the 2-0 win away to Czechia during the week.

England said that no further replacements were planned, but his City teammate Lewis has joined the squad.

He has not played for the Three Lions since November 2024 when Lee Carsley was the interim head coach.

Lewis has made two appearances for the U21s during the break - a 4-2 win over Kazakhstan and 0-0 draw with Slovakia.

The right-back, who can also play on the opposite side and in midfield, has already won five caps with the England national team.

His debut came in November 2023 when he played in a 1-1 draw with North Macedonia during Euro 2024 qualifying.

Lewis later played four matches across Carsley's interim tenure.

Tuchel selected Lewis Hall as his left-back in their 7-0 thrashing of Croatia on Saturday night.

Myles Lewis-Skelly then replaced him in the 79th minute of the Nations League victory.

At right-back, it was Jarell Quansah who started, with Trent-Alexander Arnold being rested on the bench.

2 Tuchel has opted to bring in a new face ahead of England's fourth and final match of the international break Credit: Getty

England prepare for final test

There has been clear improvement from England since losing 3-2 to Spain at the beginning of the international break.

Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane were on target when they beat ten-man Czechia in Prague.

Both players also netted against Croatia, with Jude Bellingham, Bukayo Saka and Morgan Rogers joining them in an emphatic result.

England will take a large step towards the Nations League quarter-finals with a win over Czechia on Tuesday night, live on talkSPORT.

Spain lead Group A3 with a 100 per cent record from their three matches, and will host England on November 15.

Should Tuchel's side reach the quarter-finals, they will play their two-legged tie in March.

Sports.title: ‘Volatile’ Roberto De Zerbi will not turn Tottenham around as major flaw highlighted
Sports.content:
‘Volatile’ Roberto De Zerbi will not turn Tottenham around as major flaw highlighted

Roberto De Zerbi does not have the credentials to turn the situation around at Tottenham Hotspur.

That's the view of former Premier League striker Charlie Austin, who also believes the squad lacks players who are willing to put effort in for the under-pressure head coach.

3 De Zerbi has managed to win only two points from a possible 15 during the start of his first full season at Spurs Credit: Getty

Spurs, who spent over £300million on transfers in the summer, sit bottom with just two points from a dreary winless run of five matches that includes three defeats and only two goals scored.

They went into the international break off the back of a 3-2 loss at home to Aston Villa, after which De Zerbi described how delicate his squad is.

"It's difficult to explain because, in my career, 14 years as a coach, I've never seen one team like us," he told talkSPORT. "So fragile, so inconsistent."

De Zerbi has already been warned of the sack at Spurs, despite him only taking the job in March after a spell at Marseille.

And Austin believes that the former Shakhtar Donetsk and Brighton boss doesn't have what it takes to transform the club.

Little confidence in De Zerbi at Spurs

Speaking on Saturday Session, Ade Oladipo said: "I look at someone like De Zerbi and I just look at a manager that's quite volatile, quite angry.

"If it's not going well... I don't want to say he walks because he'd rather be pushed, the money he gets if he's pushed is quite big. I just don't see how it works, I just don't see how they turn this around."

"What, in his managerial record, has he done to think he's going to turn this around?" Austin replied.

"Spurs fans, do you have the belief in him, because what has he shown at other clubs that he can turn Spurs around, and get them where you think they should be?

"Because there's no proof in the pudding."

3 Austin has questioned if De Zerbi has what it takes to drag Spurs away from what could be a third consecutive battle against relegation Credit: Getty

"Spurs fans, at the start of the season, if you were to say, 'You're going to spend nearly £300m', you want to be fighting for top four, top six," Oladipo added.

"This is a nightmare what's going on right now, you're rock-bottom!"

Austin then reflected on Spurs' 2-0 home defeat to Newcastle United on matchweek two, and compared De Zerbi's influence to that of his counterpart Matthias Jaissle.

"This is one interesting thing I don't think has been said - you see those Newcastle players?

"They're on their toes, they're ready, they look like they're going to go to war, they're going to run through a brick wall for that manager.

"Tell me the players in that Spurs dressing room that are going to run through a brick wall for him. I'm not seeing it, and I think the proof's in the pudding after these five games."

3 Spurs are only a point off safety, but have shown little to suggest they can launch themselves towards the top of the table Credit: Getty

Who do Spurs play next?

Spurs have had three weeks to mull over their alarming shortcomings in the Premier League due to the international break.

They return on October 10 with a trip to Manchester United, who are also struggling but have at least won a match so far this season.

Coventry City travel to north London nine days later, with clashes in the capital against Chelsea and Crystal Palace following.

Leeds United host them before the final international break of 2026, by which time Spurs will be desperate to be out of the bottom three.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo tipped to return to Portugal team as timeline revealed
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been tipped to return for a last dance with the Portuguese side next year despite his bombshell walkout.

The 41-year-old's international career was thrust into doubt after he departed the Euro 2016 champions' training camp in midweek.

4 Ronaldo is four goals shy of 150 international goals Credit: Getty

Ronaldo reacted furiously to being left an unused substitute for his country for the first time in 18 years during their 2-1 win at Norway.

He subsequently issued a bombshell statement on social media to announce his exit - vowing to 'tell the truth' regarding his decision.

Portuguese journalist Pedro Sepulveda told talkSPORT that Ronaldo's anger stemmed from a belief that he had been lied to about his game time by boss Jorge Jesus.

The latter has since doubled down on his stance regarding the five-time Ballon d'Or winner, which has now escalated into Ronaldo's wife, Georgina Rodriguez, voicing her disapproval in a quickly deleted social media post.

Despite the growing impasse between player and manager, CR7 has still been backed to return to the Portugal fold next year.

Ronaldo tipped to return to Portugal team

Portuguese football journalist Miguel Pereira expects Ronaldo's desire to score his 1000th career goal while playing for his country to prove to be the determining factor in his international U-turn.

He told talkSPORT's Sunday Edition: “The thing is that 21 goals that he needs to score [to reach his 100th].

“He really wanted to score the last one with Portugal the same way that Pelé mounted a show when he scored his 1000th goal, and I think he was aiming to score that goal at the end of the season in a match with Portugal.

“He was expecting to score the 15-20 goals during the season easily with Al Nassr, but he really wanted to throw up a party that celebrates himself, his ego, his history with the national side, and I do still think that is going to happen because, despite everything that we have seen and probably if we had this conversation on the day after the event, it will be more of a difficult situation to assess.

4 Jesus will again be without skipper Ronaldo for Portugal's final Nations League clash against Norway this break Credit: Getty

“But right now I really do think there are bridges being built between Cristiano’s camp, Jesus’ camp, the Portuguese federation is very much interested in having Cristiano because of all the publicity it gets, and I do think that Cristiano will be back for a last dance with the Portuguese side later next year.”

Inside the split in the Portugal camp

Ronaldo, who is the only player to score at six separate World Cups, moved onto 979 goals in total in Al Nassr's 2-1 win against Abha Club.

Two weeks later, he admitted he was happy to do whatever his new Portugal boss Jesus required of him, 'whether that means playing, coming off, coming on, coming off again, or even not playing at all...'

In the wake of his walkout, Bruno Fernandes insisted that there are 'no divisions in the national team' and that Ronaldo remains an icon.

However, Pereira claimed that the Manchester United captain is involved in a split between players who want Ronaldo to stay, and those who want him to retire.

4 Fernandes remains publicly supportive of Ronaldo, as he urged Portugal fans to not be divided by his exit Credit: Getty

He added: “Cristiano is 41 and if you look at Bruno Fernandes, Bernardo Silva, Ruben Dias, they’re almost 30, they’re around 30, so there’s a decade of difference.

“Cristiano has not been playing with the people who played throughout his career for a very long time.

“The only exception was Pepe, who said his goodbyes two years ago. So for him, those players should be in awe of him.

“And for those players who had 10, 11, 12, some of them weren’t even born when he went to Man United and played in Euro 2004 and became an international star.

“They grew up watching him as an idol, but they didn’t get the opportunity to play with him at the national side at his prime, because when they all got there, Cristiano was already in the descending phase of his career.

“So it’s a very tense situation because I do think that the players like Bruno Fernandes, like Bernardo, they think that Portugal should be doing better on the international stage.

4 No player in football history has registered as many international caps [234] or goals [146] as Ronaldo Credit: AFP

“And they do think that Cristiano Ronaldo is not making any favours to them by pressing to play all the time.

“They are happy to have him with him. They are happy to have him helping from the bench, which would be the sound decision for all parties.

“But in the end, the insistence that he has to be all the time the hero of the equation has created a sort of divide in the camp between those older players who think their time is going to pass and they will miss the opportunity to win something big for Portugal.

“And those very younger players who have only known him as an icon, as a global icon.

“So for them, it’s very hard to look at him and see the man, see the football player and see the guy who’s on the pitch.”

Sports.title: EFL boss set for new job just 26 days after being sacked for winless start to season
Sports.content:
EFL boss set for new job just 26 days after being sacked for winless start to season

Michael Duff is set to become the Bradford City manager, talkSPORT understands.

Duff was dismissed by their League One rivals Wycombe Wanderers on September 8 after a winless run of seven in all competitions.

2 Duff is returning to management in League One at Bradford after his dismissal from Wycombe less than a month ago Credit: Getty

The ex-Cheltenham Town, Barnsley, Swansea City and Huddersfield Town boss is now set to land his next job at Valley Parade.

Bradford have had Mark Trueman and Colin Doyle as joint caretaker managers since the end of September.

Graham Alexander left the club after nearly three years in charge to take charge at his former side Preston North End.

The Bantams are second in League One after drawing 1-1 at Reading on Saturday.

They have five wins from eight league matches this season and sit level on points with leaders Plymouth Argyle with a game in hand.

Bradford to battle for promotion with Duff

Duff has extensive experience in League One, having won 163 of his 376 matches in the third tier.

He is a three-time League One Manager of the Month winner, and guided Cheltenham to the 2020/21 League Two title.

The 48-year-old had been charged by the Football Association just a day before his sacking at Wycombe.

Duff allegedly used 'abusive and/or insulting words towards a match official at full-time' of a 2-1 defeat to Sheffield Wednesday.

The incident stemmed from Wycombe having a goal disallowed for handball, whilst they also had a penalty waved off for a similar claim.

2 Duff will take the reins at a Bradford side who are eyeing promotion back to the second tier, 22 years after relegation Credit: Getty

Duff is the latest manager to take a job in League One after Robbie Savage, who has joined Peterborough United.

Bradford are looking to win promotion to the Championship, 22 years after relegation from the second tier.

They finished 23rd in what was then known as the First Division and have played in the bottom two levels of the EFL ever since.

A former Premier League club, Bradford missed out on promotion at the end of last season.

By finishing fourth in League One, they were drawn against Bolton Wanderers in the play-offs.

However, Bradford were beaten 1-0 in each leg and missed out on the final at Wembley Stadium, where Bolton beat Stockport County 4-1.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino highlights why Man City should be excited by wonderkid Cavan Sullivan after making USMNT history
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino highlights why Man City should be excited by wonderkid Cavan Sullivan after making USMNT history

Mauricio Pochettino has heaped praise on Cavan Sullivan after he became the youngest international goalscorer in USMNT history.

At 17 years and five days old, USA's No.8 - who is set to join Manchester City next season - netted in a 3-0 win over Mexico.



3 Sullivan is now the youngest US international goalscorer in history Credit: Getty

Sullivan, who plays for MLS club Philadelphia Union, agreed a deal as a 14-year-old in 2024 to move to the Etihad once he turns 18.

And he underlined why there is so much hype around him with his first USA goal just a week after making his senior international debut.

Sullivan capitalised on a poor pass out from Raúl Rangel to lob the Mexico goalkeeper in the 62nd minute to double the USMNT's lead.



It was a goal that saw him break the record for his country's youngest scorer - which was set only five days ago by teammate Mathis Albert, who at 17 years and 131 days, had scored against Chile on Wednesday.

Pochettino hails US record-breaker Sullivan

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said of Sullivan.



"He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with tremendous quality with the ball in possession.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he needs to be chasing people and recover the ball.



"That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this.

"I think it's fantastic news for USA. I hope that continues in that way."

3 Sullivan - who made his MLS debut at the age of 14 - can officially join Man City next year Credit: Getty

Sullivan reacts to first USMNT goal

The teenager found himself on the scoresheet just five days after his birthday in what was only his third senior international cap.



"These are the moments you dream of when you're a three, four, five or six-year-old," Sullivan said after the game.

"I manifested this moment. Not just these past couple of hours when I found out I was starting, but my whole life."

"I just remember chipping the ball, hoping it didn't hit the crossbar or go over," Sullivan added.

"I was getting nervous when it was in the air, and then everything was a blur."



3 Pochettino's young side thrashed Mexico in Arizona Credit: Getty

Sullivan's chipped goal against Mexico came after another teen, Julian Hall, had opened the scoring for Pochettino's men inside half an hour.

The visitors' misery was compounded when substitute Luis Chavez was shown a red card, with Malik Tillman added a third late on.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino said about the performances of his team's young players.



"I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and, of course, hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo’s wife Georgina Rodriguez quickly deletes fake Sir Alex Ferguson quote slamming Jorge Jesus from Instagram
Sports.content:
Georgina Rodriguez appeared to delete an Instagram story including a fake Sir Alex Ferguson quote about her husband Cristiano Ronaldo.

Ronaldo dramatically left the Portugal camp earlier in the week amid frustration over a lack of minutes in their Nations League campaign.



4 Ronaldo's future with the Portugal national team is up in the air after a falling out with head coach Jesus over minutes

He was an unused substitute for the 2-1 win over Norway in a decision from head coach Jorge Jesus that prompted an emergency meeting with the Portuguese Football Federation.

Jesus has since doubled down on his choice to not bring on Portugal's all-time record goalscorer and appearance maker.

On Instagram, Rodriguez re-posted a quote that was attributed to Ferguson, the legendary Manchester United manager who brought Ronaldo to the Premier League in August 2003.



"If Jorge Jesus knew in his heart that he had no intention of using him, then why did he call him up in the first place?" it translated to.

"To make a point? That’s not authority, that’s insecurity."

Rodriguez then appeared to take aim at Jesus in her caption as she said: "I don't know how this man can bear the name of Christ."



However, she reportedly deleted the post soon after, with the quote from Ferguson turning out to not be real.

What next for Ronaldo and Portugal?

Ronaldo, who is on 146 goals and 234 caps for Portugal, played in the 1-0 win over Wales at the beginning of the international break.



At full-time of the victory over Norway, he stormed down the tunnel and later revealed his departure from the camp.

"In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave the national team, to which I always devoted myself," he explained.

4 Rodriguez deleted the post minutes after sharing on Instagram Credit: Instagram

4 Rodriguez showed her support for Ronaldo by re-posting what she thought was a quote from Ferguson that criticised Jesus Credit: Getty



4 However Ferguson, who managed Ronaldo for 292 matches at United, did not say those comments Credit: Getty - Contributor

Ronaldo was therefore not in the squad for Portugal's 4-2 win away to Denmark, during which Rafael Leao wore the no. 7 shirt.

Portugal are in action against Norway tonight for their final match of the international break.

Five-time Ballon d'Or winner Ronaldo will not be involved once again, and may never play for his country again.



After his exit, the 41-year-old's sister hinted that he has retired from international football.

This is a claim that Portuguese journalist Pedro Sepulveda backed up on talkSPORT.

"The information that I have is, Ronaldo took the decision - he will never, never dress in the Portugal national team jersey again."

Sports.title: Phil Foden and Cole Palmer handed England warning after missing Thomas Tuchel’s squad
Sports.content:
Phil Foden and Cole Palmer are nowhere near starting for England at the moment.

That is the opinion of talkSPORT's Tony Cascarino, who believes the Three Lions' current front four will be really difficult to dislodge.

4 One of Saka, Kane, Gordon or Bellingham was involved in every one of England's seven goals against Croatia Credit: Getty

Thomas Tuchel's preferred attack on paper all started on Saturday night as England hammered Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League.

Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka both netted twice, with Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon also getting on the scoresheet.

Three of that trio also registered assists for other goals, with at least one of the quartet involved in a direct goal contribution for everyone of England's seven in Rijeka.

And talkSPORT's Cascarino argued that those who are not in the picture at the moment have a mammoth task to break back in.

Foden and Palmer handed England warning

Chelsea talisman Palmer was recalled by Thomas Tuchel last month after missing out on the World Cup last summer.

However, the 24-year-old was one of five withdrawals alongside Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento.

Palmer's absence drew the most headlines, having missed three England camps, and withdrew from another two since Tuchel took charge of the national team at the start of 2025.

Foden, meanwhile, has been in and out of Tuchel's England squads - with the German admitting he was unsure of his best position.

Asked about the duo's current international prospects, Cascarino told Weekend Breakfast: "Well, they wouldn't be near starting at the moment.

4 Palmer's England commitment has been called into question Credit: Getty

4 Foden has also been below par compared to his past success at City Credit: Getty

"They might make squads if they play really, really well," Cascarino continued. "I can't see that at the moment.

"There's always injuries. There's always players that can be or a little bit out of form.

"But I look at that four and I think it's gonna be really difficult to dislodge them."

'England are the second-best team in the world'

England put in their best performance under Tuchel in Croatia as they recorded back-to-back wins after losing their first game of the international break to Spain.

Kane became just the fourth England player ever to find the net in six straight away games for his country.

4 Kane is just one game away from equalling Peter Shilton's record appearances [125] for England Credit: Getty

He was one of two England stars handed perfect 10/10 ratings by Adrian Durham as the Three Lions moved up to second behind the World Cup winners in Group C.

On the result as a whole, Cascarino argued: "England were really, really good. It's a bit of a one-off result.

"Don't expect England to go and beat up everybody.

"For me, England are the second-best team in the world at the moment behind Spain; I think England are the second-best team."

Sports.title: Andy Carroll confirms he was sexually assaulted by BBC Fame Academy dance coach Kevin Adams
Sports.content:
Ex-Premier League star Andy Carroll has confirmed he was sexually assaulted by a dance coach on BBC show Fame Academy.

Kevin Adams, now 59, was convicted at Chelmsford Crown Court and sentenced to 20 months in prison in 2023.

He appeared as a coach on the BBC1 talent show in 2002, as well as Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two in 2021.

The ex-Newcastle and Liverpool striker, 37, revealed the name of the 'celebrity mate' who attacked him after being made aware that Adams's name appears in publicly-available court documents.

He told The Sun on Sunday: 'Now that Kevin Adams has been named in court documents as my abuser, I can confirm it.

'Hopefully now I can finally start to put this chapter behind me.

'This had a devastating impact on my life and loved ones.'

Carroll – who now plays for National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge and serves as assistant manager – shared in his new book, Owning It, that he experienced the 'traumatic' assault several years ago but only decided 'at the last minute' to detail it, following lengthy discussions with his publisher.

Ex-Premier League star Andy Carroll has confirmed he was sexually assaulted by Kevin Adams, a dance coach on BBC show Fame Academy

Adams was sentenced to 20 months in prison in 2023 for sexually assaulting Andy Carroll

The footballer revealed he woke up after having a 'few drinks' to find his 'celebrity mate' attempting to give him oral sex.

He wrote in his new book, which was released last month: 'Other things I'd quite like to forget but can't, something happened to me a few years ago that was so traumatic I only decided to include it in this book at the very last minute.'

'I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.'

Carroll explained he was assaulted the evening after a Newcastle United game when Adams invited himself round to watch a boxing match.

Describing their relationship, he wrote: 'He was always asking me and my ex to go out with him and even buys me clothes. He is divorced with kids but I can't shift the feeling he likes me more than a platonic way.

'Whenever I bump into him at parties he is always with young boys.'

He continued: 'I was playing down south somewhere and on my way home this guy texts to ask what I am up to.

'When he texts again to ask if he can come round to watch the boxing with me, my partner tells me to stop pieing him off [putting him off].

'He takes over the kitchen, mixing drinks. I start to feel lightheaded and think has he slipped me something. "Right, time for bed", I say to him, "I'll order you a taxi".

'"Oh no," he says, "I'll stay in the spare room".'

He then claims he awoke to find Adams sexually assaulting him.

The striker, 37, shared in his new book, Owning It, that he experienced the 'traumatic' assault several years ago

Adams appeared as a coach on the BBC's Fame Academy in 2002, as well as Strictly It Takes Two in 2021
