World.title: The Jets might be improved. But they still can’t intercept a pass.
World.content:
Three weeks into the NFL season, after suffering two losses by a combined 10 points, New York Jets coach Aaron Glenn held his index finger and thumb inches apart to illustrate how close he felt his team was to a breakthrough.

“How do we close that gap?” Glenn said Sunday in Detroit, after a loss to the Lions that left the Jets 1-2. “I challenge myself, I challenge the staff, I even challenge the players on let’s identify a couple things that we need to improve on and let’s make sure that we hone in on those things.”

One area isn’t hard to find: No team has been worse at intercepting passes in NFL history than the Jets.

The league’s record-setting interceptionless streak grew to 20 games during New York’s Week 3 loss at Detroit. New York last picked off a pass on Jan. 5, 2025, when it recorded two.

Ever since, the Jets’ defense has faced 608 passes with nary a pick to show for it.

“That’s hard to do,” former NFL coach Jon Gruden said on social media this week. “You would think a ball would ricochet into somebody’s hands.”

During Glenn’s 15-year playing career as a defensive back, interceptions were a specialty. He collected 41, tied for 73rd on the NFL’s all-time list. As the Jets’ streak grew last December, Glenn admitted that “it’s disappointing that we don’t have an interception because coming from what I’ve always played, you expect those things to happen.”

During Glenn’s 15-year playing career as a defensive back, interceptions were a specialty. Focus On Sport / Getty

The Jets know all about turnover. When Glenn was hired in January 2025, after a successful run as Detroit’s defensive coordinator, he was the franchise’s fifth coach since its last winning season in 2015. Glenn told fans to “expect a winning team that you will be proud of.”

But only weeks into his first season, as the Jets staggered to a 3-14 record, the team traded two of its best defensive players in cornerback Sauce Gardner and defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. That defensive fire sale didn’t help a unit that would allow 29.6 points per game, the second most in the league.

When the streak reached 12 games last December, Glenn called it “really puzzling.”

When the streak reached 15 to break the previous record held by the San Francisco 49ers in 2024, Glenn said after a loss to New Orleans: “I hate the fact that we didn’t get an interception.” “But the thing is we got a turnover, and then we got a fourth-down stop, so these are some things we can build on.”

The Jets, seeking to address their defensive shortcomings, signed safety Minkah Fitzpatrick in the offseason. Matt Durisko / AP

Unfortunately for Glenn and the Jets, turnovers of any variety have been hard to come by. Since the start of the 2025 season, New York has forced a league-low six turnovers in 20 games. The next-lowest team produced 13. The league leader in that span, Chicago, has 39.

New York set out to address its defensive shortcomings in the offseason. In its secondary, it signed safety Minkah Fitzpatrick, drafted a safety and cornerback and signed Nahshon Wright, whose five interceptions last season helped Chicago pick off a league best 23.

Yes, Wright had heard of the streak.

“I’m on social media, so I’ve seen it, but try not to pay it any mind,” Wright said in June. But “honestly, don’t think it’s been brought up at all” during team meetings, he added.

“I think 2025 was 2025, and I think we’re trying to turn over a new leaf,” Wright said.

Three games in, the Jets’ rank in the league’s upper half by allowing just 20.3 points per game.

Yet the streak lives on.

Relief could be on the way. In three weeks, New York faces New England, whose quarterback Drake Maye has thrown 10 interceptions in his last seven games.

“We’re right here and our guys know it,” Glenn said, his fingers inches apart. “It’s this gap right here that we got to close. And we’re fighting our asses off to close that gap, and we will.”

World.title: Taylor Swift pops into ‘SNL’ to joke around with host Dakota Johnson
World.content:
Pop music icon Taylor Swift made a surprise appearance on “Saturday Night Live,” joining her friend and the episode’s host, Dakota Johnson, for some laughs.

Swift appeared onstage during Johnson’s opening monologue to address her role as the movie star’s “literal therapist,” in Johnson’s words.

00:49 Taylor Swift makes surprise appearance during 'SNL' 00:00 00:00

“I’m not your therapist, actually,” Swift said. “You just show up once a week at my house with an empty bottle of wine and ask if I want some.”

Johnson agreed: “Yeah, well, I have manners.”

Swift continued to describe a typical evening for the two.

“You flop on my couch and overshare, and every so often I just say, ‘Damn, that’s crazy,’” Swift said.

Johnson, who has been a marquee presence in the “Fifty Shades” movie franchise, stars in the new movie “Verity” and appears in the new music video for Swift’s “Patient Zero.” She said Swift’s characterization of her role hosting the actor at home seems to describe “therapist.”

But Swift had more to say about their nights.

“And then I go, ‘Oh, it’s getting late, I should probably go to bed,’ and then you say—”

Johnson chimed in: “Sleepover — yay!”

Their wine sessions end, Swift said, not with a sleepover, but with Pedialyte and a ride home via Swift’s security detail.

Swift made another appearance during the curtain call, bringing out a blue and white cake for Johnson, who turned 37 on Sunday.

“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

Turnstile was the episode’s musical guest.

World.title: Transcript: Sen. Mark Kelly on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Arizona Senator Mark Kelly. He joins us from Charleston, South Carolina, where he is campaigning for his fellow Democrats. Good morning to you, Senator.

SEN. MARK KELLY: Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Our CBS polling shows that Democrats have reason to be optimistic about taking the House, but how much harder will it be in the Senate?

SEN. KELLY: Well, Margaret, there is a lot of energy in the states I've been to recently. Whether it's Ohio or Iowa, Kansas, Georgia, now here in South Carolina, I think we have real opportunities in a lot of places. But also, I mean, this could be, you know, close elections in many of these states. But I'll tell you this: people are frustrated and they're fed up with Washington D.C. right now, and they know that this president is not addressing, you know, any of the needs that affect them and their families. I mean, the cost of living is way too high. The price of everything just keeps going up, and people can't afford their lives.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump announced Friday he's going to send $90 payments to 20 million older Americans this month, Medicare Part B enrollees. That's in addition to sending $500 in terms of checks to ACA refunds to a million people. Also said if Republicans win, then he'll send everyone $5000 bucks. Do you support any of that? And what exactly is the Democratic message on lowering costs for Americans?

SEN. KELLY: Well, certainly trying to help some working class people and seniors on a fixed income. But you got to remember, this is a guy that gave a big tax cut to the wealthiest Americans, to billionaires and millionaires, and then to partially pay for it, he's kicking people off of their health care, off of Medicaid. He's taking food benefits away from people that are having a hard time affording food, even children, in order to to help out his family and his friends, so I think people should see this for what it is, especially this $5,000 payment, if Republicans maintain control of the House and the Senate. I mean, this is just a- a payoff, and he's trying to buy votes. I mean, are you surprised with this president, who, in my view, is the most corrupt occupant of the Oval Office ever? I'm not surprised, but it's not right.

MARGARET BRENNAN 09:02:11

But what is the affirmative Democratic message here, other than we're not him?

SEN. KELLY: Well, we're going to lower costs for the American people.

MARGARET BRENNAN: How?

SEN. KELLY: We've got to win the House and, or the Senate. Well- well, how will we do this? I have legislation with- with Chris Van Hollen. We've got to get Republicans on board. It raises taxes for people who make over a million dollars a year in income, and it provides tax cuts for people, individuals, and even couples up to- who make up to about $160,000 a year- that's some relief. Ending this war in Iran that he started without a- any kind of a strategic goal or a plan, has jacked up prices for the American people- ending that would help. Getting this tariff policy reversed, these ridiculous tariffs that have also jacked up prices. The American people pay this. For some reason the president thinks that foreign countries are paying for these tariffs, that is not true. So there are things, a lot of things, we can and will do once we win back the House and, or the Senate.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Republicans have pulled funding, as I understand it, from North Carolina's Senate race, they've redirected it out to Kansas. Not typically a place a Republican would have to spend money to- to keep an advantage, but what seats specifically are you optimistic you can turn blue?

SEN. KELLY: Well, there are a lot of them. I spent some time in Kansas with Adam Hamilton. He's a pastor. He's- he's a great guy. He is the right person for Kansas. He understands what Kansans are dealing with. Josh Turek in Iowa, similar kind of situation where that's a very winnable race. Mary Peltola in Alaska, Troy Jackson in Maine, Sherrod Brown in Ohio. I'm gonna do an event, you know, here today with Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Yeah, I understand it's South Carolina, but she is a pediatrician, she's working incredibly hard, she's raising the resources to be successful. And then there are the House races. Admiral Nancy Lacore, I did an event with her yesterday here in South Carolina- can be critical to Democrats winning back the House of Representatives. She's a- she's a three-star admiral, a naval aviator like myself, who was fired by Pete Hegseth early in this administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, a number of Senate Republicans have expressed some concern about Secretary Hegseth's firing. He also announced this past week he's going to cut by 20% the number of generals and admirals. He says in order to try to change the culture and what the media calls a purge, he says is simply a matter of accountability. Do you have any insight into who he will be targeting in these cuts, and if Democrats take some control, do you have any ability to stop it?

SEN. KELLY: Well, he often fires people because of the color of their skin or because they're women. He also seems to be looking for--

MARGARET BRENNAN: He would deny that.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --loyal- of course, he would deny that. I think anybody would deny that. But it's pretty obvious when you have a list of seven people who don't promote from one-star to two-star, and five of them are either black or women. It's pretty obvious. Also, right off the bat, firing CQ Brown without giving any reason, without any particular reason why one of the most qualified professional aviators, but a four-star general, chief of staff of the Air Force, fired. Lisa Francetti--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. KELLY: --the chief of naval operations, fired. The commandant of the Coast Guard, also a woman, was fired. The- the list goes on, Margaret. This is a pattern with this Secretary of Defense, and it's damaging our readiness. And when you hurt readiness, it means that all of us, everybody watching the show, you and your family, are less safe because we have the most unqualified Secretary of Defense we've ever had in this country's history.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he gave a big speech this past week. The secretary said that every military branch has hit its recruiting targets ahead of the end of the year. He also argues military sexual assaults are on the decline. I know they have been on the decline for a few years now, but what is your response to his argument that he's doing something right?

SEN. KELLY: Well, he's doing very little right. Remember, Margaret, this is a guy that gets on a stage in front of the senior leadership of the U.S. military and runs around talking about killing people and lethality, and that the rules of engagement- I'm going to paraphrase, but he talks about how he wants to eliminate or reduce the rules of engagement, and you see the consequences of that in Iran. And he- his plan is what we went into Iran with, and he has bombed or attacked over 15,000 targets, depleting our munition supply. This thing has been a disaster because the Secretary of Defense has no idea what he's doing--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --and to some extent, he's also a yes- a yes-man for the president. Nobody seems to want to push back against this president, who--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --who I- I think is checked out from even trying to do this job.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

SEN. MARK KELLY: Got us into another war with- without- without a plan and without explaining- explaining to the American people what are we going to get out of this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, I'm sorry to cut you off, but I'm out of time, I have to leave it there. Thank you. We'll be right back.

World.title: Iowa approves pricey foreign-owned steel plant project in swing district
World.content:
"Stop the Steal" — or rather, steel — has an entirely new meaning for some Iowa voters in 2026.

Protesters at the Iowa statehouse Friday carried signs reading "No Steel Steal!" as lawmakers raced through a one-day special session to award Mesabi Metallics $1.36 billion over 10 years in tax incentives for a new steel plant in Lee County. Mesabi Metallics is owned by the Indian conglomerate Essar Group.

The Iowa House passed it 75-17, the Senate 28-19. Gov. Kim Reynolds signed it into law Friday night.

It comes after President Trump's Monday announcement that the largest steel plant in U.S. history would be built in Iowa. Mr. Trump promised the $15 billion steel plant would create 1,750 permanent jobs and roughly 6,000 construction jobs.

The announcement caught many in the state by surprise, including lawmakers who would be counted on to approve the tax incentives. When Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters at the White House "the deal is done" on Monday, lawmakers in Iowa still hadn't received details to review or timing for the special session held Friday.

Opponents of the $1.36 billion in incentives are largely supporters of the project, but they wanted more safeguards and guarantees of public benefits. The incentives roughly amount to about $777,000 in credits per permanent job over 10 years, a hefty price tag by any standards. Proponents argue that math leaves out roughly 6,000 construction jobs — which opponents point out are all temporary.

And at a time when many of Iowa's farmers are struggling, more than a billion dollars in tax credits for an India-based conglomerate is a hard sell for some.

(L-R) Mesabi Metallics President and CEO Joe Broking, Chairman Rewant Ruia, board member and Essar Capital director Ravi Ruia, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright listen as President Trump speaks in the Oval Office on Sept. 28, 2026. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

Why Iowa?

There are places in the U.S. synonymous with steel, but Iowa has never been one of them. The state has a couple scrap-fed steel mills — a small fraction of the size Mesabi is promising — and no commercial iron ore. Mesabi Metallics is based in Minnesota, and its argument is that Iowa is conveniently downriver on the Mississippi.

But Iowa has something that Minnesota doesn't: One of the most tightly contested congressional races in the nation. The state also has close Senate and governor's races.

The plant's proposed location is Iowa's 1st Congressional District, where Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending one of the GOP's most at-risk seats. In 2024, the recount had her ahead of Democrat Christina Bohannan by just 798 votes. Sabato's Crystal Ball just moved the race from "toss up" to "leans Democratic" before the steel announcement.

Bankruptcy and broken promises

Mesabi and Essar Group have a long history of missed deadlines and unfulfilled job promises. In 2008, Essar announced a $1.6 billion iron ore mine and steel plant in Nashwauk, Minnesota, home to some of the country's richest iron ore deposits. It promised more than 700 permanent jobs. But the steel mill plans were dropped in 2015. Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy in 2016, was renamed Mesabi Metallics under new owners, and later came back under Essar's control.

The India-based Essar has recueved billions of dollars in loans from the Russian state-owned bank VTB, according to local media. CBS News has not independently verified these reports.

File: Workers at an Essar Steel Ltd. facility near Pune, Maharashtra, India, in 2018. Dhiraj Singh / Bloomberg via Getty Images

There are also echoes of other regional mega-projects gone awry. No one in the Hawkeye state wants the steel plant to be the 2026 version of Foxconn. In 2017, President Trump and Foxconn promised a $10 billion plant and create 13,000 jobs in the battleground state of Wisconsin. By 2021, the plan was scaled back to $672 million and 1,454 jobs. Republican Gov. Scott Walker championed the deal — and lost his 2018 reelection bid as public support for it soured.

Tricky politics

On Friday, Republican State Senator Kevin Alons told the Des Moines Register that lawmakers needed more time ahead of Friday's vote.

"The political extortion is breathtaking," he said.

But in the end, he voted for it.

State Sen. Dave Sires, also a Republican, voted no on the project, complaining the process was rushed. State Senator Dan Dawson, another Republican, called it the "largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa's history." And Republican State Senator Jeff Taylor raised concerns that the state was already in a real budget crunch.

Taylor was swapped off the Senate Ways and Means Committee at the last minute to ensure the bill would pass committee. It passed 10-8, with 6 Republican State Senators voting against the bill.

It's a careful political calculus for Republicans in the Iowa Senate. They're trying to thread a fine needle: follow their leaders and bring home jobs, without being seen as rushing more than a billion dollars in taxpayer money to a foreign-owned company with no time for review.

File photo of the Iowa State Capitol building in Des Moines. Zhang Fengguo/Xinhua via Getty Images

Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has campaigned against corporate handouts, made a case for supporting the bill. He called the idea of an Iowa steel plant a "once in a lifetime" exception.

Democrats have been navigating tricky political territory as well, trying not to oppose job creation while pushing back on the rush to issue nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks before early voting starts on Oct. 14. Democratic nominee Rob Sand, currently the state auditor, called the steel plant "a promising idea for Lee County" but wanted to see more details first.

"You look at these data center deals that this administration has done over the last few years and we gave away the farm," Sand said. "I want to make sure this is a real opportunity, but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced."

Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner said she wants good-paying jobs and investments in the state but balked at the rapid timeline that left taxpayers out of the conversation.

"If we were doing this the right way, we would be waiting until after the election," she told CBS News on Saturday. "We have a responsibility to our taxpayers to make sure our hard-earned dollars are well spent. If it's a good deal now, it will be a good deal in January when due diligence has been done."

Meanwhile, State Representative Dave Jacoby, a Democrat, voted yes, "with the hope that this plan is real," while still cautioning, "today is not a ribbon cutting."

The ribbon cutting, if it comes, is years away. The tax credits don't kick in until the plant is running, and Mesabi says that won't be before 2030. Iowans begin to cast their votes in just a few days. So the question on the ballot isn't whether Iowa gets a steel mill. It's whether voters believe it will — and if $1.36 billion was the right price to pay for it.

Studies have shown that people who hold grudges have greater levels of cardiovascular trouble, and higher levels of depression and anxiety. But according to one survey, four out of five adults harbor some lingering resentment towards others, sometimes over the smallest of reasons. Correspondent Susan Spencer talks with experts about why some people can maintain grudges for years; how holding grudges can be counterproductive; and what it takes to have forgiveness overcome lingering ill will.

In 1964 writer Ken Kesey and his band of "Merry Pranksters" rode a 1939 school bus, named "Furthur," across the country, fueled by music, alcohol and LSD. It became an icon of the burgeoning counterculture movement, and a symbol of liberation. But in the decades since it has fallen into a rusted state. World.title: Michael Lewis on "Blockers": Profiling government workers confronted by DOGE
World.content:
Author Michael Lewis believes most Americans do not know that civil servants in the federal government take an oath of office. "I didn't know," he said. "I don't think I knew even after I'd written a whole book about them. So, I assume not."

"I, ___, do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion; and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter. So help me God."

– Civil Service Oath of Office, U.S. Code § 3331.

Michael Lewis, author of "Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State." CBS News

For Lewis, pursuing knowledge is a calling. He has conjured up bestsellers and box-office hits out of deep-dives into data, from Wall Street ("The Big Short," "Liar's Poker"), to the NFL ("The Blind Side"), to baseball ("Moneyball"). Lewis likes to challenge assumptions, including those about the occupants of Washington's federal buildings – government workers, sometimes derided as faceless bureaucrats. "That's the stereotype," Lewis said.

He believes people who distrust government don't understand what it does: "They don't like the government, or they think they don't like the government. They think they don't trust the government, but in fact they just don't know how much they trust the government. They take the trust for granted. Every time they drink water out of the tap, or fly on an airplane, or eat food, or put dollars in their bank account, they're trusting the government.

"And I thought, who are these people? We live in a society that is largely focused on personal ambition. It's a free market capitalist society and people are really interested in money and fame," he said. "To find people who are some of the most valuable people on the planet, who are interested in neither money nor fame, but have found some other purpose, who have a sense of public spirit, who are not selfish – and the government is a place where you can really do stuff that makes a difference, and it attracts these people. And thank God for them."

W.W. Norton & Co.

Lewis' latest book, "Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State" (to be published Oct. 6), profiles workers confronted by DOGE – the Department of Government Efficiency, championed by President Trump and his mega-donor, billionaire Elon Musk.

Musk promised massive savings of "at least $2 trillion" from cutting government, and targeted government workers he called "blockers."

"It's an insult," Lewis said. "A 'blocker' is a word that Elon Musk likes to toss around. He told all the 20-year-olds who came to work for him in DOGE to go find the 'blockers,' the people who would get in the way of doing what he wanted to do, and get rid of them."

Elon Musk holds aloft a chainsaw during the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), in Oxon Hill, Maryland, February 20, 2025. SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images

"I was blocking people from violating the law"

A central character in "Blockers" is Kathleen Walters. "I mean, if you want to say I was blocking people from violating the law, then I guess that's a fair term," she said.

Once a top executive in the Internal Revenue Service, Walters was responsible for protecting taxpayers' personal information. She said, of President Trump's executive order creating DOGE, "Executive orders are normal. And as long as they're lawful, our job is to administer them."

So, she wasn't trying to block executive orders? "No, no, no," Walters said. "I've been in the government for every administration since Bush, so I've worked for them all, and that's normal."

But after DOGE's arrival, nothing seemed normal to Walters. She says Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) began asking for information on undocumented workers who had been paying taxes to the U.S. Treasury. ICE would later specify in a memo they were only seeking information on individuals under criminal investigation. "They came out and said, 'Well, we're thinking of approximately, probably seven million [people],'" Walter said. "And I questioned in my head, I did not believe there could be seven million active criminal investigations going on."

Walters says she resisted for months, and ultimately she resigned. "After I left, the IRS handed over the data," she said.

The Treasury Department's Inspector General has since found that ICE did not meet "safeguarding standards"; and federal courts have ruled that privacy rights were violated. [The Trump administration continues to argue it has acted within the law.]

Former IRS executive Kathleen Walters was responsible for protecting taxpayers' personal information. She resigned after resisting ICE's demands for the Treasury Department's information on undocumented taxpayers. CBS News

Walters said, after trying to stop what she saw as a violation of the law, she left the IRS when she felt she could not stop it. Asked how tough of a choice that was for her, she replied, "In one respect, it was a simple choice. But simple isn't easy always, and it was challenging, because I'd been there almost 20 years. I was 23 days shy of qualifying for early retirement. And I'm a mom to an elementary-aged child."

Walters described her daughter's reaction to watching her mother struggle: "Well, she's a smart little kid, and I told her high level that I was asked to violate the law and I couldn't do it, so I left. And then later that week, I went into my bedroom and there was a $10 bill on my shelf. And she said, 'Mom, I just wanna help out at home.' And she wouldn't let me give it back, so I had to sneak it – hopefully she doesn't see this! – had to sneak it into her piggy bank again. And so, I know she's proud and she understands why I did what I did. And so again, I can sleep at night well knowing that my decision was the right one even though it was hard."

As for DOGE, there is intense debate over its impact. The Government Accountability Office, an independent nonpartisan federal watchdog, found in an audit that DOGE overstated its savings or could not verify them, and fell far short of its goals.

The Trump administration's Office of Personnel Management (OPM), which manages the federal workforce, praised DOGE in a statement to "Sunday Morning":

"The President is committed to stewardship of taxpayer dollars in delivering services to the American people," said Scott Kupor, director, Office of Personnel Management. "DOGE was a catalyst for these reforms that are now being institutionalized through the Vice President's leadership on fraud, waste and abuse and OPM's and OMB's cross-government focus on organizational efficiency."

But for Michael Lewis, this story is about more than numbers or budgets; it's about people. And he would like people who are skeptical of government to read this book: "Oh my God, yes. That would be my favorite reader."

Asked why some people might not see government as he sees it, Lewis replied, "Because they haven't spent the time to get to know it. This isn't knowledge I was born with. If we don't see that these people who don't make any money, and aren't famous, and don't like to talk about what they do but are working their tails off for us have value for our society, we're in trouble. And that's the message that I'm trying to get across."

Story produced by Ed Forgotson. Editor: Jason Schmidt.

World.title: Alan Alda on fighting Parkinson's with laughter
World.content:
Is it even possible to choose a favorite Alan Alda character? How about Senator Arnold Vinick on "The West Wing"? Or lawyer Jack Burroughs in "The Four Seasons"? And, of course, "Hawkeye" Pierce, the sarcastic Korean War combat surgeon, on "M*A*S*H"?

For his work on "M*A*S*H," which aired on CBS for 11 seasons beginning in 1972, Alda won five of his six Emmy Awards for acting, writing and directing.

"I have doctors coming up to me on the street all the time telling me that seeing me in the show made them want to become a doctor," Alda said. "Not a single one said it made them want to become an actor!"

Actor, writer and director Alan Alda. CBS News

Long before playing Pierce, Alda – now 90 – was on the other side of the stethoscope. As a seven-year-old he had polio, before there was a vaccine. "My father had just gotten a huge part in a movie, playing George Gershwin," he said. "And about a week after he started shooting, I got polio. And he and my mother had to administer the treatment, which was almost-scalding hot packs of wool on every limb. So, they were practically torturing their kid. I remember thinking it was hard on them."

As a boy, Alda studied his father Robert Alda's performances in vaudeville and burlesque, and also on Broadway, when Robert starred in the original cast of "Guys and Dolls." "I stood in the wings and watched that every Saturday," Alan said.

But Lady Luck dealt the family a difficult hand. His mother, Joan, a former beauty pageant winner, was complicated. "My mother was mentally ill, had schizophrenia and was paranoid," Alda said. "So sometimes the communication would be about the crack in the wall was where they had a camera taking pictures of us. I think that contributed a lot to tools I later had, trying to figure out what's real and what's not real. I had to pick one reality and try to stick with that. … It made me more observant. And I think it even helped – I'm just realizing this for the first time in this moment! – I think it made me a little more curious."

He's been especially curious about human connection, something he fostered on the set of "M*A*S*H." "We didn't go back to our dressing rooms between shots," he said. "It was just, like, an hour or two hours where they light the new set, we stayed in our chairs in a circle and made fun of one another and laughed. And that connection that we had, we carried with us onto the set."

Which had a huge impact on viewers. More than 100 million people watched the series' final episode. "They think 106. But I think it was probably more. Not that I'm greedy!" he laughed.

For years, Alda has been concerned that scientists and health care professionals often use technical language that's hard for the general public to understand. With that in mind, in 2009, New York's Stony Brook University founded the Alan Alda Center for Communicating Science. Back in 2013, our own Tracy Smith watched Alda use methods from his own acting experience, including improvisation.

He said, "Improvisation really puts you in touch with the other person, and that's when I realized the value of connection."

Connecting is one of Alan Alda's superpowers. Since 2018, on his podcast "Clear+Vivid," he's been interviewing guests like Paul McCartney, Michael J. Fox, Noah Wyle, and recently, Joy Behar.

Alan Alda interviews comedian Joy Behar for his podcast, "Clear+Vivid." CBS News

To Alda, connecting with people means being clear and honest, which is why he will openly discuss his Parkinson's disease. "I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."

At the time he had no other symptoms: "I had no twitch, no tremor, no problems with my voice."

He was 79. A few years later, Alda decided to reveal the diagnosis. "I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."

There's currently no cure for the neurological disorder, but there are medications and other treatments. "I don't let Parkinson's define me," he said. "It's not who I am. It's just a hobby."

Which brings us to what Alda considers the importance of a sense of humor: "Very important, because the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

But what is funny about Parkinson's? "I'll be at the computer keyboard writing an email, and Dr. Parkinson is moving my hand all over the screen. I have the mouse, and he's eliminating things and he's deleting things that I need," Alda laughed. "Once in a while I get frustrated. But I find what makes me laugh about it, and then I go tell Arlene. Laughing first brought us together. We were invited to dinner at a friend's house. And Arlene was sitting at one end of the table, and I was sitting at the other end. And I noticed that she was laughing at my jokes. So already I was smitten. In March, we'll be married 70 years."

They have three daughters and eight grandchildren.

Alan Alda says he feels really good, even if Arlene has to help button his shirt in the morning, which he admitted he hated. "Of course, I feel that from time to time," Alda said. "I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: what haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"
