Yet the primary task of a law enforcement system is prevention. I consider it a total failure.

Another example is the Committee for Youth and Sports. Yes, youth and sports are important to develop, but in my view, the state’s paramount priority must be education.

Georgi Berzenia: Isn’t there a deputy prime minister for education?

Adgur Ardzinba: No, there is a minister. Following that logic, I believe the Minister of Education should be the First Deputy Prime Minister. That is how priorities are defined. What happens instead? This might sound a bit dry, but it’s practical reality: the Minister of Education has to go to her deputy prime minister, and then together they must go to the prime minister.

Georgi Berzenia: Setting aside those details, what do you dislike on a global level?

Adgur Ardzinba: There are no clear priorities, and I see no development plan. A year ago, the president issued specific directives that were widely publicized. I have a report here on the execution of those directives, and the majority remain unfulfilled, while another portion was completed merely on paper. In my view, even this short one-year timeframe has been squandered. I have always said, and will continue to say, that we need a development plan, reforms, and defined priorities.

Today, the long-term priority must be education and enlightenment. Enormous focus needs to be directed here.

On a positive note in this regard, I recently spoke with the Minister of Education, and she shared very good news that you may have heard as well: the Primakov School in Moscow Oblast—in my view, one of the best schools in Russia, if not the best, because it combines modern foreign educational methods with our Soviet system—is a unique, elite institution in the Odintsovo District. They have agreed to build a branch here in the city of Sukhum. That is fantastic news. Furthermore, from what I gathered in my conversation with the minister, this school will adhere to those high standards while accommodating our local features and mentality—incorporating Abkhazian culture, language, and customs. That is precisely what we have all dreamed of. A state that fails to cultivate its own elite is doomed to failure, so this is a wonderful development. I hope it materializes quickly.

Otherwise, regarding general priorities, they remain absent.

Finally, regarding agriculture: there is talk about the “Year of the Village”—the current year was declared the Year of the Village, which is a good idea in itself. But what is happening in practice? Once again, decorative steps are taken that won’t yield long-term results. Agriculture requires a multi-year strategy. Without science, there is nothing to be done in agriculture or anywhere else.

How can we talk about developing the agricultural sector when the Institute of Agriculture is left to fend for itself? It’s simply impossible.

Adgur Ardzinba: I will also tell you something else that, in my view, illustrates this lack of systemic structure. Returning to the Ministry of Agriculture, the Ministry of Economy ought to be involved in these processes. We speak about cultivating certain crops. Yet there is such a concept as marketing, market analysis. Now, the potential target market is the Russian Federation, correct? Accordingly, economists should be tasked with analyzing the Russian Federation market to identify which crops imported into Russia—potentially adjacent ones, if working with agricultural institutes—could realistically grow in Abkhazia and yield the maximum added value. Do you understand what I am saying? Moreover, benchmarking needs to be conducted. Benchmarking means evaluating competitors. We would look foolish if, for instance, we were to visit a megamarket in Moscow, spot a particular variety of persimmon, and say, “Oh, how wonderful, a new persimmon, it costs 600 rubles, let’s plant it.” We will look foolish if, at that very same moment, tens of thousands of hectares had already been planted in Azerbaijan three or four years prior. And by the time we gather ourselves to enter the market, that product will already be right here. In other words, that is competitor analysis. It is an engaging, creative effort. That is precisely the work I do not see happening.

Handing out a million rubles to every village based on mere intuition—sure, that is better than nothing. Of course, anyone listening right now might say, “Well, at least something is being done there, it’s better than nothing.” I agree, that is also fine. But if we are talking about systemic work aimed at serious, long-term results, then without new technologies, without new crops, and without new approaches to the economy, there will be no serious results.

Georgi Berzenia: Right now, you are speaking about agriculture, providing specific examples, discussing what you dislike about education, and so forth. I just caught myself thinking how much I miss the debate format we used to have. The kind that existed previously. You are addressing each sphere now. We cannot and should not discuss every single detail. However, it seems to me it would be right if opposition figures today could sit in a single studio, for example, and discuss every topic with government representatives, where they could defend their point of view while the opposition presented theirs. Overall, that would have a positive effect.

Adgur Ardzinba: It would not have an effect, and I will explain why.

Alkhas Gagulia: We used to have that.

Adgur Ardzinba: If you recall our famous broadcasts where we debated energy policy and debated apartments. On energy, do you remember our discussions on Afganskaya’s airwaves? Where we were told, “That’s it, you were worrying over nothing.” In the end, everything we warned about occurred in the worst possible form, without them even acknowledging it.

Georgi Berzenia: That was un-systemic back then.

Adgur Ardzinba: A real application would follow the results of such a debate. But what if the state apparatus, the executive branch, completely refuses to see public opinion?

Georgi Berzenia: We are talking about a new stage now. We are talking about a new stage. I am asking what you like and what you dislike, and you are delving into details that we, as laypeople in this matter…

Alkhas Gagulia: I would like to add something regarding agriculture. There is a program in the Ministry of Agriculture…

Adgur Ardzinba: There is a subsidy program within… It is a good, decent program. But that program is insufficient. There is no science in that program. If there is no science, there will be no result. That is what I am trying to convey. First, there is no consistent, systemic work. Second, simply distributing money—yes, that too is better than nothing when people’s costs are subsidized. That is also good. But my concern lies elsewhere. I want a maximum long-term effect to be achieved. Without making our countryside competitive, we will not make this sector profitable. Consequently, we will always have a negative balance sheet. Why do we speak so much about the countryside? Because it is a cornerstone. We all say that the countryside is the cradle of our traditions. It is not merely an economic category; it is also a social, political, and cultural one. That is why we dedicate so much attention to it here.

Georgi Berzenia: Yes. That is a very interesting topic. A topic about which, truly, a great deal can be said. I simply brought it up because I asked you to provide an overall assessment. It feels to me as though, judging by what you are saying, you concentrate heavily on certain critical moments and specific details, whereas you haven’t touched upon the positive aspects at all.

Adgur Ardzinba: No.

Georgi Berzenia: You simply stated that the president does not divide people, broadly speaking, and that was essentially all.

Adgur Ardzinba: I focused on certain details because I… I articulated the premise that work is being conducted in an un-systemic manner, and I provided a series of examples. I could cite a great many such examples.

Georgi Berzenia: Perhaps you could name some positive aspects after all? For instance, even with agriculture, my association—I understand a deep conversation is one thing, but as an example—they opened a dairy plant in the Ochamchira District. That is agriculture, and as I understand it, it is a high-tech facility.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, that is the agro-industrial complex.

Georgi Berzenia: Which also engages local villagers, provides jobs, and allows us to consume local produce, even if the raw material isn’t local. Just to give such an example, broadly speaking. And if we look back at the past, Abkhazia previously had much less to take pride in and showcase. Today, there are also things that can be highlighted.

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, an economic forum was held. A rather interesting event. A great number of people came to Abkhazia—top officials, bureaucrats, ministers. I cannot recall anything like it since the time of recognition. We hosted an economic forum. That is wonderful. We introduced many people to the country and drew attention, including media coverage. Following that attention, when an ordinary Russian citizen watches the news on the Rossiya television channel and sees several federal ministers and the First Deputy Chief of the Presidential Administration in Abkhazia discussing the development of this country’s economy, a desire arises in some to go and do business there. Upon arriving here, he does not see the Deputy Chief of Staff or our president. He goes to the Technical Inventory Bureau, he goes to the district administration. And there, he gets caught in such a whirlpool that, God willing, he might escape from it only after several years. That is what needs to be addressed immediately.

Alkhas Gagulia: Back in 2024, you stated that relations between Russia and Abkhazia were at their lowest point. A couple of years—a year and a half—have passed since then. How do you assess these relations now?

Adgur Ardzinba: The most interesting part is that the very same thing was voiced on March 7 of this year during a concert here in our capital. A representative of the Presidential Administration, one of the department heads, spoke there. I cannot recall his surname at the moment, but he was a rather pleasant person. He mentioned that…

Georgi Berzenia: The Russian Administration?

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, the Russian Administration. He mentioned that our relations had cooled somewhat over the recent period, but that we need to fix all of this. By the way, I was pleasantly surprised by such a sober assessment. However, a whole host of factors contributed to that state of affairs. Without speaking of oneself, one cannot speak of others. To a greater extent, it was the activity of the ex-president, who attempted to resolve his own economic matters and tried to smear everyone opposing him as pro-Western and so forth. Naturally, when an official of such stature writes briefing notes on his fellow citizens, that information is examined at a serious level, to say the least. And when the head of state visits a district and tells people that their pensions will stop being paid unless we vote for the Pitsunda state dacha, and so on—how can that not reflect in the minds and hearts of the people? Those errors were committed. Now, over this period of time, I see that in Russia, with the arrival of a new team of individuals responsible for our direction, they have drawn the correct conclusions from what occurred previously. Once again, as we discussed above, far from everything has been rectified yet.

Alkhas Gagulia: And what specifically needs to be rectified?

Adgur Ardzinba: The persecution of citizens. That is what causes harm. On the whole, however, the agenda has shifted. All those harmful initiatives have receded into the background. Incidentally, they themselves acknowledge that those were not beneficial. Right now, as I see it, very broad opportunities are open before us, before our small country. By the way, similar opportunities were open to us right after recognition, during that flourishing period. Later, to some extent, everything experienced a slight decline, but now there is such a surge. We cited the economic forum as an example. Several federal ministers, governors, heads of republics, and the First Deputy Chief of Staff came to Abkhazia, to the city of Sukhum, to discuss the development of our economy. Those are enormous opportunities. In other words, a tremendous amount of attention is being paid to our relatively small country in this regard. And that ought to be capitalized on in the best sense. I do not see that same level of initiative from our side—from the authorized bodies and structures—to make full use of all this. Because such chances may not present themselves again in the future. Russia is a vast country. It is navigating a very complex period right now. Further escalation could follow, and people will focus on solving their own problems. Why should they travel with entire government delegations to Abkhazia, sit with us here in Sukhum, and try to help us figure out how to make our lives better? That is primarily our own responsibility. There is transportation infrastructure—the train has started running, work is underway at the border, the airport has begun operations. Most importantly, what genuinely pleases me is that very positive information about Abkhazia is circulating across the Russian Federation’s media space. There is outright promotion of Abkhazia as a resort destination. That provides a huge impetus for the growth of our tourism sector and the overall economy.

Yet, returning to those matters: when such promotion is taking place and top officials are calling Abkhazia an ally, prioritizing it, we must work proactively right here on the ground. Do you understand? Rather than simply trailing behind, picking up scattered initiatives, and failing to carry even those through to completion. That is what I am concerned about. And I will tell you why I am so concerned, Georgi. Alkhas, 2008 brought recognition. Following that, starting in 2010, Abkhazia was provided with financial assistance. Substantial financial assistance—exceeding one billion dollars. However, those funds dissolved across various projects. Back then, too, there were no clear priorities or plans. As a result, where we had the opportunity to completely resolve the situation—at least within the energy sector, given the possibilities that opened up at the time—we would not be facing these problems today. We would not be talking about a deficit today had we utilized that opportunity wisely back then. Therefore, I simply do not want history to repeat itself this time, which is why I am so concerned. The fact that there is a warming of relations, a mutual understanding, and that people are frankly paying far more attention to Abkhazia than before—that is a reality. That is a fact. The other question is what we ourselves are capable of proposing and what we ourselves are capable of achieving; that is where the problem lies.

Georgi Berzenia: And what role do you see for Sergei Vladimirovich Kiriyenko?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, I already noted above that he is a person… First of all, let us be frank. Every official possesses a certain degree of capability. There are a number of leaders in the Russian Federation, and they all have differing levels of capability. As far as I can see, this individual possesses quite substantial capabilities. Within the scope of those capabilities, he is doing everything possible to assist Abkhazia and to involve as many federal leaders in this work as possible. Let us recall—we live here after all—past periods. Let us recall the period from 2020 to 2025. How many federal leaders visited Abkhazia over those five years? The Minister of Sports came. The Minister of Economic Development came a couple of times. To my memory, that was all. Yet now, in a span of a year and a half… Again, when these people visit, our officials and top leaders have the opportunity to sit down over a cup of coffee and discuss specific issues. I assure you, I know the situation in Russia: not every governor or regional leader has the opportunity to sit down with ministers and drink coffee whenever they wish. Yet we have that opportunity. And all of this is thanks to this new team.

At the same time, I cannot fail to mention our people here. Had our people not stood up in 2024—and throughout the period leading up to November 2024—to defend their core interests, none of this would exist. Absolutely no changes would have occurred. Had that entire proposed agenda passed quietly and silently, no one would have given us a second thought. The Abkhazian people courageously defended their interests, their core interests. And the Abkhazian people—who, by the way, are exceptionally friendly toward the Russian people—stood up, protected their interests, and drew attention to themselves. That commands respect, and I observe that respect coming from these leaders.

Georgi Berzenia: Speaking of the development of relations between Abkhazia and Russia, I have also recalled with several guests in this studio the 2014 treaty. It was signed more than 12 years ago now, back in 2014, so ten years have passed. Political events were taking place back then as well, yet no review was conducted, no outcomes were summarized, and it was extended automatically. How would you evaluate these 10 to 12 years of that treaty, and where do we go from here? Does it require refinement, or is a new treaty or a new phase in relations with Russia needed?

Adgur Ardzinba: The treaty is quite thoroughly developed. Moreover, when it was adopted, as you remember, there was a certain degree of opposition here as well. The very people who in the recent past accused us of being pro-Western and anti-Russian were themselves blocking the border to prevent that treaty from being signed, to speak specifically. But the treaty itself became a foundational document following the 2008–2009 post-recognition agreements. Coming after them in 2014, it served as a foundational document that touched upon economic forms of interaction, social matters, and other areas.

Of course, time moves forward. It keeps moving forward. And I am certain that we have not fully realized the potential of that agreement. There is still much to discuss within it. However, Georgi, we can also recall other agreements. We have a whole host of agreements that remain unfulfilled. If we return to defense and security, within the framework of signed agreements regarding joint efforts to strengthen the state border along the Ingur River, nothing has been done—neither from our side nor from the side of the Russian Federation. Furthermore, matters regarding the joint group of forces in that direction remain poorly developed.

If we speak about the economy, we have an agreement on the mutual protection of investments. In that direction, too, we need to look at what genuinely concerns investors from the Russian Federation—not those who sought to create a tailored, exclusive climate for themselves, but regular businesspeople. And they do not necessarily have to be billionaires; they can simply be people capable of investing 10 million rubles, or 20 million rubles, conditionally speaking. We need to communicate with them and examine the rules and standards that exist in the Russian Federation. They could be implemented here. For instance, the public service system in the Russian Federation—the MFC system, “My Documents”—which several years ago was announced to start operating here, has seen nothing done. That system is objectively considered one of the best and most efficient in the world. So, please, let us integrate it here.

Georgi Berzenia: In Russia, which…

Adgur Ardzinba: Yes, in Russia. We all use it, as we are Russian citizens. It is an incredibly convenient system. As for tax administration, one of the most effective systems has been established in Russia. That is a reality; you can see it in all surveys. Russia has specific criteria for evaluating the investment attractiveness of various regions. At the St. Petersburg forum every year, if memory serves, a specific rating and classification is assigned to one region or another. That, too, is a positive thing. Well, as I mentioned above, the entire local economy resides in the districts.

Georgi Berzenia: In September, elections to the State Duma will take place in the Russian Federation. These elections will also be held on the territory of Abkhazia, allowing citizens of Abkhazia who are simultaneously citizens of Russia to participate. What is your view on the significance of these elections for citizens of Abkhazia, and should citizens take part in them?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, look, posters reading “Abkhazia’s Voice Matters to Russia” are currently hanging all across Abkhazia, right? If Russia, which has provided us with such immense support all these years, sends a message that our voice matters to Russia, is it really that difficult to go and vote if it truly is so important? And it is important, first of all because we are almost all Russian citizens, for the most part, when provided with such an opportunity… I remember in past periods there were issues with the number of polling stations and so forth; as far as I can see, it is being approached more systematically now. Of course, people should go and vote. Why not? It isn’t that difficult to do. If people say it is important, and one can demonstrate civic engagement in that sense, I believe one should go and vote.

As for whom to vote for, that is a separate question. I do not have the right to engage in campaigning here right now, but one should also look at the retrospective. Various political forces have existed throughout Abkhazia’s history; you are younger, but Alkhas and I remember the blockade times and the post-blockade period when the new team came in. We must also understand for ourselves which political force is minded to help Abkhazia, and which political force recognized Abkhazia’s independence. These are different teams with different viewpoints, so here too, I believe our choice is straightforward; we simply need to understand it all.

Alkhas Gagulia: We have spoken at length about relations with Russia—it is our strategic partner—but an event took place in the Turkish parliament recently. People view it in different ways, and opinions vary. In my view, it is a very landmark event when 30% of the Turkish parliament raised the issue of ending the isolation of Abkhazia. Recognition was not on the table, and there were differing opinions regarding the motives behind that speech. It turned out to be primarily the opposition party. But anticipating your answer, I would say—as one Chinese sage or general secretary put it—it doesn’t matter what color the cat is, as long as it catches mice. What is your view on this initiative, and what, in your opinion, actually happened there?

Adgur Ardzinba: Alkhas, your late relative Gennady Leonidovich Gagulia once told me a story about cats and mice too. He said that when you try to play political cat-and-mouse, make sure that you are not the mouse. Yes, of course, it is a positive signal. Incidentally, our organization issued a statement on this matter. The signal itself is positive, even if, as some note, it represents an element of internal political struggle to attract our large diaspora and secure votes. Even if that is the case, it remains positive. It shows the role and significance of our diaspora, which we utilize very weakly—and not only in Turkey. But that is a vast, separate topic. Therefore, it is a positive signal, and that is how we assess it. However, actions and deeds matter most. Words are fine—we approve and welcome them—but deeds are what count. Russia went ahead in 2008 and established diplomatic relations with Abkhazia, recognizing our independence. Those are real actions.

Alkhas Gagulia: There was a caveat there, if I am not mistaken, that there was no question of any recognition.

Adgur Ardzinba: When politicians speak about it to attract votes, again, it is still a good thing that the topic of Abkhazia and ending its isolation is being discussed, forming a positive agenda to attract votes. But I very much hope it will not remain mere words.

Alkhas Gagulia: Adgur Ardzinba of 2024 and Adgur Ardzinba of 2026. What advice would you give today to the person you were back then?

Adgur Ardzinba: That is a good question; I hadn’t thought about it. That is actually too short a time frame. I wouldn’t have changed much.

Georgi Berzenia: Significant events have occurred. First of all, the elections. They surely brought about some…

Alkhas Gagulia: Takeaways from the elections. What mistakes were made?

Adgur Ardzinba: Look, yes, of course, we made a whole host of mistakes. But it is not a given that if I had told my former self to avoid those mistakes, other mistakes wouldn’t have been made instead. Mistakes are part of any process.

Alkhas Gagulia: Nor is it a given that he would have listened?

Adgur Ardzinba: I will tell you this: it has been a rather interesting period of time. I consider myself fortunate. I feel fortunate in that—and I say this sincerely—the Abkhazian people, a portion of the Abkhazian people, and a substantial portion at that, entrusted me with this responsible mission. That is a great, immense honor. There is nothing above that, Alkhas. Any obstacles or hurdles are minor by comparison. When serving your people is not mere rhetoric but a reality—if done sincerely and from the heart—there are no obstacles. That is the highest honor.

Therefore, what would I advise my former self? I would advise him not to doubt, because a person always experiences doubt when faced with immense difficulties. Alkhas, we speak about this so casually now. For instance, when people entered the building in November 2024, some said they shouldn’t have entered, while others asked what would have happened had they not entered. Someone had to take responsibility. Other politicians were there; we were all together. While we achieved a certain goal on the one hand, on the other hand, during all those days—and I slept inside that building for three nights to ensure people wouldn’t clash with one another—it was a difficult period, followed by the election process.

Naturally, any person experiences doubt. Our recent presidential elections were unique—they were engaging and event-filled. But those elections were particularly interesting because our team faced such a formidable, serious opponent equipped with vast resources. When you have a very serious opponent, it mobilizes you immensely. I assure you, had that not been the case, the elections might have turned out very dull. Instead, they unfolded the way they did.

Alkhas Gagulia: To be honest, I dream of dull elections for all branches of power.

Adgur Ardzinba: We are speaking about personality and perception right now. Yes, I too dream that our country, like Switzerland, could have dull elections. But if we talk about what existed then versus now, it has been a very fascinating period during which I came to respect my people even more. I feel immense pride in being part of this nation—small in numbers perhaps, but possessing a grand spirit and a vast heart—a people that cannot be intimidated, no matter how hard anyone tries. And with such a spirit in our hearts, we are bound for success.

I am absolutely certain that we will succeed in everything. All those misunderstandings and unpleasantries, including those in relations between Abkhazia and Russia, are entirely surmountable. I am confident that… Look, we are talking about certain incidents right now, and they are indeed unpleasant. Yet we had a period when the entire country was under a blockade for six to seven years. We were under a blockade—the whole country. Now we are talking about a few individuals being unable to travel, whereas back then it was the entire country.

Even then… Vladislav Grigorievich Ardzinba—for which I will always be grateful to him—was a great, exceptionally wise man. He always maintained that we must orient ourselves toward a union with the Russian Federation; that time would pass, people would change, and understanding would arrive. And he was right. Although you remember, Alkhas, how many different proposals there were, delegation after delegation, yet we did not deviate from our path. All these misunderstandings taking place are simply part of the process. Just as there are mistakes on our side, there are mistakes on theirs as well.

I am confident that everything will be fine. The main thing is to remain vigilant. Times are very dangerous. I will repeat it endlessly: defense and security.

Alkhas Gagulia: Well, I want to say thank you for today’s broadcast, for coming to join us so that a thorough conversation could take place on all the questions that interested us. The only thing I would like to add, of course, is that while we spoke about priority tasks—about defense and education—all of this stems from a single overarching priority: our sovereignty and our independence. If that serves as the main guidepost, everything else is meant to serve that exact priority. There are no other options. You mentioned my age twenty times today; in any case, my generation accepts nothing less. We lost far too many people for this land, and it is thanks to them that we stand on this land today. That is what I want to say to every single politician, without exception, on both sides. Thank you for the broadcast and for coming. I look forward to our next meetings.

Adgur Ardzinba: Thank you, friends. I believe that while our conversation was lengthy, it was candid, and we answered a number of questions. If we missed anything, I think we will have another opportunity to meet. As for sovereignty, Alkhas, that concerns not only your generation. The younger generation and the youth—the rising generation with whom I interact—see no other path across all generations than the building of an independent, sovereign Abkhazian state in Abkhazia. If anyone thinks otherwise, that would be their mistake. All of us have stood, are standing, and will continue to stand for this. Fundamentally, our entire conversation has been dedicated to strengthening that sovereignty, to making our state less vulnerable.

Today, our state is vulnerable. Let us be frank. To eliminate these weak points, we need systemic work, the establishment of priorities, societal consolidation, and defense to preserve our territory, as well as our language—which you raised, Georgi—and our culture. All of this is vital, because knowing a language alone does not make you Abkhaz. The upcoming parliamentary elections are also crucial; the quality and substantive content of that body are of great importance. All of this, as was rightly stated, Alkhas, exists in order to preserve, strengthen, and pass down. Thank you.

Georgi Berzenia: Thank you for an engaging conversation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

World.title: Azerbaijan beat Lithuania in Nations League
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 4. The Azerbaijan national football team defeated Lithuania in the third-round match of Group D2 of the 2026/27 UEFA Nations League.

The match at Palms Sports Arena in Baku ended 1-0 in favor of the hosts.

The only goal was scored in the 25th minute. Abdullah Haibullayev found the back of the net to put the national team ahead.

In the 51st minute, Haibullayev received a second yellow card and could have been sent off. However, after VAR intervention, the referee reviewed the decision and overturned the dismissal.

The score remained unchanged in the second half, and Azerbaijan secured its first victory in the current Nations League campaign, taking its tally to five points and moving into first place. Lithuania dropped to second with four points. Liechtenstein are third with one point.

It should be recalled that the teams drew 1-1 in their previous match in Lithuania. Azerbaijan will play its next match in the tournament away against Liechtenstein on November 13.

World.title: Verstappen ends drought with win, Russell retires with five laps to go
World.content:
Max Verstappen's long wait for another Formula 1 race win is finally over, and the drivers' championship race might be over, too.

Verstappen took his first victory of an often-frustrating year for the four-time champion at Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Sunday.

A retirement for George Russell handed a huge title boost to Kimi Antonelli.

Verstappen was leading from Antonelli and Russell behind the safety car with five laps to go when Russell suddenly pulled over in his Mercedes.

Antonelli further stretched his lead over teammate Russell from 66 points to 84, with seven races remaining on the schedule, including those in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Mercedes told Antonelli over the radio it appeared Russell had suffered a power unit problem.

Antonelli finished second and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton passed Verstappen's Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar for third.

Four-time champion Verstappen had not won since the final race of last season, but upgrades to his Red Bull car made him competitive again in Malaysia this week.

"Good job guys, wow," he told the team over the radio, thanking them for a "fantastic weekend".

Delays for rain and software issues

The first wet-weather race for F1 in 2026 started more than 90 minutes later than planned.

The start was first delayed 40 minutes for heavy rain, then suspended again when cars had apparent software problems on the formation lap.

When it finally did get underway, Verstappen was slow off the line and lost places to Antonelli and Russell. He chased down Russell and then got past Antonelli in a side-by-side fight after a safety-car restart.

After Verstappen took the win, he had another small delay before hearing his anthem. Crowd chants filled an awkward silence as Verstappen waited on the top step of the podium before the Dutch anthem finally began.

The race was relocated because of the Iran war, becoming F1's first event at the Sepang circuit in Malaysia since 2017.

Ferrari recovers from early blunders

Hamilton's third place capped a remarkable recovery for the seven-time champion and ends a run of five races without a podium finish for the Italian team.

It seemed almost impossible early in the race as Hamilton, and his teammate Charles Leclerc, were near the back of the pack. Ferrari had gambled on sending them to the start on dry-weather tyres as the track began to dry after rain, causing Hamilton to drop from second to near the back.

Leclerc also overtook Hadjar late on to follow Hamilton into fourth place, as Hadjar ended up fifth. Oscar Piastri was sixth for McLaren after a punchy late battle with Liam Lawson of Racing Bulls, who was seventh after racing near the front at the start.

Fernando Alonso was eighth in Aston Martin's best result of the season, Lando Norris ninth after going off-track and losing places, with Lawson's teammate Arvid Lindblad 10th.

AP

World.title: Newcastle's magic NRL premiership tilt ends in defeat, pride and honour
World.content:
In the end, the final mountain proved too high for Newcastle to climb even if they got a good, long look at the summit.

The Knights gave that mountain everything they had and then a little bit more. Until the very end of their 19-18 loss to the Roosters, they never stopped fighting for their miracle.

It was perhaps the cruellest fate of all, to come so far, to do so much, to play so proud and strong, only to fall short by the narrowest margin possible, to come so close to defying the odds one last time.

The Newcastle hordes were sent home dissappointed. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It is easy, when you’re not of a Novocastrian persuasion, to say they lost no admirers, or that they did themselves proud.

Such words are of cold comfort in the quiet void of defeat, and truth doesn’t always cut through the pain.

But it is still important to say it, because there is still honour to be had, and they earned that with their effort and their toughness and their ability to save at least half a dozen tries.

When Kalyn Ponga went the length of the field midway through the first half, completing a play where he started out making a try-saving tackle on Billy Smith in one corner and finished scoring in the other, running about as far as a person can on a rugby league field, it felt like the moment that would last forever from this match.

Ponga's try was a magnificent grand final moment. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gut-busting effort to cover so much ground in the first place, the long journey towards the very heart of the Newcastle fans who had turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter and the fact that the Knights had, yet again, scored from a thousand miles out gave a feeling that maybe this really was destiny.

Those tries from the ends of the Earth have been Newcastle’s hammer of the gods through this finals run, but in the second half the Roosters gave them no Earth to run from because the Tricolours were as inevitable as the tide through the middle of the field.

They tried to starve the Knights to death and just about did it.

Newcastle had six tackles inside the opposition all night compared to 51 for the Roosters as the newly minted premiers went direct and they did it hard and often.

Newcastle's fans tried to will their team home. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It was a game plan made for Clive Churchill Medal winner James Tedesco as he put up a run metres total that may as well have been the distance back to Newcastle itself.

But he was not alone. Naufahu Whyte showed why he is a man of iron and Spencer Leniu ran like he didn’t care what happened to him next.

They bent the Knights up like pretzels, so much so that the underdogs could have started charging rent inside their own 20. But Newcastle would not break.

The tries they did concede came from one of those Mark Nawaqanitawase efforts that only he could do, a Billy Smith barge-over that came after three try-saving efforts in as many plays beforehand and a wicked bounce off the posts that fell just right for Tedesco to fire a ball out for Nawqanitawase’s second.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The Knights barely kept it together when they held up Lindsay Collins and stopped Robert Toia from going in, but they did.

They were hanging on by a thread, but they used that thread to haul themselves back into it.

They were rewarded for their courage under fire when they wound up for their last big punch, because it landed true. Greg Marzhew’s late try was just about the only chance they had in the entire second half.

By rights, they shouldn’t have been near. But by rights they shouldn’t have been here at all. Defeat was in the air but they refused to breathe until the siren.

This time, almost 30 years after their first premiership, the Darren Albert moment did not come for them. There are no premiership heroes but that doesn’t mean there aren’t heroes still.

Francis Manuleleua, in just his 15th NRL game, was magnificent in defeat, scoring a try in the first half after running a line that was a piece of rugby league art.

He and backrow partner Jermaine McEwan call themselves “The Bruise Crew” and they’ll have as many as they dished out while prop Cody Hopwood made 46 tackles which is more than his age (20) and his number of NRL appearances (18) combined.

Ponga was their best and not just for his try. His defence was stellar; he threw himself into collisions and refused to give up on anything.

The captain – and he is the captain now, when once he was just the bloke who led them onto the field – was close to tears at the end of the match.

His people left the ground in the horrible daze that comes only when the greatest prize has been ripped from your hands, but they could not have asked for more from their team.

The Knights could have played better – a couple of passes were loose and some of their work under the high ball wasn’t great — but it is difficult to imagine a way they could have fought harder.

They cannot take a premiership trophy home, but they can take plenty of hope.

The future might feel like it doesn’t matter now but between the young forwards, the return of Dylan Brown, Trey Mooney, Jacob Saifiti and Phoenix Crossland combined with Newcastle, it makes it very unlikely they’ll have to wait another 25 years for another shot.

But you never know. Each chance at a premiership can be the last.

That’s why it’s important, if they were fated to go down, that they did it like this, why men of steel and coal had to leave a little piece of themselves out there.

Their city will be proud of them. Their people will be proud of them.

There is little glory in defeat, but after a game like that, there is no shame either.

World.title: Tedesco wins Churchill Medal after leading Roosters to grand final win
World.content:
James Tedesco has won the Clive Churchill Medal as player of the match in the 2026 NRL grand final as his Sydney Roosters defeated the Newcastle Knights 19-18.

The Roosters skipper completed his set of the game's greatest individual awards as the Roosters won their first men's premiership since 2019.

Roosters win NRL premiership A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The honour will sit alongside Tedesco's Wally Lewis Medal, earnt in the 2019 State of Origin series, and his Dally M gongs from 2019 and 2025.

Tedesco was instrumental for the Roosters on Sunday evening, pulling off two clutch kick receptions when the match was on the line in the final few minutes.

He churned through 385 run metres, the most by a player in any NRL finals match.

A constantly elusive presence, the fullback racked up 14 tackle breaks and was close to faultless under the high ball.

Tedesco was a back-to-back premiership winner with the Roosters in 2018 and 2019, but this title marks his first time captaining a side to a grand final win.

James Tedesco led the Roosters by example in a player-of-the-match performance. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"So proud of this team, what a game," Tedesco said immediately after the match.

"Honestly, it felt like we had them on the ropes, but they just kept coming back.

"There's so many great attacking players and that game could've gone either way."

Retired Parramatta great Peter Sterling presented Tedesco with the medal, 40 years after becoming the first winner of the iconic award.

"To our boys, to our supporters that came out supported us all year, thank you," Tedesco said on stage.

AAP

World.title: Play School presenter Alister Smart dies aged 90
World.content:
Australian actor and beloved Play School presenter Alister Smart has died aged 90 at his home in East Gippsland, Victoria.

Mr Smart died on September 9, but the news of his death has only recently become public.

Born in Adelaide on November 30, 1935, and raised in part around Nowra, Mr Smart left school and joined his family's piano restoration business.

He soon developed an interest in pianos which prompted him to study at Sydney's Conservatorium of Music.

He later turned to acting.

Veteran Play School presenter and actor Alister Smart has died aged 90. (ABC TV)

He started his career in theatre in the early 1950s and appeared in television productions in Australia and the UK from the 1950s until the mid-1990s.

His credits include Number 96, Skippy, The Sullivans, Sons and Daughters, A Country Practice and Neighbours.

Mr Smart featured on the very first episode of ABC's Play School which aired in 1966.

He would continue to appear as a presenter on Play School, now Australia's longest running children's show, for the next 27 years.

World.title: Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters prevailed in a classic grand final, holding off a spirited Newcastle Knights outfit who threatened to complete one of the great premiership wins.

In a match where the Roosters statistically dominated, but the Knights managed to lead in the second half, these were the key moments from the 2026 NRL grand final.

1. Early bomb hits the Spidercam wire

There are no shortage of camera angles in professional sport these days.

One of rugby league's favourite angles used by the Nine Network in its broadcasts is Spidercam, an overhead view of the action.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The camera is hoisted by high wires well above the action, but not high enough for a bomb from Sydney Roosters five-eighth Daly Cherry-Evans.

The Roosters' playmaker, in his final NRL match, hoisted an early kick that hit the cable holding Spidercam.

Newcastle Knights fullback Kalyn Ponga was cool under pressure as the trajectory of the footy quickly changed and plummeted to the turf.

Ponga adjusted well and caught the footy. A knock-on would have been a major controversy.

2. Teddy fumes as Ponga avoids sin-bin for high shot

Ponga was always going to be a central figure at Stadium Australia, and he was involved in an incident of some controversy midway through the first half.

Ponga may well have been fortunate to avoid a spell in the sin bin. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The Knights captain may well have been lucky to not have been sent to the sin bin when his shoulder collected the head of Victor Radley in the tackle.

The Roosters were clearly unhappy with the tackle, with Naufahu Whyte scuffling with Jermaine McEwan.

But referee Adam Gee and the bunker opted against sending Ponga to the bin.

James Tedesco (left) believed opposing captain Kalyn Ponga (right) should have been sent to the sin bin in the first half. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"If we're consistent with the rules, that's a shoulder to the head," Roosters captain James Tedesco was heard on the Nine broadcast telling Gee.

"It's been a sin bin all year."

It would prove to be a massive call.

3. From dislocated elbow to first GF try in five weeks

Francis Manuleleua dislocated his elbow in Newcastle's final home and away match on August 30.

Just 35 days later, the 22-year-old from Auckland scored the first try of the NRL grand final.

The Roosters seemed to have the better of the early momentum, but it was the Knights who scored first, with Manuleleua running through a huge gap to score under the posts.

The Roosters' defenders appeared to be focused on Ponga who was running wide, but a beautiful pass from Fletcher Sharpe hit Manuleleua in full stride for the opening score.

"It looked way too easy – didn't look like there was anything wrong … absolutely brilliant football, outstanding pass, but it all looked too easy for the Knights," two-time premiership winner Luke Lewis said on the ABC Sport call.

The Roosters would have felt hard done by. The Knights were able to get into an attacking position off the back of a penalty against prop Lindsay Collins for a head-high tackle.

Replays appeared to show Collins made contact with the chest and shoulder of Newcastle's Mat Croker, but ref Adam Gee ruled in favour of the Knights.

4. Ponga runs 95 metres as Knights fans go wild

If the Knights were going to win the grand final, Ponga needed to have a big impact.

He made a diving effort midway through the first half to knock the ball out of the grasp of Mark Nawaqanitawase, denying a certain Roosters try.

A few minutes later, Ponga produced a moment of individual brilliance.

He stood at marker near the right touchline, then sprinted across the field as the Roosters put up a kick to the opposite corner.

It was another Roosters' kick for Nawaqanitawase who tapped the ball back for a teammate.

But Ponga, who had just sprinted across the field, swooped on the bouncing ball and ran 95 metres in the opposite direction as Knights fans went wild at Stadium Australia.

Ponga was chased all the way by Cherry-Evans, but the Newcastle number one had enough speed, and just enough energy, to score and help the Knights take a 12-0 lead.

5. Nawaqanitawase with one more for the highlight reel

Few have made such an impact on the NRL in two seasons as Sydney Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

The walking highlight reel has produced many memorable moments since joining the competition, with Sunday's NRL grand final the final chapter of his NRL career (for now) before he returns to rugby union.

Nawaqanitawase got the Roosters on the scoreboard in the grand final, showing off his soccer skills for the Tricolours' opening try.

As the ball bounced to him on the final play, Nawaqanitawase decided to kick the ball towards the in-goal.

It was not the smoothest display of soccer skills, coming off his right shin, then trapped under his right boot, before then being kicked forward with his left foot.

Nawaqanitawase was able to keep his feet, and sprinted to the goal-line to score a grand final try and get the Roosters back into the contest.

6. DCE shows his experience with a clutch field goal

No off-season switch was more high-profile than Daly Cherry-Evans leaving Manly for the Sydney Roosters.

But the former Queensland State of Origin captain had his decision vindicated by guiding the Roosters to the grand final.

And it was Cherry-Evans who put the Roosters in a match-winning position with 10 minutes to play.

Holding a six-point lead after second-half tries to Billy Smith and Nawaqanitawase, Cherry-Evans showed off his years of experience to slot a smartly taken field goal, giving the Roosters a vital seven-point lead.

How vital that one point would turn out to be.

7. Marzhew scores and Knights fall one-point short

The Newcastle Knights never gave up. They fought until the final second as they tried to become the first team since the 1930s to go from wooden-spoon to premiers.

Down by seven points with less than four minutes to play, the Knights showed a never-say-die attitude that will define their 2026 campaign.

Left winger Greg Marzhew broke two tackles to score in the corner, giving the Knights a glimmer of hope.

Sandon Smith, who was a Rooster before moving to the Knights, landed the most fantastic conversion from the sideline to reduce the deficit to just one point.

The Knights had two more uses with the ball, but could not get close enough to the Roosters' goal-line to snatch the premiership.

World.title: Eight-bed outback hospital costs $67m, three times original budget
World.content:
WA's Health Minister Meredith Hammat has defended the cost of a new eight-bed outback hospital, which has reached practical completion at a cost of $67.6 million, or more than three times the original budget from 2015.

Construction of the new Laverton Hospital began last year to replace the aging facility, which was built in 1973 for the northern Goldfields community, about 950 kilometres north-east of Perth.

WA Premier Roger Cook and Ms Hammat flew into Laverton on Sunday to announce practical completion of the new hospital, which includes a 24-hour, telehealth-equipped emergency department.

The hospital also has flexible care beds, specialist facilities for visiting clinicians as well as outpatient services for community health, mental health, and space for an onsite private GP clinic.

Pat Hill (left) with Ali Kent, Roger Cook and Meredith Hammat at the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

When pressed on the cost of the build, Ms Hammat said it reflected the reality of delivering major infrastructure in remote locations.

"What we see with all our health infrastructure projects, particularly in regional Western Australia, is that it's always challenging to deliver them," she said.

"But we are absolutely committed to deliver the health services and the health infrastructure that people need.

"A look at the old Laverton Hospital confirms the reality that this facility is incredibly needed for the community, and we've taken the opportunity to co-locate services like community health, child health, as well as a GP service."

The entrance to the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

Long road to new hospital

The Shire of Laverton has been lobbying for a hospital redevelopment for more than a decade.

The former Liberal-National government promised a $19.5 million redevelopment of Laverton Hospital in 2015, before funding was cut by WA Labor when it came to power in 2017.

Mr Cook, who was minister for health in 2017, said the new Laverton Hospital would open its doors to patients from Wednesday.

"I'm a previous health minister and this project has been on the books for a long time," he said.

"It's with a sense of deep relief but great pride that we're now in a position to welcome patients here."

Roger Cook on a visit to the new Laverton Hospital. (ABC Goldfields: Nick Ward)

After years of delays, the state government announced in February 2025, on the eve of the March election that year, that ADCO Constructions had won the tender to build the new hospital at a cost of $37.5 million.

Minister for Health Infrastructure John Carey confirmed in October last year those costs had blown out to $63.6 million.

The final cost of $67.6 million includes a federal government contribution of $16.8 million towards the project.

Hospital vital for Outback Way

Shire of Laverton president Pat Hill said the new hospital would be vital in emergencies due to the projected increase in traffic once the Outback Way was sealed.

The Outback Way stretches 2,719km through central Australia, from Laverton in Western Australia's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland, and it is hoped the final stretch can be sealed by 2032.

"It's been on the cards for over 15 years … I know they've had challenges but it's completed and it's a beautiful, first class facility," he said.

"With the development of the Outback Way and more people coming through these isolated, remote communities, and also the mining interests around Laverton, we've got over 7,500 people working fly-in, fly-out, so it's great to see governments working to put infrastructure into these remote areas."

The Outback Way in WA begins at Laverton with the Great Central Road. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Hill has been chairman of the Outback Highway Development Commission since 1997 and is set to attend its annual general meeting in Alice Springs on Tuesday.

Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent echoed Mr Hill's sentiments on the hospital's importance due to the Outback Way.

"Laverton is in the middle of the desert, it's a long way from the Perth CBD and to have a hospital of this standard delivered here … it's been a difficult journey because we were putting tenders out and couldn't get builders that could do it," she said.

"When the Outback Way goes through, this hospital is going to become even more important."

World.title: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute for Jai Arrow
World.content:
Tens of thousands of fans have united by making the arrow gesture during a moving pre-grand final lap by the NRL's Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who were both diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.

Arrow, who had the month of July dedicated to him when NRL players would make the arrow gesture after scoring, was forced into retirement following his diagnosis, rocking the Australian sporting community.

Charles, who played four rugby union Tests for Australia, revealed his diagnosis this week.

The pair were driven around Stadium Australia before the NRL grand final, with Australian music artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamison performing.

Shark began with a rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone as Arrow and Charles began their lap.

Amy Shark performs as the NRL pay tribute to Jai Arrow and Nathan Charles. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Thousands in the crowd did the arrow gesture as they drove past, as prompted in a pre-packaged video by NRL Hall of Fame member Ray Warren.

"Jai's fight against MMD has reached far beyond the football field," Warren said.

"He has and continues to inspire others facing difficult times.

"The way Jai has faced this challenge with his head held high is showing us what true bravery really looks like.

"This is what our game is about. Strength, courage, community and making sure when life gets tough someone is there beside you."

After Shark sang You'll Never Walk Alone, Newcastle legend Dave Gleeson walked onto Stadium Australia to sing What's Up? by 4 Non Blondes.

Grinspoon's Phil Jamieson then joined Shark and Gleeson to end the tribute with the famous Tina Turner rugby league anthem, The Best.

The tribute came after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through.

The NRL has pledged $1 million, which was to be spent on pre-match entertainment, to help underprivileged kids who can not afford to play rugby league play rugby league," Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC this week.

World.title: Thousands of motorcyclists join pothole rally outside Victorian parliament
World.content:
Thousands of motorcyclists descended on Victoria's parliament on Sunday to voice their concerns about safety issues stemming from the state of the road network, with a focus on potholes.

Chants of "fix the roads" could be heard alongside the roar of motorbikes outside state parliament as more than 3,000 attendees joined the rally, which began at 11am.

The so-called broken roads rally was organised by Michael White and Paul Povh, who host a motorcycling YouTube channel.

"We're not here because we're bloody happy," Mr White said as he addressed the crowd.

"We're not here because we care about Labor, Liberal, Greens, One Nation, anyone.

" We're here because of the bloody state of the roads and we're sick of burying our mates. "

The rally was organised in the wake of the death of 71-year-old Peter "Tiki" Mason, who died while riding his motorbike on the Western Highway near Trawalla last month, after he was believed to have struck a pothole.

Police have said they were still investigating the cause of the incident, while Mr Mason's family have shared their heartbreak and said they did not want his death to be used to promote "political agendas".

Police say the rally attracted more than 3,000 attendees. (ABC News)

In recent days, heavy rain in some parts of the state has resulted in fresh potholes on the road network.

Concerns about potholes and poor road maintenance have become a key topic in the lead-up to the November state election.

A recent report from the Victorian Auditor-General's Office on the maintenance of the state's roads found that the proportion of state-managed roads in poor or very poor condition had increased from 39 to 48 per cent between 2021 and 2024.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson attended the rally, while Premier Ben Carroll spoke with the rally's organisers on Saturday.

Ahead of the state election, Labor has promised $1 billion for road maintenance, and has also doubled the amount allocated to fixing potholes this year with an additional $352 million. The Coalition has promised to spend $5 billion over four years to improve the state's roads.

World.title: Liberals pledge ‘transit lounges’ to free up hospital beds
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Liberals pledge ‘transit lounges’ to free up hospital beds Angelica Snowden October 5, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hospital overcrowding and ambulance ramping would be eased by a “transit lounge” scheme to shift patients out of emergency department beds sooner, the state opposition said in its latest election pledge. According to the $99 million plan, 10 new or expanded lounges would be reserved for patients who are ready to leave hospital but are awaiting medication or transport, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said. Jess Wilson has announced a plan to ease pressure on hospitals with “transit lounges”. Luis Enrique Ascui The lounges would free up hospital beds sooner for patients in emergency departments, while the fund would also support the rostering of extra staff as well as extended operating hours, according to the Liberal plan. Hospitals where ramping is most severe will be prioritised, but Wilson did not confirm their locations. Ramping occurs when paramedics are forced to wait with their patients in ambulances outside hospitals until beds become available.



“Victorians shouldn’t be stuck waiting for hours in an emergency department because a hospital bed is being occupied by someone who is ready to go home,” Wilson said. “We will deliver up to 10 new or expanded patient transit lounges to free up beds faster and help get patients out of emergency departments and into the care they need.” Before the latest announcement, Premier Ben Carroll earlier on Sunday accused the state opposition of trying to “Americanise our public health system”. “You’re seeing today, the Liberal Party announcing a policy to fund public dollars into private healthcare,” Carroll said. “One Nation have a policy to do the same, to Americanise our public health system,” he said.



“Sending public taxpayers’ dollars to the private health system is not supporting public beds, public nurses [or] public doctors.” The premier was reacting to an earlier Liberal election pledge in which the party promised to divert thousands of public patients to private hospitals for elective surgery at no cost. Wilson said the policy would deliver an extra 25,000 surgeries per year, and tackle the state’s ballooning elective surgery waiting list, which has grown from 58,062 to 68,730 in the past 12 months. Premier Ben Carroll called the Liberal Party’s health policy a plan to Americanise the state’s public health system. Justin McManus This policy would cost $1.27 billion over four years, and would be funded by cash offset by the winding up of Breakthrough Victoria, the state-owned venture capital firm.



Asked on Sunday if it was bad to “Americanise” the state’s healthcare system, Wilson responded: “Not at all.” Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Closed theatres, empty beds: The problems plaguing Melbourne’s new $1.5b hospital “This is happening in Queensland today. In fact, the Labor government has implemented it here in the past,” she said. “We have capacity in our healthcare system. We need to be partnering ... our private hospitals with the public system to make sure that Victorians get surgery sooner.” Last week, The Age reported 170 beds at the brand new Footscray Hospital remain closed due to a lack of operational funding to meet surging demand.



Footscray Hospital is administered by Western Health, where demand for emergency surgery has increased by 51 per cent in the past five years. The Victorian Agency for Health Information reported the median waiting time for a triage nurse or doctor after arriving at the hospital’s emergency department was 31 minutes. This is double the statewide average of 15 minutes. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Knights coach ‘couldn’t be prouder’ as Roosters celebrate grand final victory
World.content:
The Roosters have won the 2026 premiership after defeating the Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium.

Newcastle tried, but despite a late try for winger Greg Marzhew, they couldn’t quite get there.

It means veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans has begun and ended his NRL career with premierships. He did it in his first season with the Manly Sea Eagles in 2011, and now, 15 years later, he’s done it with the Roosters.

And it was Cherry-Evans who slotted the match-winning field goal with 11 minutes left in the match. What a fitting end to his career.

Loading

It’s also a sensational comeback for Sam Walker, who had surgery on a syndesmosis injury only weeks ago and somehow made it back on the field to play in the preliminary final last weekend and the final dance today.

It also means second-rower Angus Crichton will end his rugby league career with a premiership ring before moving to rugby next year.

The stadium of mostly Knights fans have gone quiet as James Tedesco and his Roosters celebrate their first premiership victory since 2019.

World.title: False dawn of a Newy era as brave Knights run out of steam
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion False dawn of a Newy era as brave Knights run out of steam Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer October 4, 2026 — 10:35pm

October 4, 2026 — 10:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you told any rugby league fan in March that the Knights, wooden-spooners last season, would be up by 12 points in this year’s grand final, they would have laughed at you. Is it worse to not be in the contest at all, like Parramatta against Penrith in 2022, or lead by two converted tries and then lose the decider by a solitary point? Loading You will have to ask the Newcastle players, whose rags-to-riches story missed out on its happy ending on Sunday evening as the Roosters secured a 19-18 victory. The Newcastle spirit, cited so often this week, took them so close to the ultimate prize. In the end, a Daly Cherry-Evans field goal 10 minutes from the death was all that separated them from the premiership.



As Roosters players sprinted into the middle of Accor Stadium, toasting their first title since 2019, dejected Knights players slumped on the turf. Newcastle were pinned in their own half for the majority of the match, and it was emblematic of their fighting season. They were always going to have to do it the hard way and were worn down by the Roosters’ completion rate (90 per cent) and stabbed in the heart by Mark Nawaqanitawase’s terrific second try in the right corner in the 59th minute. Kalyn Ponga holds his head at full-time, with the Knights pipped 19-18. Audrey Richardson Nawaqanitawase’s last game in the NRL – for now – was phenomenal. In two seasons, he has elevated his status to superstardom, with rugby league in disbelief at his looming departure for Japanese rugby. All square with 26 minutes to go is a broadcaster’s dream, but was a nightmare for Novocastrian heart rates. The makings of one of the great rugby league tales was in motion. Adversity, underdogs and battlers punching above their weight are intoxicating for neutrals. Newcastle had it all.



Saturday’s horrific car accident in Newcastle had added a sombre element to the narrative. A city that prides itself on producing hard-working people hadn’t come together like this since the Knights’ last grand final in 2001. There was an unmistakable energy around Newcastle this week and the players leant into it. But vibes and houses painted red and blue don’t win grand finals. The Roosters’ NRLW and NRL teams celebrate. Audrey Richardson Last to first is the stuff reserved for sporting movies. Even then, it would be a script almost too far-fetched to believe. The Roosters showed why with a meticulous game plan executed perfectly by its senior players. Andrew Johns, his heart with Newcastle but his head with the Roosters, said during the week the boys from Bondi should win by 30 points. Even he knew it was going to be a monumental task for his beloved Knights to keep riding the emotional wave they had surfed deep into September.



A Roosters ambush, on the same turf onto which players had sprinkled sand from Bondi Beach on Saturday, never eventuated as Newcastle weathered the storm and defended their line with vigour. Referee Adam Gee raised eyebrows when he allowed Kalyn Ponga to stay on the field after a high shot on Victor Radley. How the Knights captain escaped the sin bin for direct contact with the head was mystifying. Coach Trent Robinson celebrates with the Roosters players. Audrey Richardson James Tedesco was immense with ball in hand, Cherry-Evans got his fairytale ending, while Spencer Leniu took his angry pills and came good when it mattered on the grand stage. When Ponga crossed for his length-of-the-field try in the 29th minute, the Knights were suddenly 12-0 up. “I could imagine Newcastle is rocking,” Johns said in commentary.



Related Article NRL grand final Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights But there will be no limousine back to the Hunter for Joey this time. No “kidnapping” of Silverchair’s Daniel Johns to get the party started like in 1997. New York is the city that never sleeps, but Newcastle was primed to give the Big Apple a run for its money this week. The Knights faithful will get to bed eventually. But the nightmare of losing a grand final after being 12-0 up will haunt them for a long time. Let’s hope it’s not another 25 years before they’re back. World.title: Despite heartbreaking result, Knights remain the people’s choice
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion Despite heartbreaking result, Knights remain the people’s choice Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author October 4, 2026 — 10:05pm

October 4, 2026 — 10:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We knew what would happen in this grand final – and it didn’t. All the smarties, and all the rest of us besides, knew that however much popular sentiment was behind the Knights in this NRL grand final, last year’s wooden-spooner workers beating the uppity glory boys of the eastern suburbs would be wonderful – but elite sport just doesn’t work like that. The Knights, we knew, had left their best on the field by beating Penrith last week, and would have nothing left to give. The Roosters, obviously, had too much firepower, too much big-match experience, too much sheer talent, to lose against the sweaty proletariat from the north. No-one would be surprised by a 20-point victory, if not 30 points. Francis Manuleleua gets first blood for the Knights. Audrey Richardson And yet?



And yet all through the first half it was obvious we had a real contest on our hands. Despite the Roosters dominating possession and territory, the Knights had something the Roosters did not. Firstly, the ability to successfully strike. While the Roosters always threatened to score, the only thing they had to show for it from the first half was a piece of individual brilliance from their rugby-bound winger Mark Nawaqanitawase to not just toe it through as we’ve seen players do many times, but use two toes – a tap with the left to bring it under control, and a thrust with the right to perfectly push it over the try-line to dive on top of it. (How many times are we going to see “Marky-Mark” do things that we’re not quite sure that we’ve ever seen before?) Loading Secondly, the Knights had a bit of luck. There is no doubt that opening 40 minutes the Novocastrians had the rub of the green, with the ball bouncing their way, including right into Kalyn Ponga’s arms just when they needed it most to score a runaway try – their second after a great early effort by Francis Manuleleua. Going into the break, the Knights 12-6 lead was a fitting reward for their efforts. To that point the Roosters had showed very little bar two tactics endlessly repeated: the up and the under. Sooner or later, was their clear reckoning, the individual brilliance of Marky-Mark must make the difference from whatever scraps their kicks delivered.



Sadly – you heard me – the Roosters were pretty much correct. Related Article NRL grand final Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights Though the Roosters centre Billy Smith scored a good try to close early in the second half to make it 12-12 and Sam Walker nailed a penalty to give the Roosters a 14-12 lead, with 20 minutes to go – who else could it be but? – Marky-Mark went over in the corner again to make it 18-12. (A pause here, for rugby folk. As I write, let us rejoice that this superb athlete is coming home to the Wallabies. Good Lord willing and the creeks don’t rise, at about this time next year he’ll be wreaking havoc on the All Blacks, Springboks and French in the World Cup. With Joseph Aukuso Suaalii also in our corner, no team in the world will be better equipped to dominate the aerial game. We now resume our normal service.) In the meantime?



In the meantime, as the game went on the Channel Nine coverage gave us regular crosses to the folk watching at home. “The cutaways to the Paddington Inn,” a mate noted, “look like a casting call for Australia’s Next Top Model. The cutaways to Newcastle look like a gathering of great Aussies.” The casting call people looked as if they were pleased. The Novocastrians looked as if they were hanging on every tackle, every pass. They were the ones we wanted to be rewarded for their passion. Please, can the Knights pull this off against all odds? Can the team showing all the heart, all the grit, all the refusal to give up, actually triumph against the team just endlessly kicking the damn thing? Alas it was not to be. In the end the smarties were right. The Roosters really just did have too much firepower, too much Marky-Mark and too many up-and-unders to be denied. When Daly Cherry-Evans put over a field goal with 10 minutes to go to make it 19-12, it was going to need a miracle and there wasn’t to be one …. WAIT!



With just three minutes to go, Greg Marzhew sails over for the Knights in the corner against all odds! Converted, the score closes to 19-18, and an ordinary match is set for a superb finish! There would be no more miracles. The Roosters won with that score. They are the premiers, and good luck to them. But the Knights remain the people’s choice. They displayed all the qualities we most admire in sport – courage, creativity, refusal to bend – but just didn’t get there in the end. Bugger.
