World.title: Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights Adrian Proszenko October 4, 2026 — 9:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Grand final hero. That’s the latest label that can be attached to Mark Nawaqanitawase. Apparently, being a dual-code international, State of Origin star and Olympic representative wasn’t quite enough. As speculation surrounds whether the Roosters winger will return to the NRL after switching back to rugby union, let us take a moment to appreciate his ability to deliver the biggest plays on the biggest days. Loading “Marky Mark” was at it again in Sunday’s NRL decider. The Roosters had enough possession to win not only this game, but half a dozen others. Yet, it took a couple of moments of brilliance from Nawaqanitawase to sink the valiant Knights 19-18 in a thriller. Few others could have scored his first try. When centre partner Rob Toia came down with an attacking kick and batted the ball back, it bobbled tantalisingly on the turf. Not only did Nawaqanitawase regather it to score, he kicked it ahead twice – using both his feet to do so.



There was also an air of freakishness about his second try, when a Daly Cherry-Evans kick ricocheted off the uprights before the ball ended up in the safest of hands. When he wasn’t scoring, he was flying above the pack to either defuse a short dropout or soar for one of the many attacking kicks that came his way. Mark Nawaqanitawase (left) celebrates after scoring his second try with Rob Toia. Audrey Richardson His contribution ensured he finished on top at the Roosters and the 13-man game. It’s often said that, whenever a player switches codes, they are replaceable. But is that really the case with Nawaqanitawase? He was a star in a team full of them. Cherry-Evans earned his own fairytale farewell after kicking the field goal that proved the difference. James Tedesco ran for more than 300 metres. Spencer Leniu, meanwhile, had the game of his life.



All of that and more was required to defeat a Newcastle side that had no right to get this close. From the very first set, the Roosters powered up the field to ram home a territorial advantage. It set the tone: 84 per cent of the game was played on Newcastle’s side of halfway. Kalyn Ponga scores for Newcastle after the Roosters had dominated the opening half. Audrey Richardson For anyone else, that statistic would have been the death knell. Yet, for these Knights, this is where they are most dangerous. No other team has scored more tries from its own side of halfway, and they would soon add to the tally. The opening try came from a rare sojourn into opposition territory, and in somewhat controversial circumstances. It was made possible when the Roosters conceded a penalty for a supposedly high shot on Mat Croker, who dropped the ball before contact.



From the ensuing set, with the Roosters defence fixated on Kalyn Ponga lurking out the back, Fletcher Sharpe hit Francis Manuleleua with a pass as he ran back against the grain. The rising back-row star, three weeks after dislocating his elbow, ran a superb line that led him all the way under the posts. As the fans went berserk, the DJ chose – of all the celebratory songs at his disposal – to play Dance Monkey. Make of that what you will. The Roosters celebrate their first NRL title in seven years. Audrey Richardson Despite being under intense pressure, everything was going Newcastle’s way. On any other day, Ponga would have spent time in the sin bin – if not worse – for his challenge on Victor Radley. While Radley was falling in the tackle, Ponga’s shoulder clearly collected the forward in the head. A crowd of 80,814 held its collective breath as the bunker had several looks at an incident that changed the game. Would Ponga – Newcastle’s captain, fullback and talisman – be removed from the fray?



Video referee Chris Butler decided that putting him on report was sufficient. Related Article Analysis

NRL grand final NRL grand final player ratings: Who shone brightest on league’s biggest day In those 10 minutes that Ponga probably should have been off the field, he came up with two plays that could have altered the result. The first came when Nawaqanitawase flew high above Greg Marzhew, grabbed the football and seemingly scored yet another try. But just as he was about to put the ball down, Ponga created just enough interference to prompt the smallest of bobbles. Try saved. And then, another example of why you can never switch off on this Newcastle team. It was again the same protagonists: Nawaqanitawase tapped the ball back, but rather than finding a teammate, Ponga pounced, scooped the ball up and ran the length of the field to score.



As he made the 95-metre dash for glory, with Cherry-Evans running in pursuit in vain, the question had to be asked: should Ponga have been on the field? Related Article Opinion

NRL grand final False dawn of a Newy era as brave Knights run out of steam Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer It will be a point debated long after the final siren. There were other strokes of fortune for the underdogs. When Cherry-Evans kicked early in the tackle count, it wasn’t just the Knights caught out of position. The kick was partially charged down by, of all things, the cable holding the Spidercam camera. And when Ponga accidentally made incidental contact with the referee, again no action was taken.

World.title: Liberals pledge ‘transit lounges’ to free up hospital beds
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Liberals pledge ‘transit lounges’ to free up hospital beds Angelica Snowden October 5, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hospital overcrowding and ambulance ramping would be eased by a “transit lounge” scheme to shift patients out of emergency department beds sooner, the state opposition said in its latest election pledge. According to the $99 million plan, 10 new or expanded lounges would be reserved for patients who are ready to leave hospital but are awaiting medication or transport, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said. Jess Wilson has announced a plan to ease pressure on hospitals with “transit lounges”. Luis Enrique Ascui The lounges would free up hospital beds sooner for patients in emergency departments, while the fund would also support the rostering of extra staff as well as extended operating hours, according to the Liberal plan. Hospitals where ramping is most severe will be prioritised, but Wilson did not confirm their locations. Ramping occurs when paramedics are forced to wait with their patients in ambulances outside hospitals until beds become available.



“Victorians shouldn’t be stuck waiting for hours in an emergency department because a hospital bed is being occupied by someone who is ready to go home,” Wilson said. “We will deliver up to 10 new or expanded patient transit lounges to free up beds faster and help get patients out of emergency departments and into the care they need.” Before the latest announcement, Premier Ben Carroll earlier on Sunday accused the state opposition of trying to “Americanise our public health system”. “You’re seeing today, the Liberal Party announcing a policy to fund public dollars into private healthcare,” Carroll said. “One Nation have a policy to do the same, to Americanise our public health system,” he said.



“Sending public taxpayers’ dollars to the private health system is not supporting public beds, public nurses [or] public doctors.” The premier was reacting to an earlier Liberal election pledge in which the party promised to divert thousands of public patients to private hospitals for elective surgery at no cost. Wilson said the policy would deliver an extra 25,000 surgeries per year, and tackle the state’s ballooning elective surgery waiting list, which has grown from 58,062 to 68,730 in the past 12 months. Premier Ben Carroll called the Liberal Party’s health policy a plan to Americanise the state’s public health system. Justin McManus This policy would cost $1.27 billion over four years, and would be funded by cash offset by the winding up of Breakthrough Victoria, the state-owned venture capital firm.



Asked on Sunday if it was bad to “Americanise” the state’s healthcare system, Wilson responded: “Not at all.” Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Closed theatres, empty beds: The problems plaguing Melbourne’s new $1.5b hospital “This is happening in Queensland today. In fact, the Labor government has implemented it here in the past,” she said. “We have capacity in our healthcare system. We need to be partnering ... our private hospitals with the public system to make sure that Victorians get surgery sooner.” Last week, The Age reported 170 beds at the brand new Footscray Hospital remain closed due to a lack of operational funding to meet surging demand.



Footscray Hospital is administered by Western Health, where demand for emergency surgery has increased by 51 per cent in the past five years. The Victorian Agency for Health Information reported the median waiting time for a triage nurse or doctor after arriving at the hospital’s emergency department was 31 minutes. This is double the statewide average of 15 minutes. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Knights coach ‘couldn’t be prouder’ as Roosters celebrate grand final victory
World.content:
The Roosters have won the 2026 premiership after defeating the Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium.

Newcastle tried, but despite a late try for winger Greg Marzhew, they couldn’t quite get there.

It means veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans has begun and ended his NRL career with premierships. He did it in his first season with the Manly Sea Eagles in 2011, and now, 15 years later, he’s done it with the Roosters.

And it was Cherry-Evans who slotted the match-winning field goal with 11 minutes left in the match. What a fitting end to his career.

Loading

It’s also a sensational comeback for Sam Walker, who had surgery on a syndesmosis injury only weeks ago and somehow made it back on the field to play in the preliminary final last weekend and the final dance today.

It also means second-rower Angus Crichton will end his rugby league career with a premiership ring before moving to rugby next year.

The stadium of mostly Knights fans have gone quiet as James Tedesco and his Roosters celebrate their first premiership victory since 2019.

World.title: False dawn of a Newy era as brave Knights run out of steam
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion False dawn of a Newy era as brave Knights run out of steam Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer October 4, 2026 — 10:35pm

October 4, 2026 — 10:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you told any rugby league fan in March that the Knights, wooden-spooners last season, would be up by 12 points in this year’s grand final, they would have laughed at you. Is it worse to not be in the contest at all, like Parramatta against Penrith in 2022, or lead by two converted tries and then lose the decider by a solitary point? Loading You will have to ask the Newcastle players, whose rags-to-riches story missed out on its happy ending on Sunday evening as the Roosters secured a 19-18 victory. The Newcastle spirit, cited so often this week, took them so close to the ultimate prize. In the end, a Daly Cherry-Evans field goal 10 minutes from the death was all that separated them from the premiership.



As Roosters players sprinted into the middle of Accor Stadium, toasting their first title since 2019, dejected Knights players slumped on the turf. Newcastle were pinned in their own half for the majority of the match, and it was emblematic of their fighting season. They were always going to have to do it the hard way and were worn down by the Roosters’ completion rate (90 per cent) and stabbed in the heart by Mark Nawaqanitawase’s terrific second try in the right corner in the 59th minute. Kalyn Ponga holds his head at full-time, with the Knights pipped 19-18. Audrey Richardson Nawaqanitawase’s last game in the NRL – for now – was phenomenal. In two seasons, he has elevated his status to superstardom, with rugby league in disbelief at his looming departure for Japanese rugby. All square with 26 minutes to go is a broadcaster’s dream, but was a nightmare for Novocastrian heart rates. The makings of one of the great rugby league tales was in motion. Adversity, underdogs and battlers punching above their weight are intoxicating for neutrals. Newcastle had it all.



Saturday’s horrific car accident in Newcastle had added a sombre element to the narrative. A city that prides itself on producing hard-working people hadn’t come together like this since the Knights’ last grand final in 2001. There was an unmistakable energy around Newcastle this week and the players leant into it. But vibes and houses painted red and blue don’t win grand finals. The Roosters’ NRLW and NRL teams celebrate. Audrey Richardson Last to first is the stuff reserved for sporting movies. Even then, it would be a script almost too far-fetched to believe. The Roosters showed why with a meticulous game plan executed perfectly by its senior players. Andrew Johns, his heart with Newcastle but his head with the Roosters, said during the week the boys from Bondi should win by 30 points. Even he knew it was going to be a monumental task for his beloved Knights to keep riding the emotional wave they had surfed deep into September.



A Roosters ambush, on the same turf onto which players had sprinkled sand from Bondi Beach on Saturday, never eventuated as Newcastle weathered the storm and defended their line with vigour. Referee Adam Gee raised eyebrows when he allowed Kalyn Ponga to stay on the field after a high shot on Victor Radley. How the Knights captain escaped the sin bin for direct contact with the head was mystifying. Coach Trent Robinson celebrates with the Roosters players. Audrey Richardson James Tedesco was immense with ball in hand, Cherry-Evans got his fairytale ending, while Spencer Leniu took his angry pills and came good when it mattered on the grand stage. When Ponga crossed for his length-of-the-field try in the 29th minute, the Knights were suddenly 12-0 up. “I could imagine Newcastle is rocking,” Johns said in commentary.



Related Article NRL grand final Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights But there will be no limousine back to the Hunter for Joey this time. No “kidnapping” of Silverchair’s Daniel Johns to get the party started like in 1997. New York is the city that never sleeps, but Newcastle was primed to give the Big Apple a run for its money this week. The Knights faithful will get to bed eventually. But the nightmare of losing a grand final after being 12-0 up will haunt them for a long time. Let’s hope it’s not another 25 years before they’re back. World.title: Despite heartbreaking result, Knights remain the people’s choice
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion Despite heartbreaking result, Knights remain the people’s choice Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author October 4, 2026 — 10:05pm

October 4, 2026 — 10:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We knew what would happen in this grand final – and it didn’t. All the smarties, and all the rest of us besides, knew that however much popular sentiment was behind the Knights in this NRL grand final, last year’s wooden-spooner workers beating the uppity glory boys of the eastern suburbs would be wonderful – but elite sport just doesn’t work like that. The Knights, we knew, had left their best on the field by beating Penrith last week, and would have nothing left to give. The Roosters, obviously, had too much firepower, too much big-match experience, too much sheer talent, to lose against the sweaty proletariat from the north. No-one would be surprised by a 20-point victory, if not 30 points. Francis Manuleleua gets first blood for the Knights. Audrey Richardson And yet?



And yet all through the first half it was obvious we had a real contest on our hands. Despite the Roosters dominating possession and territory, the Knights had something the Roosters did not. Firstly, the ability to successfully strike. While the Roosters always threatened to score, the only thing they had to show for it from the first half was a piece of individual brilliance from their rugby-bound winger Mark Nawaqanitawase to not just toe it through as we’ve seen players do many times, but use two toes – a tap with the left to bring it under control, and a thrust with the right to perfectly push it over the try-line to dive on top of it. (How many times are we going to see “Marky-Mark” do things that we’re not quite sure that we’ve ever seen before?) Loading Secondly, the Knights had a bit of luck. There is no doubt that opening 40 minutes the Novocastrians had the rub of the green, with the ball bouncing their way, including right into Kalyn Ponga’s arms just when they needed it most to score a runaway try – their second after a great early effort by Francis Manuleleua. Going into the break, the Knights 12-6 lead was a fitting reward for their efforts. To that point the Roosters had showed very little bar two tactics endlessly repeated: the up and the under. Sooner or later, was their clear reckoning, the individual brilliance of Marky-Mark must make the difference from whatever scraps their kicks delivered.



Sadly – you heard me – the Roosters were pretty much correct. Related Article NRL grand final Mark of a champion: Nawaqanitawase’s brilliance sinks valiant Knights Though the Roosters centre Billy Smith scored a good try to close early in the second half to make it 12-12 and Sam Walker nailed a penalty to give the Roosters a 14-12 lead, with 20 minutes to go – who else could it be but? – Marky-Mark went over in the corner again to make it 18-12. (A pause here, for rugby folk. As I write, let us rejoice that this superb athlete is coming home to the Wallabies. Good Lord willing and the creeks don’t rise, at about this time next year he’ll be wreaking havoc on the All Blacks, Springboks and French in the World Cup. With Joseph Aukuso Suaalii also in our corner, no team in the world will be better equipped to dominate the aerial game. We now resume our normal service.) In the meantime?



In the meantime, as the game went on the Channel Nine coverage gave us regular crosses to the folk watching at home. “The cutaways to the Paddington Inn,” a mate noted, “look like a casting call for Australia’s Next Top Model. The cutaways to Newcastle look like a gathering of great Aussies.” The casting call people looked as if they were pleased. The Novocastrians looked as if they were hanging on every tackle, every pass. They were the ones we wanted to be rewarded for their passion. Please, can the Knights pull this off against all odds? Can the team showing all the heart, all the grit, all the refusal to give up, actually triumph against the team just endlessly kicking the damn thing? Alas it was not to be. In the end the smarties were right. The Roosters really just did have too much firepower, too much Marky-Mark and too many up-and-unders to be denied. When Daly Cherry-Evans put over a field goal with 10 minutes to go to make it 19-12, it was going to need a miracle and there wasn’t to be one …. WAIT!



With just three minutes to go, Greg Marzhew sails over for the Knights in the corner against all odds! Converted, the score closes to 19-18, and an ordinary match is set for a superb finish! There would be no more miracles. The Roosters won with that score. They are the premiers, and good luck to them. But the Knights remain the people’s choice. They displayed all the qualities we most admire in sport – courage, creativity, refusal to bend – but just didn’t get there in the end. Bugger. World.title: New postgraduate training pathway needed for rural GPs - doctor
World.content:
A Far North doctor is calling for a new postgraduate training pathway to better equip GPs for work in rural areas.

Katharina Blattner said working as a doctor in the rural Far North wasn't easy, but it was rewarding.

"I work at Hauora Hokianga Rawene Hospital, one of the smallest hospitals in the country, and my job is fantastic," she said.

She said working in a remote area had much different demands to working in the city.

"Practising medicine in a rural area, that's shaped by a lot of interrelated factors but the notable one is geographic distance from specialist services and resources," she explained.

"That rural context means clinicians need to be able to work across a really broad generalist scope of practice and with the capacity to manage a really wide range of presentations to quite a depth, because it might be a two-hour drive to the closest ED."

Dr Blattner had trained as both a GP and a rural hospital doctor.

Katharina Blattner. Supplied / University of Otago

"It's a pretty long training process to get a fellowship in rural medicine and general practice, they're both specialties in their own right," she said.

"That would be a minimum four or up to eight years of training [after graduating medical school] before someone is a fully qualified rural medicine specialist."

The rural hospital medicine specialisation was introduced in 2008 in recognition that urban and rural hospitals required different skillsets.

"Being a rural-specific programme, that's had a real impact in terms of the doctors coming out the other end making a difference to the workforce in rural hospitals," she said.

But no such specialisation existed for rural general practice.

"What hasn't happened, and what would be great if it did happen, would be if there was also a parallel rural-specific training programme for general practice. If within the general practice programme there was a rural-specific stream."

Dr Blattner, who also worked as an associate professor at the University of Otago, last week published a study in the New Zealand Medical Journal highlighting the gap.

She said working as a general practitioner in a rural area was often seen as a "lesser" option for graduates, and offering a full postgraduate training pathway would go a long way to breaking that illusion.

"Sometimes what I'm hearing or what I'm observing is that it's seen as a dead-end choice. Graduates would like to see they can have career progression in rural medicine in the same way they would if they chose another specialty," Blattner said.

"As a clinician you want to be able to do the whole career-progression thing, work to the top of your scope, be involved in teaching and do some research.

World.title: Two men jump into river after failing to stop for police
World.content:
Police in the Ōpōtiki area in the Bay of Plenty are appealing for sightings of two men who failed to stop for officers before jumping in a river.

Duty Inspector Phil Edwards said about 3.45am on Sunday a vehicle ran a red light in Wainui.

"Road spikes were successfully deployed about 10km from Ōpōtiki shortly after 4am, before the vehicle came to a stop down Snell Road, by the Otara River," he said.

"The two occupants have then got out of the vehicle and jumped into the water."

A search and rescue operation was launched, with assistance from the Harbourmaster, Coastguard Ōpōtiki, and a rescue helicopter, but the two men have not been found.

"Police Search and Rescue staff are continuing the search this morning, and are appealing to the public for help," Edwards said.

Edwards said a "large-scale" operation was underway and police had searched the river and deployed helicopters and ground crew across farmland to find the men.

"If you are one of these males, you know who they are, or you have any other information which may help us locate them, please get in touch. We're also after information about any suspicious behaviour in the area."

Edwards said the priority at this time was ensuring the men were safe.

Urgent information could be passed on via 111, referencing job number P067829874.

World.title: 'I just wanted to get him out' - Man who saved 89-year-old from burning home
World.content:
One of the men who helped rescue an 89-year-old from his burning Gisborne home early Saturday morning, before quietly slipping away, says he did not want to make a fuss about it.

Local police hailed Tim Morris as a 'hero' yesterday after the rescue.

The 37-year-old Gisborne man was driving on Aberdeen Road at about 1am Saturday with a friend, when they saw the blaze and pulled over.

They were able to pull the 89-year-old through a broken window to safety, before checking to see if anyone else was in the property and going to neighbours for help.

Police said the rescued man was recuperating well in hospital.

Police said, once emergency services arrived, Morris and his friend quietly slipped into the night, but he revealed his involvement, after he saw an appeal from police for the hero to come forward.

"I just wanted to get him out," he said. "It's been a bit emotional.

"At the end of the day, helping people makes me feel good."

Detective Senior Sergeant John Love said the fact Morris did not want to make a fuss when he arrived at the Gisborne Police station on Sunday morning said a lot about him.

"However, thanks to his quick actions, the house occupant was able to escape a life-threatening situation.

"We put out an appeal, because we wanted to find him, not because he was in any trouble. We wanted the opportunity to shake his hand and say 'thank you'.

"We got that opportunity today.

World.title: Coloured solar panels hold potential for NZ vegetable growers
World.content:
A renewable energy researcher says coloured solar panels have "tremendous" potential for New Zealand vegetable growers.

Published in Cell Reports Physical Science, a Swedish study has found broccoli grows well beneath magenta-coloured solar panels, although the vegetable takes 25 days longer to get to full size and has lower levels of micronutrients.

Victoria University School of Engineering and Computer Science associate professor Ramesh Rayudu said further research was needed, but the initial study was a bit of a game-changer.

Rayudu told RNZ that, every now and then, researchers came across a paper that sparked the reaction: "Oh, that was so obvious, why haven't we thought of that?"

"It was one of those situations when I read that paper," he said. "It is a great idea."

The Swedish researchers said conventional dark-blue solar panels were typically opaque, creating too much shade for crops. so customised semi-transparent panels were designed for the study.

The basic concept was straightforward, according to author Silvia Ma Lu of Mälardalen University.

"The solar panels use part of the incoming sunlight to generate renewable electricity, while allowing part of the light to pass through to the crops growing underneath."

The solar panels offered a potential tool for farmers to harvest renewable energy, while sustaining crop yields, the study said.

Ramesh said it was a promising demonstration of producing both food and electricity from the same land, and opened the door for New Zealand vegetable growers to one day offset their electricity bills or sell energy back to the grid.

"If they haven't got any solar panels, now they can consider putting in solar panels. What that means is that whatever energy is generated from the solar panels is an added advantage for these growers."

He said the technology likely needed further development to make such a scheme viable, as the semi-transparent panels generated less electricity.

"Depending on the value of electricity and the price received for broccoli, that lost electricity could require roughly 1.2 to 3.2 tonnes of additional broccoli per hectare to offset its value."

However, if the benefits outweighed the cost, coloured solar panels shouldn't be limited to broccoli growers, he said.

"We can use it for other things, like cabbages, cauliflower, carrots."

Canterbury University electric power research engineer Sharee McNab said investigating how to make food production and energy generation viable and efficient was potentially crucial.

World.title: As it happened: Election campaign 4 October
World.content:
Election 2026 heated up on Sunday, when Labour released its long-awaited fiscal plan and National immediately claimed it fell billions of dollars short, which would be made up in more borrowing and taxes.

Among the promises from Labour leader Chris Hipkins was a pay rise for 65,000 care and support workers, costing $2.5b over four years, while also re-implementing pay-equity legislation.

National finance spokesperson Nicola Willis accused Labour of lying to the country, claiming an $8.5b hole in its policy.

Why aren't young people signed up to vote? Let's ask them! Afternoons Download MP3 11m

Meanwhile, National leader Christopher Luxon visited the Takanini Gurdwara Sri Kalgidhar Sahib Sikh Temple, which has hosted several previous prime ministers.

National also launched its blue campaign bus and pledged $1.75b to build South Auckland's Mill Road, which NZ First leader Winston Peters claimed his party first announced in July.

National's Mt Roskill MP Carlos Cheung also had billboards burnt down overnight.

ACT leader David Seymour insisted government policies had attacked wealth creation for decades and other parties would "destroy wealth" with their solutions to the current cost-of-living crisis.

Instead, he promised to remove tax on KiwiSaver earnings.

The Green Party pledged to make public transport free for eligible groups, like children, students apprentices, community services cardholders and total mobility users, and cap bus and train fares at $2 for everyone else.

Te Pāti Māori announced its one-person party list, with general secretary Lance Norman the only extra candidate.

World.title: Greens eye free, fast and reliable public transport with election promises
World.content:
The Green Party has pledged to make public transport free for eligible groups and cap bus and train fares at $2 for everyone else.

It says its transport plan offers fast, frequent and affordable services.

Under the Greens' policy, public transport would be free for children, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders and Total Mobility users, while everyone else would pay a maximum fare of $2.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406186515112

It would also build mass rapid bus and light rail services in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, offer more frequent inter-regional bus services, strengthen rural bus services and allow councils to pedestrianise more inner-city areas and increase safe walking and biking spaces.

The party has also promised overnight passenger trains from Auckland to Wellington, as well as bringing back the Southerner between Christchurch and Dunedin and extending Te Huia to Tauranga.

"In the middle of a fossil fuel crisis, these common sense investments will save New Zealanders money, stress and time," said co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick.

"It'll cut emissions and improve quality of life."

Swarbrick and transport spokesperson Julie-Anne Genter addressed media in Auckland on Sunday from outside Maungawhau City Rail Link station.

Swarbrick referred to the more than a million trips that have been taken on the CRL since it opened last month.

"What that tells us and shows us so clearly is that when we build transport infrastructure that makes it easy, affordable, and even fun to get around, people will use it.

"But right now, too many New Zealanders are driving around with the fuel light on, hoping and praying that petrol prices will drop," she said.

Swarbrick said the government could not control oil shocks like that caused by the Middle East war - but it could make investments that reduce the cost of living and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

She described the party's plan as "straight up common sense".

Swarbrick said meaningful change could be made immediately, but some parts of the plan like light rail networks could take a decade or so.

The major investments would go through the Infrastructure Commission's assurance process, she said.

The entire plan would cost around $23.9b: $21b for mass rapid transit and rail investments, $1.3b for capped and free fares, $75m for electric buses, $290m for councils to expand walking and biking spaces, $824m for public transport improvements and $406m for inter-regional buses.

"What we are proposing today is to meet the needs not only of our immediate cost of living crisis, but also our medium and longer term needs to build infrastructure that is fit for purpose for the future. Yes, that will cost money," Swarbrick said.

She cited the Greens' wealth tax as a way of paying for some of it, but said the party's full fiscal plan would be laid out in the next few weeks.

But Public Transport Users Association national co-ordinator Jon Reeves questioned the viability of the Greens' plan.

He supported cheaper fares, but said the proposal sounded like wishful thinking.

"I'd like to see some of these things come true. On a $2 fare for everyone, it's good, it may change the attitudes of some people into using public transport but how many is the question," he said.

"The other area is who is going to fund it.

"When we do give out free transport to someone, someone else has to pay for it. Does it come at the cost and the expense of running services?" he said.

Reeves said one way to reduce the cost of public transport would be to bring services back into New Zealand ownership to keep profits in the country.

"In New Zealand multinational corporations are pretty much the ones who operate all the services, whether it's Auckland or Wellington trains or the bus services around the country. They're all majority owned by overseas foreign companies," he said.

"We need to bring it back to New Zealand and cut out the middleman, bring that money back and make it stay here so we can invest in more public transport and give cheaper fares to users."

World.title: Labour releases its fiscal plan, promises pay rise for care and support workers
World.content:
Labour has released its long-awaited fiscal plan saying every election promise is paid for, but it has not provided a cost for fully re-implementing pay equity legislation.

It does however promise an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers, costing $2.5 billion over four years, and Labour leader Chris Hipkins says there's "plenty of headroom" within the plan to pay for pay equity overall.

Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds says Labour will keep operating allowances - that is, new day-to-day spending - at the $2.4 billion set by the coalition government in Budget 2026.

The party said it wouldn't rely on a larger operating allowance, stating new investment "must fit within these allowances, alongside cost pressures and other priorities".

"Our announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances," said Edmonds.

"We also have almost $10.5 billion of future operating allowances unallocated. We can deliver what we have promised without increasing those allowances."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406191627112

Edmonds also said Labour would return the books to surplus in 2028/29 and bring net debt down below 20 percent of GDP "over time", maintaining it will use the OBEGAL measure, rather than the government's preferred OBEGALx measure.

"We can do that because we have made better choices about where public money goes and will make every dollar work harder."

Labour has previously labelled the government's spending decisions austere, but Edmonds denied that matching allowances could also be considered austere.

"We're providing real cost of living relief pressure for our families. We are moving as much as we can to ensure that the money goes to the places it needs to," she said.

"It all comes down to choices."

Labour's already announced capital commitments were:

$200 million capital injection for the New Zealand Future Fund

$420 million for the initial student loan write-off

$200 million for hospitals

$400 million for schools

$2.9 billion for Kāinga Ora housing, spread over four years

$7 million for Ratepayer Assistance Scheme (RAS) solar expenditure

Hipkins said most of the party's big election policies had been announced.

No cost indicated for restoring pay equity law

Last year the government overhauled the Equal Pay Act, retrospectively stripping nurses, teachers, carers and other female-dominated workforces of the right to pursue pay equity claims under the existing law.

The controversial legislation stopped the 33 claims underway and raised the threshold for proving work has been historically undervalued.

On Sunday Labour confirmed it would restore pay equity legislation in its first 100 days and give an immediate pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers.

That specific payrise would cost $2.5 billion over four years, but the full cost for restoring pay equity was not provided.

"You'll see there's plenty of headroom within the fiscal plan that we've released today," Hipkins said.

"We have a $10 billion unallocated amount of headroom, we've got multi billion dollars for health cost pressures - and many of the pay equity claims are within the health system - so we're confident we will be able to meet the costs of pay equity within the flexibility that we built into the plan."

The legislation would include transitional rules so the claims that had been underway could continue, rather than be started from scratch.

Hipkins said the care and support worker payrise was a stopgap.

"This is not a final deal for care and support workers, but that could still take... a year, maybe, to negotiate and to conclude that process."

Some public sector cuts reversed

Labour promised to reversed half of the first tranche of public sector cuts announced in the government's Budget, and fully reverse the second tranche.

The party is working on the assumption that the government is already halfway through that first tranche of cuts.

"In many cases the cuts have already been made, and we're not going to reverse cuts that have already been made," Hipkins said.

"The current government aren't releasing that information, so we've had to make some assumptions about that."

Hipkins said Labour would scrap the Ministry for Regulation, and the savings realised would largely be divvied up among other agencies.

Labour stands by its promises, ridicules National's

Hipkins said National promised to grow the economy and get the books in order.

"It has done neither," he said.

"171,000 New Zealanders are unemployed, growth is weaker and debt has continued to rise. They have cut jobs and services, and New Zealanders have been left to pay the price."

Hipkins said the choice was clear: "more cuts and decline under National, or a Labour Government that will balance the books without shrinking the economy, get costs under control and back the people and businesses doing the work."

Edmonds said every election commitment Labour had made was fully costed and fully funded.

"The numbers add up and we have left room to confidently respond to whatever comes next," she added.

World.title: Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal
World.content:
As the merciless Roosters ran away with the NRLW grand final it was hard to think of a less fitting end for a career as legendary as Ali Brigginshaw's.

The 36-year old and the rest of the Broncos were helpless to stop a Tricolour massacre that ended 30-6 as the Roosters earned a manner of vengeance for last year's grand final defeat to complete a perfect season.

It was over by half-time because Brisbane did not pick up their guns, let alone fire a shot.

NRLW grand final quick hits The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos. Here are the quick hits from the NRLW grand final.

They completed just three sets in the entire first half as they drowned under a sea of Roosters points.

From the 15th minute to the 34th minute they only touched the ball to kick it off, drop it or be driven back into the in-goal.

For almost 20 minutes they did not play the ball once, with the Roosters running in six straight tries and between the 15th and 39th minutes they did not complete a set.

All of the weapons that have made Brigginshaw great — her skill, her guile, her cunning and class as a playmaker, which she has carried through her 17 years at the top of women's rugby league — were blunted before she even got a chance to use them.

She did manage to sneak through for a line-break in the second half, a 35 minutes of football that felt like it only happened because it had to happen so we could get to the end, as she held up a pass before hitting a gap with exquisite timing, but had no support.

In the end, her last day was destroyed by a monster of a team who are without question the best NRLW side ever assembled.

They are the culmination of a transformation in women's rugby league that Brigginshaw herself helped bring about through a career that stretches all the way back to the primordial days of women's rugby league.

Brigginshaw's Broncos were helpless before the Roosters onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

When she started playing for Queensland and Australia in 2009 her Broncos teammate Reegan Hicks was three years old.

Club football was ad hoc, pathways barely existed and the NRL may as well have been a different universe. For the committed few who kept the women's game going it was day-to-day as much as it was hand-to-mouth.

Interstate matches were not played under the State of Origin banner and were held at suburban grounds in front of tiny crowds.

A World Cup final was the only game that could get on television and even then, only if the network was feeling generous.

Footage of those days leading up to the first NRLW season in 2018 is grainy and hard to find. Even basic details of matches — things like team lists, scorers and attendances — aren't always easy to track down.

Brigginshaw has been a top-level footballer for almost as long as some of her teammates have been alive. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

In a very literal sense of the word, it's almost prehistoric.

Today it's a new world, a world Brigginshaw helped create as the premiere footballer and one of the biggest stars of the transitional era and into the early NRLW years.

For proof, look no further than the words of Julia Robinson, who has played with Brigginshaw ever since that first Broncos season.

“She’s a true leader, on and off the field, she’s the heart of the Broncos, she’s going to be this legacy that carries on for generations," Robinson told ABC Sport.

“She’s going to be missed, missed by the team, missed by everyone but she’ll still be around and make a big impact on the rugby league community.”

“I’m so grateful I had the opportunity to play with Ali, she’s one of the greats.”

Brigginshaw was a pioneer and a trail blazer, who set a new mark and standard for others to aspire to and acted as a legend for an entire game to believe in.

To see the Tricolours complete their perfect season is to see the end product of that belief. Today's players are bigger, faster, stronger and more skilful.

They play together for longer and the improvements to the sport are plain to see. They are better athletes and better footballers and so many of the best of them play at the Roosters.

John Strange's side are the culmination of almost a decade of progress, the ultimate example of what's possible when a club with some serious muscle decides to really invest in a women's program.

As Brigginshaw proved what was possible for the women's game in terms of star power and sheer class, the Roosters prove what is possible when those attributes are taken to their very limit.

Now they are what Brigginshaw was — a star for the entire league to sail by, and they are filled with players who can trace their lineage to the retiring Bronco.

In a cruel irony, without Brigginshaw there might be no Tarryn Aiken, who was named the Karyn Murphy medallist with a brilliant display at halfback for the Roosters or Jocelyn Kelleher, Brigginshaw's opposite number, who tortured Brisbane with her kicking game.

Closer to home might be no Tamika Upton, who succeeded Brigginshaw as the world's best player but just could not get into the game for the Broncos until she set up a late try, or Jesse Southwell, who scored that try and is so clearly an evolution of an archetype that Brigginshaw pioneered — not an athlete, but a pure footballer.

She is one of the players who entered the NRLW having played league all their lives, unlike Brigginshaw who had to stop when she was 12 because there were no more teams to play on and that's just one change Brigginshaw has born witness too.

Origin matches are ratings gold and attracts crowds that dwarf what they were even five years ago, the NRLW has been born and expanded twice over and the product and support is edging towards the point where a standalone grand final doesn't just feel possible, it feels like a logical step for a game that continues to grow.

Brigginshaw helped raise that profile as a mainstay in Brisbane's early premierships and a Queensland regular. She was not just a star, she was the star.

She didn't just adapt to the new world, she brought it to heel as she became a legend and now retires as an icon — if they were to rename the women's Dally M after a modern player, the Ali B certainly has a fine ring to it.

NRL live The Sydney Roosters won their third NRLW premiership, thrashing the Brisbane Broncos by seven tries to one in a blowout of a grand final. Follow live.

When you are a player of that stature, to whom greatness has been a constant companion for years and who remained a threat right to the end — even at 36, Brisbane did not win a game this year without Brigginshaw — a grand final massacre is no way for a career to end.

She has given the game so much but the game could not give her the perfect ending.

But as she prepares for the rest of her life, Brigginshaw leaves the game as a figure that sits astride two eras, who helped bring her game to life and make it bigger than anyone in the old days could have dreamed.

There is still progress to be made and in retirement Brigginshaw will not stop pushing for it.

She believes in a brighter future and she knows one is possible, because she has already built one. We are living in it right now.

World.title: NRLW quick hits: Roosters complete 101-year first as Aiken stars
World.content:
The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos.

Twelve months on from a heartbreaking loss to the women from Brisbane, the Roosters not only won the premiership, but did something no other top-flight rugby league team has achieved in Australia for more than a century.

Here are the quick hits from Sydney's NRLW grand final win over Brisbane.

1. Origin wingers make uncharacteristic errors

It doesn't matter how much experience you have, every player feels some sort of pressure on grand final day.

And the pressure of a grand final was on display in the opening minutes, with a pair of State of Origin representatives making uncharacteristic errors.

Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal Ali Brigginshaw's decorated rugby league career ended with a heavy defeat but there can be no doubt about the impact the Broncos playmaker has had on the game.

Sydney Roosters winger Jayme Fressard had a proper shocker to begin the grand final, failing to gather the opening kick-off and nudging it into touch.

As the ball came to the NSW State of Origin rep, she tried to trap it with her foot but kicked the footy over the sideline.

The Roosters were able to defend their goal-line and then it was a Broncos Origin rep to have a shocker.

It was Fressard's opposing winger, Julia Robinson, who dropped the ball stone cold in her own half, which gifted the Roosters a golden chance to open the scoring.

Unlike the Broncos, the Roosters were able to score when winger Brydie Parker fielded a great cross-field kick from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and touched down in the corner.

2. Tarryn Aiken takes over in 7-minute blitz

The Roosters were dominating the grand final in the first half, as multiple errors from Brisbane kept them under immense pressure.

But Brisbane's goal-line defence was one aspect of their game that was withstanding the impressive Roosters.

That was until Sydney halfback Tarryn Aiken, who missed last year's decider due to an ACL injury, produced three moments of brilliance in a 7-minute stretch that led to a trio of tries for the Roosters.

First Aiken grubbered for herself and when the ball bounced off the arm of Brisbane winger Kerri Johnson, the Sydney halfback caught the ricochet and scored the game's second try.

Four minutes later, Aiken was setting up the third try of the match. The halfback lined up at lock in an attacking scrum 10 metres from Brisbane's goal-line. Aiken passed from the base of the scrum to the left, wrapped around and retook the footy, then gave a perfect short pass to captain Isabelle Kelly who charged over.

The Roosters then charged down the field again and when a sixth tackle play looked to be coming unstuck, it was Aiken again who produced a great kick which Brisbane's Deleni Paitai fumbled, and the Tricolours regathered and Fressard scored in the corner.

3. Brigginshaw on report in her farewell game

The trailblazing career of Ali Brigginshaw, someone who has been instrumental in the growth of women's rugby league, came to an end with an NRLW grand final.

But the legendary Broncos, Maroos and Jillaroo might have considered herself lucky not to have been sin-binned in her farewell game.

With the Roosters on top, Brigginshaw was desperate not to let Aiken put in an attacking cross-field kick.

Aiken did, which led to a try, but Brigginshaw's low dive resulted in her clattering into the planted leg of Aiken.

A hit under the knee led to Aiken landing hard on her back and could have easily resulted in Brigginshaw being sent for a 10-minute break on the sideline.

But referee Belinda Sharpe decided that putting Brigginshaw on report was the only action necessary, which really is academic considering this was her farewell outing.

4. Dally M medallist pulls off one of season's best tackles

Down 26-0 early in the second half, Brisbane's misery looked destined to continue when the Roosters were about to cross over for what would have been their seventh try of the grand final.

Jessica Sergis of the Roosters is tackled by Tamika Upton of the Broncos. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

A high bomb from the Roosters was allowed to bounce, the ball took a wicked turn and landed in the arms of Brydie Parker, and a brilliant flick pass on the inside looked set to end with Jessica Sergis scoring in the corner.

But Brisbane's captain and fullback Tamika Upton, the Dally M medalist this season, produced a try-saving tackle as good as any seen this season.

The Brisbane number one screamed across in cover and was able to twist her body in the tackle and make sure she was under the ball as Sergis fell to the line.

With Upton around her like a snake, Sergis was unable to get her arm free and ground the ball. It didn't change the outcome, but it was another example of why Upton is the best player in the competition.

5. Roosters complete first perfect season in 101 years

The Roosters came into Sunday's decider with plenty of confidence.

They had won 30 of their previous 31 NRLW matches. There only loss was last year's grand final, to the Broncos, denying them an undefeated season.

But the Tricolours regrouped in 2026, won every match on their way to the decider, then exacted revenge with a commanding win to complete the perfect season.

The Sydney Roosters became the first men's or women's side in top grade rugby league to go the entire season without suffering a loss since the 1959 ST George Dragons.

That Dragons team recorded 17 wins, and one draw, on their way to a fourth consecutive premiership, in a dominant era of 11 straight titles.

But the 2026 Roosters NRLW side had no draws, just 13 wins from 13 matches. The last team to win every match in a season was South Sydney, way back in 1925.

World.title: Kangaroos thrash Swans as Demons, Eagles claim crucial wins
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have lost star ruck Ally Morphett to a knee injury in their humiliating 55-point defeat to North Melbourne.

But while the 10.11 (71) to 2.4 (16) victory returned the Kangaroos to the top of the ladder, the reigning premiers have injury concerns of their own, as Emma Kearney sustained a hamstring injury.

In the first quarter at Arden Street Oval on Sunday, Morphett looked to make a tackle but collapsed in the lead-up.

She was left holding her right knee in agony, later emerging from the rooms wearing a brace and on crutches.

St Kilda kick solitary point St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The 22-year-old has played a starring role for the Swans this season, spearheading them into top-four contention.

Kearney, an eight-time All Australian, left the field in the fourth quarter, just two months after missing the Australia-Ireland clash with a hamstring injury.

The loss of the 37-year-old defender would be massive, considering she adds a plethora of experience to the Kangaroos, who are in a tight race for the minor premiership.

"Disappointing way to finish the game. I've been pretty lucky throughout my career not to have too many injuries," Kearney told the Seven Network.

"Probably my age has something to do with it. Hopefully it's not too bad, but we'll get it scanned."

The Kangaroos' Tess Craven (17 disposals, two goals), Tahlia Randall (three goals) and Jasmine Garner (31 disposals, 10 clearances) dazzled, as the Swans were held goalless until midway through the third term.

By that point, the home team had already booted four goals and kicked another six afterwards to demote the Swans to seventh position.

Mia Austin (right) kicked three goals in the Demons' triumph. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

At Victoria Park, Melbourne secured a 6.6 (42) to 2.9 (21) win over a wasteful Collingwood, despite the absence of injured captain Kate Hore.

Fresh off a 31-point defeat to the Kangaroos last round, the Demons rebounded with forward Mia Austin slotted three first-half majors to help the visitors lead 29-10 at the main break.

From this point of the match, midfielders Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, 12 tackle and one goal) and Olivia Purcell (32 disposals) sparkled.

The win moves the Demons into second position, while the Magpies will hope defender Sarah Rowe quickly recovers from a leg injury sustained in the second half.

Meanwhile, the West Coast Eagles thrust themselves firmly into finals contention by beating Fremantle 5.9 (39) to 4.3 (27) in Perth.

Midfielder Ella Roberts (22 disposals, one goal) produced a masterclass to help the Eagles claim their first regular-season win over their cross-town rivals and move level on points with the eighth-placed Dockers.

The Eagles' fourth straight win comes after they lost their first four matches.

AAP

World.title: Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have held off a fast-finishing Newcastle to win 19-18 in a pulsating NRL grand final at Stadium Australia.

The Roosters seemed to have the premiership wrapped up late in the match, until Greg Marzhew scored a 76th-minute try down the Knights' left edge.

Sandon Smith converted from wide out, sending Knights' fans into a frenzy.

But the Roosters held on in the dying stages, with captain James Tedesco pulling off two kick receptions in a Clive Churchill Medal-winning performance to deny the Knights their first men's premiership in 25 years.

The win completed a premiership double for the Roosters, with the club earlier winning their third NRLW title following a 30-6 thrashing of the Brisbane Broncos.

Daly Cherry-Evans was sent out a winner in his final NRL appearance, giving the 37-year-old a second premiership ring to go with the one he claimed with Manly in 2011.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson also added another premiership to his tally, the fourth of his decorated career at the Tricolours.

It was clear from the opening whistle Newcastle was going to enjoy the larger share of the crowd's support, with most neutral fans among the 80,814 spectators jumping on board the Knights' bandwagon.

They had reason to cheer when the Knights scored first in the 15th minute after Francis Manuleleua ran a brilliant angle off a Fletcher Sharpe short ball to cross for the opening try.

The crowd was firmly in Newcastle's corner. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Smith landed the conversion to establish a 6-0 lead, before the Knights were given a life when the Roosters had a try disallowed 10 minutes later.

Mark Nawaqanitawase leapt high in the air to mark a Sam Walker kick in the right-hand corner, but the bunker ruled he knocked on as he attempted to ground the ball in the in-goal area.

The Knights built on their advantage in the 29th minute via the standout play of the first half, when captain Kalyn Ponga ran 95 metres to score his side's second converted try.

Nawaqanitawase had tapped back the ball in an aerial contest near the Knights' line, but it was pounced upon by Ponga, who proceeded to outsprint the Roosters' cover defence.

The Roosters showed no sign of panic, though, and Nawaqanitawase got them on the scoreboard with a trademark opportunist try five minutes shy of half-time.

The Roosters did not panic as their dominance eventually took its toll on Newcastle. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Walker's conversion reduced the Knights' lead to 12-6, which they held through to the break.

The Knights' defence was under pressure early in the second half, as the Roosters launched a series of attacking raids.

The dam wall eventually burst in the 47th minute, with Billy Smith touching down despite the Knights' best efforts to hold the Roosters centre up over the goal line.

Walker added the extras to level scores, and he gave the Roosters the lead for the first time in the match following a 54th-minute penalty goal.

Nawaqanitawase's second try, scored midway through the second half, pushed the lead out to 18-12, before Cherry-Evans nailed a field goal with 11 minutes left in the contest.

It appeared the seven-point margin would see the Roosters through to full-time, prior to Marzhew's heroics setting up the grandstand finish.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Up There Cazaly singer vowed to make AFL grand final after horrific fall
World.content:
He is a name synonymous with the AFL grand final.

While teams change, pre-game acts change and even the rules themselves change, Mike Brady's performance of unofficial AFL anthem Up There Cazaly has been a fixture of the big day for decades.

Last weekend's grand final was no different — but that was not always a given.

In January, the 78-year-old suffered a horrific fall during a routine evening walk near his Great Ocean Road home.

Mike Brady performed on ABC's Countdown program in 1979 to promote his Up There Cazaly single. (ABC News)

"I fell and landed on my ample backside," he said, laughing.

But the injury was no laughing matter.

Brady described the horror of having to twist his ankle back into place before dragging himself to a nearby fire station, "leaving a trail of blood and mud".

Brady would later learn he had fractured his leg, ankle and foot in 12 places.

With his doctor telling him not to push himself and that it was unlikely he would be able to walk anytime soon, his grand final call-up nine months later was all but certainly out of the picture.

Mike Brady performed before the 2013 AFL grand final between the Hawthorn Hawks and the Fremantle Dockers. (AAP: David Crosling)

When the AFL asked if he would still be up to performing, he vowed to be there even if he had to crawl on stage.

"I said, 'Try and stop me,'" he said.

"Because I love it. It's a part of me."

'The place was closing in on me'

A self-described "outdoors person" who relishes being active, Brady is the first to admit that even he doubted he would make it during parts of the nine-month journey that followed.

"I wasn't doing well," he said.

"I was waking up and felt like the place was closing in on me.

" I was put in a palliative care place, and that was tough because I felt like I shouldn't be there. "

Mike Brady performed during the 2022 AFL grand final match between Geelong and Sydney. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

After five months in hospital, he was able to return home with the help of a wheelchair.

He slowly transitioned to crutches, and now mostly gets around using a walking stick.

But Brady defied all expectations and ditched the walking stick to walk out on stage on September 26.

The 100,000-strong crowd gave him the strength not just to walk, he said, but to fly.

"At the beginning of the song, I'm singing it kind of normally, but then I thought, 'I've got this, I'm going to be able to sing it!'

Mike Brady was interviewed about his famed football anthem in 2002. (ABC News)

"I sang harder than I've ever sung before.

"One hundred thousand people reacted, and the roar — I've never heard anything like it.

"It was fantastic. I felt absolutely vindicated for pushing myself so hard."

Musician vows to perform for years to come

Brady says he is not one to dwell on the past and spent much of his recovery writing new poetry and music.

But many hours alone with his thoughts left him to reminisce on a career he never expected.

As an English immigrant, Brady moved to Melbourne at the age of 11.

Mike Brady performed at the 1979 VFL grand final. (Supplied)

The musician and jingle-maker had never even been to a full AFL game when he was asked to create a tune to market the Victorian Football League.

"What an honour," he said.

He went on to pen what would become a footy phenomenon.

Recalling the day he first performed Up There Cazaly at the 1979 VFL grand final, introduced by his friend John Farnham, Brady said it was the first time he felt truly at home in the country he had lived in for nearly two decades.

"I really felt like I belonged in Australia," he said.

"I'd never felt that before. But hearing men and women in the crowd shouting, 'Good on ya, Mike', I really felt the warmth."

Even 48 years later, the feeling remains every time the words "up there Cazaly" leave his mouth.

"I often say the smile on my face when I sing it is actually me chuckling at the irony," he said.

"I love the irony of being a Pommy immigrant that was taken to heart by so many Australian people, and if that's not a great honour, I don't know what is."

Mike Brady says the 1979 VFL grand final, which featured Carlton legend Alex Jesaulenko (pictured), was a key moment in his Up Their Cazaly journey. (Getty Images)

While the honour of performing the track has been handed to other performers over the years, he wants to perform for the next two years, taking it to the song's 50-year anniversary and his own 80th birthday.

"I just hope the crowd is as kind to me as they have been for all those 48 years," he said.

In fact, Brady was more determined than ever to take to the stage this year, fearing the AFL might not ask him back if he did not.

If the crowd's reaction was anything to go by, it was an unlikely fear.

World.title: Aussie duo and new world number one fall at China Open
World.content:
Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties.

World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night.

Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes.

Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end.

For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits.

The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired.

Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes.

The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia.

Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina.

The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2.

Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round.

It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month.

Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one.

Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL and NRLW grand final day has arrived. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW seasons is here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held today.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.

The Sydney Roosters are undefeated in 2026, winning all 11 matches in the home-and-away season, then defeating the Canberra Raiders in last week's preliminary final.

What pre-match entertainment is taking place at the NRL grand final?

After talks between the NRL and Australian artist Tones And I, the grand final appeared set to take place without any pre-match entertainment.

However, on Friday it was revealed that an all-star ensemble of Australian musicians, led by Amy Shark, will lead a tribute to recently retired player Jai Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year.

Shark will be joined by members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

Electronic duo Peking Duk revealed on Instagram on Sunday morning that despite rumours to the contrary, they would not be part of the performance.

Shark previously performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and is set to perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

World.title: Verstappen claims pole at Grand Prix in Malaysia
World.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed his first pole position of the season at the Formula One Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Saturday, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton joining him on the front row.

It is the first time two great rivals have shared the front row of the grid since the Hungarian Grand Prix in 2023.

Verstappen's teammate, Isack Hadjar, was third fastest but will start eighth due to a grid penalty, with championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third alongside Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Oscar Piastri was pipped to sixth by his teammate Lando Norris, but will move up a position as a result of Hadjar's penalty to start sixth as McLaren locked out the third row of the grid.

George Russell, who so spectacularly won the last Grand Prix in Azerbaijan last week, will start seventh in what was an alarming performance for Mercedes, who came to Malaysia with a big upgrade package.

"It's very difficult to understand," Mercedes boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports.

"We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year.

"But then you can say it's very hot, with the tarmac very different to all the tracks.

"[We] looked really good in the morning; we seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then in qualifying, it was a little bit back to what we saw before — just no performance."

Verstappen was the last driver to win a Grand Prix in Malaysia in 2017, in what was his second career victory, before the race was taken off the calendar after the government said it could not justify the costs.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the front row of the grid together for the first time in three years. (Getty Images: Formula 1/Mark Sutton)

Nine years and four championships later, the Dutchman showed he was still the man to beat in Sepang with a time of 1 minute 35.130 seconds.

"It's fantastic, we've been trying for many Grands Prix to get more, sometimes a bit closer to the others. But to finally get it from where we started the season [it's] pretty incredible," said Verstappen as he eyes his first win of the season.

Hamilton, who also has one victory in Sepang, struggled with tyre degradation in practice sessions but the veteran Briton snatched second from Hadjar in the dying stages of the final qualifying session.

"It's so hot here, I keep saying it. But that's made it a massive challenge for the tyres, for the car, for the mechanics in the garage," Hamilton said.

"We made so many changes through all these practice sessions because the cars are sliding, these tyres are overheating. It was really, really hard to find a good balance. We made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot."

Hadjar had exceeded his seasonal allowance for engines, which resulted in a five-place grid penalty.

"It's a bit unfortunate we take the penalty on a track that fast," Hadjar said.

"But you know, from P8, I'm confident we can go through the field and come back for a good result."

Reuters/ABC

Tech.title: The AirPods Pro 3 are a fantastic deal at $179
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been a while since we’ve seen a good discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3, but like the latest iPad Mini and the M5 MacBook Airs, a great one is happening now for October Prime Day. You can snag a pair of the noise-canceling earbuds that include five ear tip sizes, live translation, and fantastic sound for $179 at Amazon (originally $249). I expect other retailers to offer a similar price in the coming days.

This is the first time the price has gone below $190 since Prime Day in June. Since then, Apple launched the AirPods 5, and the most feature-complete version with a wireless charging case costs $149.99. Those are great if you prefer earbuds that don’t form a seal in your ears, but for everyone else, the AirPods Pro 3 are a much better value at just $30 more right now.

Tech.title: The MacBook Air M5 is $200 off for the first time in months
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon’s October Prime Day has effectively chopped off Apple’s June price increases. Usually $1,299, the 13-inch MacBook Air with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is on sale for $1,099 at Amazon. That’s a more palatable price for a machine that’s significantly faster than Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo.

The 15-inch version, also with 512GB of storage, is $1,299 at Amazon (was $1,499). In addition to the larger screen, it has two additional speakers, for a total of six, and two additional GPU cores for better overall graphical performance.

The latest update to Apple’s midrange laptop includes a noticeable improvement to the speed of both the processor and storage. Even without flashy new features compared to the last-gen model, it’s still one of our favorite laptops, thanks to its long battery life, bright screen, and excellent speakers.
